member.name: T:g3.PrimitiveFit3
member.summary: Robust fit of a plane, sphere, cylinder or cone to points (eg scan points or mesh vertices), with optional normals. Two stages: 1. RANSAC (Fischler and Bolles, "Random sample consensus", CACM 1981) over minimal samples, with the minimal sets of Schnabel, Wahl and Klein, "Efficient RANSAC for point-cloud shape detection" (Computer Graphics Forum 2007): plane from 3 points, sphere from 2 points with normals (4 points without normals), cylinder from 2 points with normals, cone from 3 points with normals. (Their localized sampling is not used: it finds some small part quickly, which suits detecting many shapes, but stops before the largest one.) Candidates are scored with the truncated quadratic loss of MSAC (Torr and Zisserman, "MLESAC", CVIU 2000); a point counts as inlier when it is within InlierDistance and, if normals are known, its normal is within MaxNormalAngle of the surface normal (unoriented). The number of samples adapts to the inlier ratio (Confidence). Every new best candidate is refined by least squares on its inliers and scored again (LO-RANSAC, Chum, Matas and Kittler, "Locally optimized RANSAC", DAGM 2003; LocalOptimization). 2. Least squares on the inliers: orthogonal regression (PCA) for the plane, Levenberg-Marquardt on the geometric (orthogonal) distances for the other primitives, then the inliers are selected again; repeated until the inlier set no longer changes (at most RefineIterations). Without RANSAC (UseRansac = false) all points are fitted by least squares, starting from closed form estimates: the algebraic sphere fit (Kasa 1976), and for cylinder and cone the axis and apex from the normals (every cylinder normal is orthogonal to the axis; every tangent plane of a cone passes through the apex, and the directions from the apex make the same angle with the axis). Cylinder and cone need normals; if none are given they are estimated by PCA of the NormalNeighbors nearest points (Hoppe et al., "Surface reconstruction from unorganized points", SIGGRAPH 1992), iteratively reweighted (Cauchy weights of the plane distances) so that outliers among the neighbors do not tilt them; where the weighted neighborhood is not flat the normal is unknown, and such points are judged by their distance only. Deterministic for a given Seed.

member.summary: RANSAC stops when a better model is found with at most this probability

member.name: F:g3.PrimitiveFit3.MaxRadius
member.summary: largest sphere / cylinder radius, and the distance of a cone apex from the points; 0 = 10 times the bounding box diagonal. Larger shapes would only imitate a plane (a sphere of radius R deviates from a plane by D^2/(8R) over an extent D). Behaviour change against the first version (limit 100 times the diagonal, cone angle below 89.94 degrees): a genuinely flat cap, eg a lens surface with R above 10 times its extent, needs a larger MaxRadius (Result is RejectedByLimits if nothing else fits).

member.name: F:g3.PrimitiveFit3.LocalOptimization
member.summary: LO-RANSAC: refine every new best candidate by least squares on (at most 2000 of) its inliers. On the 400 Thingi10K meshes of benchmarks/MeshRepairBenchmark, at about the same median time (-13 % to +7 % per primitive): somewhat better models (better / worse by more than 1 % of the points on 32/15 meshes for spheres, 46/42 cylinders, 52/44 cones), but a rotated input reaches another quality slightly more often (27/29/23 instead of 21/16/16 meshes). false = plain RANSAC with the same bail-out pre-test.

member.name: T:g3.Arrangement2d
member.summary:
Arrangement2d constructs a planar arrangement of a set of 2D line segments. When a segment is inserted, existing edges are split, and the inserted segment becomes multiple graph edges. So, the resulting DGraph2 should not have any edges that intersect.
Calculations are performed in double-precision, so there is no guarantee of correctness.

member.name: T:g3.ConstrainedDelaunayMesh2
member.summary: Constrained Delaunay triangulation of points, segments, rings, holes and regions, with exact predicates; the output coordinates are doubles and the mesh is valid on them (decision D1).

remarks.para: Crossing, touching and overlapping constraints are split at their intersections (noding, spec O10). A crossing is computed exactly and rounded to the nearest double; the pieces then run through it, at most a few units in the last place off their input segment. A vertex within the automatic tolerance (2^-41 of the larger of the largest coordinate and the extent, about 2.6 um at UTM northings; spec O11, Q14) of a segment becomes a vertex of it, so every piece stays within that tolerance of each of its input segments. Input points within that tolerance of each other become one vertex (the first of them; maps the others to it), so no ulp-wide triangle is made between them. With off, a crossing gives .

The domain: a point belongs to it iff the innermost ring containing it (each ring by the even-odd rule) is an outer ring, or, without outer rings, iff it is in the convex hull and in no hole (decision D5, owner 2026-11-01). So an island in a lake is meshed, a lake in it removed again, a hole in a hole stays removed; a hole removes the free segments inside it, not the rings whose role is outer (Q7). Rings that overlap without nesting: the latest decides, with a diagnostic. Hole seeds remove the bounded cell of the constraints around them (D6). Regions by ring or seed label the triangles, the last one wins (I6, D16).
Vertex ids: input point i is vertex i; crossings get ids from the input count on (Q8). Deterministic; independent instances may run concurrently.

member.name: F:g3.ConstrainedDelaunayMesh2.ResolveCrossings
member.summary: Split crossing and overlapping constraints (default). Off: a crossing is a failure, never an invalid mesh.

member.name: F:g3.ConstrainedDelaunayMesh2.AutoToleranceFactor
member.summary: The automatic tolerance as a fraction of the larger of the largest coordinate and the extent.

member.name: F:g3.ConstrainedDelaunayMesh2.SnapTolerance
member.summary: Snap tolerance in coordinate units (spec O11); 0 (default): only the automatic tolerance. With a tolerance the input is snap rounded first (decision D14): every input point moves to the centre of its pixel on a grid of this width anchored at the origin (so input on that grid stays put), constraints are routed through the hot pixels, and every vertex ends at least half a pixel from every constraint edge not incident to it. With quality refinement every vertex it adds is on the grid as well. A point on the grid and a segment closer than half the tolerance (per axis) merge, features more than twice the tolerance apart never do, and in between the grid decides; two points off the grid merge if they fall into one pixel, so close points on either side of a pixel boundary stay apart. Collapsed rings and segments and dropped seeds are reported in the diagnostics. At least 2^-40 of the largest coordinate.

member.name: M:g3.ConstrainedDelaunayMesh2.Builder.Shortens(System.Int32,System.Int32,System.Int32)
member.summary: splitting piece u-w at v (a vertex within the tolerance of it, not on it) leaves two pieces each strictly shorter than u-w: the condition for a tolerance split to make progress. Without it, two vertices within the tolerance of each other's piece, where refinement has made pieces about as short as the tolerance, split the piece at each other in turn for ever (the order along a piece is not reliable in doubles at that scale; found with ext/cdt/island at 32 and 34 degrees, constrained mode: NodingLimit "a segment split did not settle"). Squared lengths in scaled units: deterministic, so the length of the piece being inserted strictly decreases along every chain of such splits. All three tolerance splits (the existing edge, the start triangle, the walk) use it; the exact splits (a vertex on u-w) shorten anyway.

member.name: M:g3.ConstrainedDelaunayMesh2.Builder.RatioToDouble(System.Numerics.BigInteger,System.Numerics.BigInteger,System.Int32)
member.summary: num / den * 2^scale (den > 0) rounded to nearest, ties to even, in integer arithmetic only: no conversion of a large BigInteger to double, whose rounding may differ between runtimes. Below the normal range a second rounding to the subnormal grid follows: the result is then within one unit in the last place, not always the nearest.

member.name: M:g3.ConstrainedDelaunayMesh2.Builder.RingParity(System.Int32[]@,System.Collections.Generic.List{System.Int32[]}@,System.Boolean[]@)
member.summary: Domain membership from scratch, by ring parity (D5): per triangle slot the interned set of rings it lies inside of (each ring by the even-odd rule), and per set whether it is in the domain: the innermost ring of the set decides by its role (owner decision of 2026-11-01: islands in lakes are meshed, a hole in a hole stays removed). Ring r is inside ring q when every triangle inside r is inside q, read off the sets of the real triangles; the innermost ring of a set is inside all the others. Rings that overlap without nesting have none: the latest ring of the set decides, reported in overlaps.

member.summary:
Incremental 3D Delaunay triangulation of points inside a box (Bowyer-Watson insertion with exact predicates, ExactPredicates.Orient3d / InSphere). The eight box corners are vertices 0 to 7 and the box is the convex hull, so there are no infinite cells: a facet on the box has neighbour -1. Points are inserted strictly inside the box.
Cells are positively oriented (Orient3d(v0, v1, v2, v3) > 0). Facet i of a cell is the one opposite its vertex i; FacetVertices(c, i) lists it oriented outwards (counter-clockwise seen from outside the cell). Cell ids are reused after cells are removed; CellStamp(c) changes whenever id c gets a new cell.
With cospherical points (eg the box corners) the triangulation is one of the Delaunay triangulations. The conflict region of a new point is grown, where needed, until it is star-shaped from the point, so every cell has positive volume (exactly) and the adjacency stays valid also for degenerate input.
Sources (docs/SOURCES.md): A. Bowyer 1981, D. F. Watson 1981 (insertion by cavities); O. Devillers, S. Pion, M. Teillaud, "Walking in a triangulation", 2002 (point location by a stochastic walk).

member.name: T:g3.DelaunayKernel2
member.summary: The constrained phase of the kernel: points inserted one at a time by splitting and Lawson flips that never cross a constrained edge (Lawson 1977; the constrained Delaunay property of Lee and Lin 1986, Chew 1989), segments recovered by a walk and flips (Sloan 1993). Ghost triangles take part like any other (Cheng, Dey, Shewchuk 2012), so a point outside the hull extends it.

The incremental Delaunay kernel of the 2D mesher: Bowyer-Watson insertion (Bowyer 1981, Watson 1981) into a triangulation closed by ghost triangles with one vertex at infinity (Cheng, Dey, Shewchuk, "Delaunay Mesh Generation", 2012, chapter 3), points ordered by biased randomized insertion rounds (Amenta, Choi, Rote 2003) along a Hilbert curve, located by a visibility walk (Devillers, Pion, Teillaud 2002) from the last insertion. All decisions use the exact predicates; no coordinate is invented (no supertriangle).
member.remarks: Storage: triangle t has vertices V[3t..3t+2], counter-clockwise for a real triangle. Half-edge 3t+k runs from V[3t+k] to V[3t+(k+1)%3]; H[e] is its twin. Ghost triangles carry the vertex ; a ghost (a, b, inf) lies on the outer side of the hull edge from a to b (the interior is to its right). The number of triangles, ghosts included, is 2 (vertices) - 2 at all times, so a cavity of k triangles is replaced by k + 2; only a vertex deletion (DelaunayKernel2.Deletion.cs) frees slots, two, by moving the last slots into them.
member.summary: Vertex deletion in the constrained phase. Removing a vertex p leaves the star-shaped polygon of its link; the triangles outside it keep their empty circumcircles (they were empty with p, so they are without it), so only the polygon is triangulated anew (Devillers 1999, "On deletion in Delaunay triangulations"). Here by ear clipping with exact orientations, then Lawson's flips inside it until every new edge is locally Delaunay: the flip algorithm turns any constrained triangulation into the constrained Delaunay one (Lawson 1977; for constraints Lee and Lin 1986, Chew 1989), and the polygon's edges stay locally Delaunay throughout, so the flips never leave it. The ear search is O(k^3) in the worst case; the degree of a vertex is small in practice, and Devillers' O(k log k) priority queue would not pay for its code.

member.name: M:g3.DelaunayKernel2.DeleteVertex(System.Int32,System.Int32)
member.summary:
Deletes vertex p and restores the constrained Delaunay property. Only a made vertex can be deleted: one made by the constrained phase, or an input vertex whose input index (its representative, the smallest with its coordinates) is at least (on the snap grid, a hot pixel centre that snap rounding appended to the input). It must lie inside the hull (no ghost triangle at it), have no constrained edge and one tag on all its triangles; otherwise nothing changes and the result is false.
Triangle slots are renumbered: the star's k triangles become k - 2, and the last two slots move into the two freed ones. A caller that holds triangle ids must not call this; , if set, receives every slot written.

member.name: T:g3.DelaunayMesh2
member.summary: Delaunay triangulation of a 2D point set over its convex hull, with exact predicates and without Steiner points.

remarks.para: Vertex ids are input indices. Exact duplicates are mapped to their first input index and are in no triangle; signed zeros count as equal. Fewer than three distinct points, or all collinear, give an empty mesh.

Cocircular points (ties of the Delaunay property) are resolved by a rule that depends only on the points and their indices: each Delaunay cell with more than three vertices is triangulated as a fan from its vertex with the smallest index. The result is therefore the same for any insertion order, and bit-identical across runs, threads and power-of-two scalings of the input.
The finished mesh is verified in linear time (orientation, adjacency, local Delaunay property, convex hull); a defect, which is not expected, gives instead of an invalid mesh.
Independent instances, and one instance on different threads, may compute concurrently. Expected time O(n log n).

This class extracts the set of loops bounding the "cells" of a DGraph2, ie each cell is a connected region with a polygonal boundary. Precondition: the graph has no self-intersections. Precondition: at any vertex, the edges are sortable by angle (ie no outgoing edges overlap) ** numerically this may not be 100% reliable....
Both "sides" of each edge are included in some cell boundary, ie so for a simple polygon, there are two cells, one infinitely large. The "inside" cells will be oriented clockwise, if converted to a Polygon2d.

member.name: T:g3.QualityMesh2
member.summary: Quality mesh of a domain: the constrained Delaunay triangulation of , refined by Delaunay refinement until every triangle meets the minimum angle, the maximum area and the size function, or the Steiner limit is reached. Conforming: every output triangle has an empty circumcircle, also across segments, except across locked segments, which are never split (spec O2, O9).

remarks.para: Ruppert's algorithm (1995) with Shewchuk's refinements (2002): encroached subsegments are split first, a bad triangle gets a vertex at its circumcentre unless that would encroach a subsegment, which is then split instead; a subsegment at an input vertex is split at a power of two from it (concentric shells), so that small input angles do not make refinement run away. Triangles whose small angle lies between two constrained edges are not refined for their angle. Split points are computed on the original input segment, so they stay within rounding of it however often a piece is split (spec O12).

Without (the default), a subsegment counts as encroached only by a vertex in its diametral lens (Shewchuk 2002, section 6.4: the points that see it under at least 120 degrees, a narrower region than the diametral circle) when the angle bound is at most arcsin(sqrt 3 / 4) = 25.65 degrees, the bound the paper proves for lenses; above it the diametral circle is used. As the paper's rule says (after Chew 1993), before a subsegment is bisected the free vertices (made by refinement, on no constraint) in its open diametral circle that see its midpoint are deleted. The paper's termination proof is for circumcentres and midpoint bisection; this mesher also inserts off-centres, splits at concentric shells next to input vertices and, on the snap grid, rounds every point to a pixel centre, so termination here is measured (catalogue, corpus, Herne tiles), not proven, and the Steiner limit bounds every run. With Conforming the circle is always used (O2).

Terminates: angles up to about 33 degrees converge on ordinary input; any input stops at the Steiner limit (default 10 x (points + segments) + 100 000, spec Q13). Pieces that are too short to split in doubles stay as they are.

Locked segments (spec O9) keep their vertices and the mesh stays valid, but the bounds are not guaranteed near them yet: a triangle whose circumcentre lies behind a locked segment is left as it is, so its neighbourhood may keep triangles below the angle or above the area (listed in when below the angle). Meeting the bounds there is the open work item m3.locks.

member.name: T:g3.QualityMesh2.Refiner.TriangleQueue
member.summary: The queue of triangles to look at. Worst first: a binary heap keyed by the triangle's sin^2 of its smallest angle when queued (, scale-free), ties in the order queued, so the order is deterministic; only triangles below the angle bound, the others follow in the order queued. Splitting the worst triangle first lets its new vertex remove the slightly bad triangles around it before they are split for themselves, which gives fewer triangles (measured: MESHING2D_GRADING.md; the ordering is a known heuristic, see MESHING2D_PROVENANCE.md). An entry may be stale (its slot refilled or freed); the main loop judges the triangle as it is when taken out.

member.name: M:g3.QualityMesh2.Refiner.CarveOutside
member.summary: Removes what lies outside the domain before refinement (spec Q7: a hole removes everything inside its ring; O2: the output's triangles are judged against the output's vertices, owner 2026-11-03). A constraint with the outside on both sides is lifted if it is a piece of free segments (rings stay), and the triangulation made constrained Delaunay again across it; then every made vertex (a crossing, a hot pixel centre that snap rounding added) whose triangles all lie outside is deleted. member.name: M:g3.QualityMesh2.Refiner.ApexExempt(System.Int32,System.Int32)
member.summary: The small-angle rule (MESHING2D_SMALL_ANGLES.md, owner decision 2026-11-06; in the conforming mode with the Delaunay check of Encroached, MESHING2D_SMALL_ANGLES_CONFORMING.md, owner decision 2026-11-08): subsegment e is not split for vertex v when all of these hold. - v is a vertex refinement made on exactly one source c: not an input vertex, not a crossing, no third source (Shewchuk 2002 section 6.2 applies its cure only then: not for a parent that "is an input vertex or lies on a nonincident segment"). - c and a source a of e make an input angle below the bound, their closed input segments meeting exactly (PairOf). - (i) an end u of e is a vertex on c too (e starts at the apex, or at the crossing of a and c), and v lies on e's side of u; or (ii) v and an end of e lie at distances from the apex within a factor of 1.5, on the same side (NearSmallAngle). Splitting e for such a v is the partner's follow-up in section 6.2's figure-eight cycle (a circumcentre halves a subsegment at the apex, the partner follows by encroachment, and the next free edge is shorter; found with ext/cdt/island: 38 octaves of splits towards a 2.6 degree apex of a hull edge and a segment). Only this vertex encroachment is exempt: a circumcentre or off-centre that is behind e or would encroach it still splits it, and the rule excuses no triangle.

member.name: M:g3.QualityMesh2.Refiner.GridSplitPoint(System.Int32,g3.Vector2d,g3.Vector2d,System.Collections.Generic.List{System.Int32},System.Double,g3.Vector2d@)
member.summary: The split point of constrained edge u-w on the grid (MESHING2D_SNAP.md section 3g): the point at the given fraction between u and w is taken on the input segment the edge comes from (O12), and its pixel's centre is used if it is valid; else the neighbouring pixels of the input segment's envelope between u and w, nearest first. Valid: no constraint crosses its pixel, and the new edges u-q, q-w cross no vertex's pixel and no other constraint. A vertex already at q is fine: the chain is then routed through it, as snap rounding routes a segment through every hot pixel of its envelope (a Steiner point there would otherwise block the split and leave the subsegment encroached; found by the fuzz test).

member.name: M:g3.QualityMesh2.Refiner.OffCentre(g3.Vector2d,g3.Vector2d,g3.Vector2d,System.Double,g3.Vector2d@)
member.summary: The off-centre of triangle abc (Ungor 2004): on the perpendicular bisector of the shortest edge pq, on the side of the circumcentre, where the triangle of pq and the point has the angle bound theta at the point: |pq| cot(theta / 2) / 2 from the midpoint of pq. False if the circumcentre is not farther than that (it is then the point to insert) or nothing can be computed in doubles. Computed in the triangle's frame scaled by a power of two (): an input scaled by 2^k gives the point scaled by 2^k, bit for bit

member.name: F:g3.QualityMesh2.Refiner.BisectorCandidates

member.name: M:g3.QualityMesh2.Refiner.BestCandidate(System.Int32,g3.Vector2d,System.Boolean,g3.Vector2d,g3.Vector2d@)
member.summary:
The split point of a triangle t bad by its angle, chosen among candidates: the default point (the off-centre if there is one, else the circumcentre) and the candidates in the petal of t's shortest edge pq (; grading step 2). With off, step 1's candidates on the perpendicular bisector of pq instead: the circumcentre and six points evenly from the nearer of the off-centre and the circumcentre to 1.3 times the circumcentre's distance from the midpoint of pq (from the circumcentre with off-centres switched off). On the grid the default point is the pixel centre refinement inserts without the choice, the others are rounded to their pixel centres. A candidate counts only where it would be inserted as it is: reached from t without crossing a constraint, encroaching on no subsegment, with t in its cavity, and on the grid with no constraint across its pixel. Of those the one wins that removes the most triangles bad by their angle (in its cavity) less those it makes (in the fan of new triangles), ties to the larger insertion radius (the distance to the nearest vertex of the fan), then to the earlier candidate. The fan's count takes the angle bound only (a new triangle at a small input angle counts as bad although refinement would leave it): it skews the score, not the mesh. When the default point wins, nothing is chosen.
The floor: a candidate's insertion radius must be at least the default point's, so every point inserted is at least as far from the mesh as the point refinement would insert without the choice, and the insertion radius argument of termination (Ruppert 1995; Shewchuk 2002; Ungor 2004 for off-centres) holds as for the default point. When the default point itself does not count (it is blocked, encroaches or lies in a constraint's pixel), nothing is chosen: refinement goes on as without the choice (it splits the subsegment, or falls back to the circumcentre). Choosing among several points is the idea of Erten and Ungor 2007 (locally optimal Steiner points, SGP 2007), with step 1's score instead of their farthest point (MESHING2D_GRADING.md 4.3.1).

member.name: F:g3.QualityMesh2.Refiner.PetalArcPoints
member.summary: the arc points of the petal on each side of its far end ()

member.name: F:g3.QualityMesh2.Refiner.PetalSearch
member.summary: at most this many triangles near t are searched for circumcentres in the petal

member.name: M:g3.QualityMesh2.Refiner.PetalCandidates(System.Int32,g3.Vector2d,System.Int32,g3.Vector2d,g3.Vector2d,System.Double,System.Collections.Generic.List{g3.Vector2d})
member.summary: The candidates of the choice besides the default point (), in the petal of t's shortest edge pq (Erten and Ungor 2007): the disk through p and q from which pq is seen under the angle bound theta or more, on t's side of pq. It lies in t's circumdisk, and its far end on the bisector is the off-centre. Their point is the petal's point farthest from every vertex, at a Voronoi vertex inside the petal or on its boundary; here the candidates are where it can lie, and step 1's score decides among them (measured better than the farthest point: MESHING2D_GRADING.md 4.3.1): - the circumcentres (Voronoi vertices) of the triangles reached from t across unconstrained edges whose circumdisks meet the petal, at most of them, that lie inside it; - seven points of its boundary arc: the far end and three on each side, by the half-angle parameter s = tan(psi / 2) of the angle psi from the bisector at the petal's centre, s = cot(theta / 2) (i / 4) |i / 4| for i = -3 ... 3, spaced quadratically: 0 at the far end, and cot(theta / 2) = would be p and q. Rational in s: no trigonometric function (whose last bit may differ by runtime); the quadratic spacing puts more points near the far end (measured better than linear). In t's frame of (an input scaled by 2^k gives the candidates scaled by 2^k, bit for bit), returned in the mesh's coordinates

member.name: F:g3.QualityMesh2.Refiner.MinRoundedSplitExponent
member.summary: The exponent below which a piece's split point must lie exactly on its source: the piece's larger coordinate difference () is below 2^-1026. The computed point A + dir * tt is off the line by its last two roundings, each at most half a unit in the last place of the result: relative to the coordinates in the normal range, but at least half the subnormal step 2^-1074 below it, whatever the coordinates. From 2^-1026 on that absolute part is at most 2^-49 of the piece, so the error is as small against the piece as a relative rounding; below, at 2^-1054 say, it is 2^-21 of it and the point lies visibly off the segment. (A piece below 2^-1026 between normal coordinates near 2^-1000, whose rounding is relative to the coordinates, is refused too: conservative, the mesh stays valid, only its refinement there is weaker.)

member.name: M:g3.QualityMesh2.Refiner.DeleteFreeInCircle(System.Int32,g3.Vector2d,g3.Vector2d,g3.Vector2d)
member.summary: Chew's deletion with lenses (Chew 1993; Shewchuk 2002, section 6.4, "Terminator Chew": "all free vertices that are inside the diametral circle of s and visible from the midpoint of s are deleted before s is bisected"): deletes every vertex made by refinement (not one of the input, its crossings or snap rounding's hot pixels: those come before firstSteiner) that lies in the open diametral circle of the subsegment e = pu pw, sees its midpoint (no other constrained edge meets the segment between them, closed: a touch blocks too), and is not on a constraint (DeleteVertex refuses those, so a vertex a chain is routed through stays). The split point p itself, if a vertex is there already (a reroute on the grid), stays. Called once the split point is found and the Steiner limit allows the split: a split refused before that deletes nothing. The midpoint is (pu + pw) / 2 rounded in doubles. The circle is local: the triangles are searched from e across unconstrained edges that come within twice the radius of the midpoint, in a frame centred on it and scaled by a power of two (no underflow at small scales; the margin is far above the rounding of these distances, and searching more only costs time: what is deleted is decided exactly). Returns the number deleted.

member.name: T:g3.SnapRounding2
member.summary:
Snap rounding at an explicit tolerance (spec O11, decision D14 of 2026-11-01): snap rounding on a grid of pixel width tol anchored at the origin (J. D. Hobby, Practical segment intersection with finite precision output, CGTA 1999), followed by the restore step of Snap Rounding with Restore (A. Belussi, S. Migliorini, M. Negri, G. Pelagatti, ACM TSAS 2016), so that every vertex ends at least half a pixel from every edge not incident to it.
Pixels are half-open, closed on the left and bottom (Hobby). A pixel is hot if it holds an input point or a crossing of two input segments. Every input point moves to the centre of its pixel; every input segment becomes the chain through the centres of the hot pixels it touches, in order along it. A hot pixel whose interior an output edge crosses, its ends outside the pixel, is critical; SRR's ChoosePixel picks a pixel next to it in the envelope of the edge's input segment (rules R1 to R3) and makes it hot; by SRR's Proposition 4.14 the result is snap rounding on the grown set of hot pixels, so every round routes all segments again, which keeps SR's guarantees (no crossings, topology up to collapse) at every step. Splitting only the critical edge, as SRR's listing does, can make the new edge cross another chain away from any hot pixel (found by the fuzz test). Only pixels that are not hot yet are chosen, so every round adds one; all lie in the envelopes of the input segments, so the rounds end.
Arithmetic: every double is an integer times a power of two; with the common exponent of all input coordinates and the pixel width, twice every coordinate is an integer, and so are the pixel corners (2k ± 1) W and centres 2 k W. Every decision is exact.

member.name: M:g3.SnapRounding2.Restore(System.Collections.Generic.List{System.ValueTuple{System.ValueTuple{System.Int64,System.Int64},System.Int32,System.Int32}})
member.summary: SRR's Restore with ChoosePixel (their Table II), for each critical pixel and edge, among pixels not hot yet: a free pixel next to it in the envelope of the edge's input segment that routes the edge around it, nearest to the segment (R1, spread); else the nearest such pixel even if not free (R3, spread). R2 (the critical pixel itself) cannot apply here: a segment crossing it would have been routed through it. If no pixel next to it qualifies, the nearest pixel of the envelope within two pixels on the edge's span is taken (Widened). All choices of a round are made on the same arrangement, so the result does not depend on the order (their Proposition 4.17).

member.name: T:g3.SnapGrid
member.summary: The pixel grid of a snap tolerance (D14): pixels of width w centred on the points k w, half-open (closed left and bottom), anchored at the origin. Every decision is exact: the coordinates and w as integers on their common power of two.

member.name: M:g3.SnapGrid.Pixel(System.Double)
member.summary:
the pixel index of x: floor(x / w + 1/2), exactly. A filter first, else the exact quotient (). Refinement on the grid rounds every candidate point (profiled: the BigInteger quotient was a tenth of the split-point choice).
The filter needs no error bound, only that rounding is monotone (w > 0; for any other w the exact path alone, as before). Let q = x / w exactly, r = fl(fl(q) + 1/2) and f = floor(r), and suppose f < r (r is no integer; then |r| < 2^52, beyond which every double is one, and f + 1/2 is a double). If q + 1/2 < f, then q < f - 1/2, so fl(q) <= fl(f - 1/2) and r <= fl(fl(f - 1/2) + 1/2) = f (at f = -2^52, f - 1/2 is no double, but q < f - 1/2 then forces fl(q) <= f - 1, and fl(f - 1 + 1/2) = f, the tie rounding to the even f), a contradiction; if q + 1/2 >= f + 1, then fl(q) >= f + 1/2 and r >= f + 1, again. So f <= q + 1/2 < f + 1: the index is f. Where r is an integer (q + 1/2 may lie just below it), infinite or NaN, the exact quotient decides

member.name: M:g3.SnapGrid.PixelExact(System.Double)
member.summary: the pixel index of x: floor(x / w + 1/2), from the exact quotient

member.name: M:g3.SnapGrid.CrossesInterior(g3.Vector2d,g3.Vector2d,System.Int64,System.Int64)
M:g3.SnapGrid.CrossesInteriorFilter(g3.Vector2d,g3.Vector2d,System.Int64,System.Int64)
member.summary: The filter of : 1 crosses, -1 does not, 0 undecided (the exact test decides). u = 2^-53. - The pixel's sides: (k -+ 1/2) is exact for |k| < 2^52, and the product with w rounds once, s = fl(S) of the true side S. - The box test compares exact coordinates v (doubles) with the sides. Rounding is monotone, so v < s implies v < S (if S <= v, then s = fl(S) <= fl(v) = v), and v > s implies v > S; where v = s, undecided. No error bound is needed. - A corner's orientation against ab, O = DX EY - DY EX (DX = bx - ax, EY = CY - ay for the true corner (CX, CY)), in doubles: dx = DX (1 + d1); ey = (CY (1 + d0) - ay)(1 + d2) = EY (1 + d2) + CY d0 (1 + d2); l = dx ey (1 + d3), and r alike; o = (l - r)(1 + d4). With |di| <= u: |o - O| <= (3u + O(u^2)) (|DX| |EY| + |DY| |EX|) + (u + O(u^2)) (|DX| |CY| + |DY| |CX|) + u (|l| + |r|) <= 5u (1 + 4u) (|dx| (|ey| + |cy|) + |dy| (|ex| + |cx|)), the computed values standing in for the true ones within (1 + 2u). The bound used is 1e-14 times that sum, more than 17 times 5u (1 + 4u): an orientation beyond it has its true sign; within it, undecided. Valid where no rounding is absolute: every input, side, product and the bound normal and far from overflow, in [1e-140, 1e140] or zero (Ok; else undecided), and a difference of doubles that is subnormal is exact. The decisions then equal the exact test's, step for step (the box test, then the four signs; a degenerate segment, a == b, has every orientation 0 and goes to the exact test)

member.name: T:g3.ContMinCircle2
member.summary: Fit minimal bounding-circle to a set of 2D points. Incremental construction in random order (Welzl 1991, written as three nested loops), expected O(N), on the points translated to the first one and scaled by a power of two of their extent. So the decisions depend on neither the position nor the size of the set, and any finite coordinates work. One limit: with a coordinate at or above 2^1021, all coordinates are first divided by 4, which rounds away the last two units of a subnormal coordinate in that set. The radius is up to about 16 eps of the extent above the minimal one, plus the rounding of the center to a coordinate. Circle2d.Contains is true for every input point, as long as the radius is above about 1e-150: below that, squared distances lose bits as subnormal numbers (and from about 1e-162 they are 0, so Contains is simply true). A radius above the double range is +Infinity. The same input gives the same bits (fixed seed). Scaling the input by a power of two scales the result by it, bit for bit, unless a subnormal coordinate rounds in that scaling.

member.name: M:g3.ContMinCircle2.#ctor(System.Collections.Generic.IList{g3.Vector2d},System.Double)
member.param: Dimensionless (it was an absolute squared length in upstream): three points are treated as collinear if the sine of their triangle's largest angle is at most this, and the circle over their longest edge is used. Below about 0.866 this takes only obtuse triangles, for which that circle is the minimal one. From about 0.866 (the sine of 60 degrees, the least that the largest angle of an acute triangle can have) it also takes acute triangles: the result still contains every point but is not minimal, with no error or status, which is what an upstream caller gets who passes a large absolute epsilon. Negative or NaN mean the default.

member.name: T:g3.HBitArray
member.summary:
HBitArray is a hierarchical variant of BitArray. Basically the idea is to make a tree of 32-bit blocks, where at level N, a '0' means that no bits are true in level N-1. This means we can more efficiently iterate over the bit set.
Uses more memory than BitArray, but each tree level is divided by 32, so it is better than NlogN

member.name: F:g3.JitHints.Optimize
member.summary: MethodImplOptions.AggressiveOptimization (.NET Core 3.0 and later; not part of the netstandard2.0 enum, and ignored by the .NET Framework): the method is compiled fully optimized at its first call. For the loops of the exact boolean pipeline: with tiered compilation they otherwise start as unoptimized code and are replaced only after many iterations, which made a single boolean of a mesh with 10k-50k triangles 2-3 times slower than the optimized code (benchmarks/BooleanComparison/README.md, profile). The generated code computes the same IEEE results (no contraction to FMA), only faster.

member.name: T:g3.RefCountVector
member.summary:
RefCountedVector is used to keep track of which indices in a linear index list are in use/referenced. A free list is tracked so that unreferenced indices can be re-used.
The enumerator iterates over valid indices (ie where refcount > 0)
**refcounts are shorts** so the maximum count is 65536. No overflow checking is done in release builds.

member.name: M:g3.RefCountVector.allocate_at(System.Int32)
member.summary: allocate at specific index, which must either be larger than current max index, or on the free list. If larger, all elements up to this one will be pushed onto free list. otherwise we have to do a linear search through free list. If you are doing many of these, it is likely faster to use allocate_at_unsafe(), and then rebuild_free_list() after you are done.

member.name: M:g3.RefCountVector.allocate_at_unsafe(System.Int32)
member.summary: allocate at specific index, which must be free or larger than current max index. However, we do not update free list. So, you probably need to do rebuild_free_list() after calling this.

member.name: M:g3.RefCountVector.Indices
member.summary: the valid indices in increasing order, as GetEnumerator gives them but without boxing each index (the end is max_index when the enumeration starts)

member.name: T:g3.SmallListSet
member.summary:
SmallListSet stores a set of short integer-valued variable-size lists. The lists are encoded into a few large DVector buffers, with internal pooling, so adding/removing lists usually does not involve any new or delete ops.
The lists are stored in two parts. The first N elements are stored in a linear subset of a dvector. If the list spills past these N elements, the extra elements are stored in a linked list (which is also stored in a flat array).
Each list stores its count, so list-size operations are constant time. All the internal "pointers" are 32-bit.

member.name: T:g3.PolySimplification2
member.summary:
2D Polyline/Polygon simplification.
This is a more complex approach than Polygon.Simplify(), which uses sequential vtx clustering and then runs douglas-peucker algorithm. That method can end up modifying long straight segments, which is not ideal in many contexts (eg manufacturing).
Strategy here is : 1) find runs of vertices that are very close to straight lines (default 0.01mm deviation tol) 2) find all straight segments longer than threshold distance (default 2mm) 3) discard vertices that deviate less than tolerance (default = 0.2mm) from sequential-points-segment, unless they are required to preserve straight segments
[TODO] currently doing greedy search in 1,3. Could do more optimal search. [TODO] currently measuring deviation of p1...pN-1 from line [p0,pN] for points [p0,p1,...pN]. could alternately fit best segment to p1...pN (p0 is already fixed). [TODO] 2d variant of variational shape segmentation?

member.name: T:g3.CachingMeshSDF
member.summary:
[RMS] this is variant of MeshSignedDistanceGrid that does lazy evaluation of actual distances, using mesh spatial data structure. This is much faster if we are doing continuation-method marching cubes as only values on surface will be computed!
Compute discretely-sampled (ie gridded) signed distance field for a mesh The basic approach is, first compute exact distances in a narrow band, and then extend out to rest of grid using fast "sweeping" (ie like a distance transform). The resulting unsigned grid is then signed using ray-intersection counting, which is also computed on the grid, so no BVH is necessary
If you set ComputeMode to NarrowBandOnly, result is a narrow-band signed distance field. This is quite a bit faster as the sweeping is the most computationally-intensive step.
Caveats: - the "narrow band" is based on triangle bounding boxes, so it is not necessarily that "narrow" if you have large triangles on a diagonal to grid axes
Potential optimizations: - Often we have a spatial data structure that would allow faster computation of the narrow-band distances (which become quite expensive if we want a wider band!) Not clear how to take advantage of this though. Perhaps we could have a binary grid that, in first pass, we set bits inside triangle bboxes to 1? Or perhaps same as current code, but we use spatial-dist, and so for each ijk we only compute once? (then have to test for computed value at each cell of each triangle...)
This code is based on the C++ implementation found at https://github.com/christopherbatty/SDFGen Original license was public domain. Permission granted by Christopher Batty to include C# port under Boost license.

member.name: T:g3.IntrRay3Triangle3
member.summary: Ray-triangle intersection. Whether the ray hits is decided exactly and watertight (ExactRayTriangle): the ray is the half line from Origin through Origin + 2^m Direction (rounded; 2^m from the exponents, so 2^k scaling is exact), the triangle is closed (a ray onto an edge or a vertex hits every triangle there, so it never misses all triangles of a shared edge or vertex), a ray in the plane of the triangle never hits it (as upstream), and a ray that starts on the triangle hits it at t = 0. No tolerance: upstream rejected rays within about 1e-8 of the plane as parallel and rounded edge tests on and near edges either way. RayParameter and TriangleBaryCoords are computed in doubles (the barycentrics clamped into the triangle).

member.name: T:g3.TriangleTriangleFilter
member.summary:
A filter in front of the exact triangle-triangle test ExactTriangleIntersection.IntersectsBeyondShared, for the self-intersection checks (Reducer, Remesher). It decides the pairs a projection onto an axis plane settles, with the exact ExactPredicates.Orient2d only, so it adds no error bound of its own:
- both triangles in one axis plane (all six coordinates on that axis equal): the problem is 2D, and the projection decides both ways. The exact 3D test would spend its Orient3d calls (all exactly 0, so all in the exact stage) to find that out.
- otherwise, projected along the dominant axis of A's normal: a projection that separates them separates the triangles in 3D (the projection is linear). Without a shared vertex, an edge line of one projected triangle with the other strictly outside (for triangles in 2D such a line exists iff they are disjoint). With a shared vertex s, the projected corners at s overlap only at s; with a shared edge, the far corners lie strictly on opposite sides of it. Both need A's projection to be one to one (its projected corners not collinear), then the triangles meet only at s, or only on the edge. Nearly coplanar neighbours, which the exact test decides in its slow stage, are decided here.
- one triangle in an axis plane, the other not crossing it: Orient3d against the first is the sign of one coordinate difference times its projected Orient2d, so the sides are exact comparisons, and where the other touches the plane (a point, a segment) Orient2d decides both ways. Caps and walls of CAD parts that touch at a rim, where Orient3d is exactly 0 and its exact stage slow.
Anything else is left to the exact test (Undecided). The filter only answers where the exact answer is known, so it never changes a decision of the exact test (checked against it, also on coplanar slivers whose floating-point normal is 0, in TriangleTriangleFilterTests).

member.name: T:g3.GLTFReader
member.summary:
Read glTF 2.0 files, as .gltf (JSON) or .glb (binary container); the variant is detected from the data. https://registry.khronos.org/glTF/specs/2.0/glTF-2.0.html
Every node of the default scene that references a mesh becomes one mesh (if there is no scene, all root nodes are used; if there are no nodes, every glTF mesh is read once). Node transforms (matrix or TRS, including parents) are applied to positions and normals unless ApplyNodeTransforms is false. All primitives of a glTF mesh are combined; if there is more than one primitive, the primitive index is stored as face group. The glTF mesh name is stored as "name" metadata if the builder supports it. Reads POSITION, NORMAL, COLOR_0 (RGB) and TEXCOORD_0, including sparse and normalized-integer accessors. Triangle lists, strips and fans are read; point and line primitives are skipped. Materials, textures, skins and animations are ignored. Coordinates are not converted (glTF is Y-up, in meters). Draco and meshopt compression are not supported (FormatNotSupportedError). Buffers can be the GLB BIN chunk, base64 data URIs, or external files loaded through ResolveUri. Errors are returned as an code, exceptions are caught.

member.name: T:g3.GLTFWriter
member.summary:
Write glTF 2.0 files, as .glb (binary container, ) or .gltf (JSON with embedded base64 buffer, ). No external .bin files are written. https://registry.khronos.org/glTF/specs/2.0/glTF-2.0.html
Each mesh becomes one node with one mesh and one primitive, named by WriteMesh.Name. Writes POSITION and, if enabled in the options (bPerVertexNormals/Colors/UVs) and present in the mesh, NORMAL, COLOR_0 (RGB, clamped to [0,1]) and TEXCOORD_0. Meshes without triangles are written as point primitives, empty meshes as nodes without mesh. No materials are written.
glTF stores positions as 32-bit floats. With CenterNodes = true (default), each mesh is written relative to the center of its bounding box and the center is stored as node translation (in double precision), so large coordinates (eg UTM) keep their precision. GLTFReader applies the translation again when reading. Coordinates are not converted (glTF is Y-up, in meters). The write methods return Ok; exceptions are not caught here.

member.name: T:g3.HeightGrid
member.summary: Regular height grid (a DGM / DTM raster): node (i, j) lies at (X0 + i CellSize, Y0 + j CellSize), row j = 0 is the south row, Z[i + NX j] is its height, NaN = no data. The grid's TIN splits each cell along the diagonal from node (i, j) to node (i+1, j+1) (); interpolates on that TIN, so it is exactly the surface of the mesh. A cell with a no-data corner (NaN or infinite height) has no surface.

member.name: T:g3.HeightGridReader
member.summary:
Readers for height grids (DGM / DTM rasters). Heights are node values: node (i, j) of the is a point of the file (XYZ) or the center of a raster cell (ESRI ASCII). All readers return a status instead of throwing on bad input.
XYZ ASCII: one point per line, "x y z" separated by blanks, tabs, commas or semicolons (further columns are ignored; empty lines and lines starting with # are skipped). The points need not be sorted. They must lie on one regular square lattice; nodes without a point are NaN (gaps). Otherwise the status says why not.
ESRI ASCII Grid (.asc): the header ncols, nrows, xllcorner | xllcenter, yllcorner | yllcenter, cellsize (or dx = dy), optional NODATA_value, then nrows rows of ncols values, north row first.

member.name: M:g3.HeightGridReader.Lattice(System.Collections.Generic.List{System.Double},System.Double,System.Double@,System.Double@,System.Int32@,System.String@)
member.summary: The regular lattice of one coordinate: origin = smallest value, count, and step = extent / (count - 1). The lattice position of each distinct value follows from its gap to the previous one in units of the typical gap (the smallest gap above the jitter), so that jitter within the tolerance does not accumulate. A lattice is recognised if adjacent positions occur somewhere; a position that no point shares with its neighbour column (eg x = 0, 2, 5) is not. False with error == null: fewer than two different values; with an error: not on a lattice.

member.name: T:g3.HeightGridWriter
member.summary: Writers for , the inverse of . ESRI ASCII round trips exactly (origin, cell size and heights are written as given). XYZ round trips the heights and the node positions up to rounding of the cell size (the reader takes the spacing from the extent), and only grids whose border rows and columns hold data: an all-NaN border has no points to recover it from.

member.name: T:g3.OBJReader
member.summary:
gradientspace OBJ mesh format parser
Basic structure is: 1) parse OBJ into internal data structures that represent OBJ exactly 2) convert to mesh objects based on options/etc
Reads v (optionally with r g b vertex colors), vn, vt and f lines (polygons are fan-triangulated, negative indices are supported), "g" groups as triangle groups, and with ReadOptions.ReadMaterials mtllib/usemtl materials (set ). "o" objects are ignored, so all objects become one mesh. Lines that fail to parse are skipped with a warning. A file without vertices or triangles returns (point clouds are not read). Only the TextReader overload is implemented.
[TODO] major current limitation is that we do not support multiple UVs per-vertex (this is a limitation of DMesh3). Similarly no multiple normals per-vertex. So, in the current code, such vertices are duplicated. See append_vertex() and use of Index3i triplet (vi,ni,ui) to represent vertex in BuildMeshes_X() functions
[TODO] only a single material can be assigned to a mesh, this is a current limitation of DMesh3Builder. So, in this case we are splitting the input mesh by material, IE multiple meshes are returned for a single input mesh, each with one material.

member.name: T:g3.OBJWriter
member.summary:
gradientspace OBJ writer
Writes all meshes into one OBJ file (no "o" lines, indices continue across meshes). Vertex colors are written as "v x y z r g b". Normals, colors and UVs are written if enabled in the options and present in the mesh; a separate UV layer in WriteMesh.UVs replaces per-vertex UVs. With options.bWriteGroups, triangles are written sorted by group under "g" lines. With options.bWriteMaterials, OBJMaterial entries of WriteMesh.Materials are written to options.MaterialFilePath (via OpenStreamF) and referenced with mtllib/usemtl. Coordinates use default double formatting (options.RealPrecisionDigits is ignored). Only the TextWriter overload is implemented.
[TODO] if mesh has groups, usemtl lines will not be written (see TODO below) [TODO] options to preserve vertex and triangle indices

member.name: T:g3.PLYReader
member.summary:
Parse PLY (Stanford polygon) mesh format, ascii and binary (little or big endian) http://paulbourke.net/dataformats/ply/
Reads the vertex element (x,y,z and optionally normals nx,ny,nz, colors red/green/blue and UVs s,t or u,v) and the face element (vertex_indices or vertex_index list) into one mesh. Polygons are fan-triangulated; faces with fewer than 3 or out-of-range indices are skipped with a warning. uchar/ushort colors are scaled to [0,1]. Files without faces are read as point sets (a mesh with only vertices). Other elements (edges, materials, ...) and other properties are skipped. Use the BinaryReader overload (as does), which handles all PLY variants. Errors are returned as an code, parse exceptions are caught.

member.name: T:g3.PLYWriter
member.summary:
Write PLY (Stanford polygon) mesh format, ascii or binary_little_endian http://paulbourke.net/dataformats/ply/
The TextWriter overload writes ascii, the BinaryWriter overload binary_little_endian (StandardMeshWriter picks one from options.bWriteBinary). PLY only stores one mesh, so all input meshes are combined. Positions are written as double if options.RealPrecisionDigits > 7, otherwise as float. Normals, colors (uchar) and UVs (s,t) are written if enabled in the options and all meshes have them. options.AsciiHeaderFunc lines are written as header comments. Meshes without triangles are written as point sets. WriteMesh names, materials and UV layers are ignored. Always returns Ok; exceptions are not caught here.

member.name: T:g3.StandardMeshReader
member.summary:
Reads mesh files, choosing the format reader from the file extension (case-insensitive). Supports: * .obj : Wavefront OBJ (optionally with .mtl materials, see ) * .stl : ascii and binary STL (vertices are welded, see ) * .off : ascii OFF * .g3mesh : internal binary format for DMesh3 * .ply : ascii and binary PLY * .3mf : 3D Manufacturing Format (core spec), converted to millimeters * .gltf / .glb : glTF 2.0
Easiest use is the static , which returns the first mesh or null. To get all meshes and error details, use with a and read builder.Meshes afterwards. Read errors are returned as an code, exceptions thrown by format readers are caught and returned as . Coordinates are not converted (except 3MF units to millimeters).

member.name: T:g3.StandardMeshWriter
member.summary:
Writes various mesh file formats. Format is determined from extension. Currently supports: * .obj : Wavefront OBJ Format https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Wavefront_.obj_file * .stl : ascii and binary STL formats https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/STL_(file_format) * .off : OFF format https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/OFF_(file_format) * .g3mesh : internal binary format for packed DMesh3 objects * .ply : ascii and binary (little endian) PLY format http://paulbourke.net/dataformats/ply/ * .3mf : 3D Manufacturing Format (core spec) https://3mf.io * .glb / .gltf : glTF 2.0 binary, or JSON with embedded buffer https://www.khronos.org/gltf/
Each of these is implemented in a separate Writer class, eg OBJWriter, STLWriter, etc
Easiest use is the static , eg WriteMesh("out.ply", mesh, WriteOptions.Defaults). Start options from ; bWriteBinary selects binary STL / PLY. Coordinates are written as stored, no unit or axis conversion is done (3MF is labelled millimeter). Errors are returned as an code; exceptions during writing (including failing to create the file) are caught and returned as .

member.name: T:g3.STLReader
member.summary:
Read ASCII/Binary STL file and produce set of meshes.
Since STL is just a list of disconnected triangles, by default we try to merge vertices together. Use .RebuildStrategy to disable this and/or configure which algorithm is used. If you are using via StandardMeshReader, you can add .StrategyFlag to ReadOptions.CustomFlags.Integers (value is a Strategy) to set this.
Each ascii "solid" becomes one mesh; binary STL is always one mesh. Facet normals are ignored. Vertices are read as float. STL has no units. A truncated binary file is read up to the last complete triangle without error; an ascii file without solids reads Ok with no meshes. Use the BinaryReader overload for binary STL and the TextReader overload for ascii ( detects which one to use).
TODO: document welding strategies. There is no "best" one, they all fail in some cases, because STL is a stupid and horrible format.
STL Binary supports a per-triangle short-int that is usually used to specify color. However since we do not support per-triangle color in DMesh3, this color cannot be directly used. Instead of hardcoding behavior, we return the list of shorts if requested via IMeshBuilder Metadata. Set .WantPerTriAttribs=true or attach flag .PerTriAttribFlag (in ReadOptions.CustomFlags.Flags). After the read finishes you can get the face color list via: DVector<short> colors = Builder.Metadata[0][STLReader.PerTriAttribMetadataName] as DVector<short>; (for DMesh3Builder, which is the only builder that supports Metadata)

member.name: T:g3.ThreeMFReader
member.summary:
Read 3MF (3D Manufacturing Format) files, core specification https://github.com/3MFConsortium/spec_core
Each build item becomes one mesh (with the object name as "name" metadata, if the builder supports it). Components and item/component transforms are applied to the vertices, and objects in other model parts (production extension "path" attribute) are followed. Vertices are converted to millimeters unless ConvertToMillimeters is false. Invalid triangles are skipped with a warning. Materials, colors and extensions (beam lattices, slices, ...) are ignored. ReadOptions are ignored. Errors (not a zip package, missing model part, bad XML or numbers, result larger than ) are returned as , exceptions are caught. A file without build items reads Ok with no meshes. The stream is left open.

member.name: T:g3.AdaptivePredicates
member.summary:
Stages B, C and D of Shewchuk's adaptive predicates ("Adaptive Precision Floating-Point Arithmetic and Fast Robust Geometric Predicates", 1997), after the floating-point filter (stage A, in ExactPredicates): B evaluates the determinant exactly from the rounded coordinate differences (an expansion of a few dozen doubles), C adds the first-order terms of the differences' rounding errors; each decides the sign when its error bound allows. D adds all terms with rounding errors exactly to B's expansion: the exact determinant, so D always decides. Rounding errors that are zero are skipped, which keeps D's expansions short.
Only valid without overflow and underflow: the caller checks that all coordinates are 0 or in [2^-100, 2^100] (Expansion.InRange). Then all coordinates are multiples of 2^-152, so are the differences' rounding errors, and every product of up to four of them (and its rounding error) is a normal double. Signs follow Shewchuk: orient2d > 0 for counter-clockwise, orient3d > 0 if d is below the plane of the counter-clockwise (seen from above) a, b, c, incircle > 0 if d is inside the circle of the counter-clockwise a, b, c.

member.name: T:g3.ExactInterval
member.summary: A closed interval of doubles that contains an exact real value, for floating-point filters. Every operation rounds to nearest and then widens the result by one unit in the last place on both sides, so the exact result of the operation on any values in the operand intervals lies inside: round to nearest is off by at most half the spacing to the next double on the side of the exact value, and the widening moves by a whole spacing. This holds for subnormal results too (the spacing there is 2^-1074). A NaN (eg infinity minus infinity) gives the whole line. So a sign decided by Sign() is a proof, without a hand-derived error constant.

member.name: T:g3.ExactRayTriangle
member.summary:
Exact decisions whether a line or a ray crosses a triangle, shared by IntrRay3Triangle3 (every ray query of DMeshAABBTree3), DMeshAABBTree3.IsInside and the exact winding number of VolumeSampleCells.
The line is given by two double points o and p (for a ray: its origin and SecondPoint(origin, direction)). The line meets the triangle (a, b, c) iff the three edge signs Orient3d(o, p, a, b), (o, p, b, c), (o, p, c, a) do not have opposite signs (Plücker coordinates); all three are 0 iff the line lies in the triangle's plane. Two rules for an exact zero (the line meets the line of an edge: through an edge or a vertex): - closed (ClosedCrossing, RayHitClosed; the hit queries): the triangle is closed, a line through an edge or a vertex meets every triangle there. Watertight: a ray onto a shared edge or vertex, or onto the boundary of an open mesh, never misses all of them, at any scale; a line in the plane of a triangle does not meet it. - perturbed (EdgeSign, LineCrossing, RayHitPerturbed; counting): Simulation of Simplicity (Edelsbrunner and Mücke, ACM TOG 9(1), 1990): p is moved by (ε, ε², ε³), o by (ε⁴, ε⁸, ε¹²), the same for every triangle, so the decision is that of a line in general position that no edge meets. EdgeSign(o, p, a, b) = -EdgeSign(o, p, b, a) exactly, so a line through an edge or a vertex crosses exactly one triangle of a closed fan: no crossing is lost or counted twice, the parity and the signed crossing count are right. Every decision is an exact sign (ExactPredicates, a floating-point filter in the common case) or a comparison of coordinates, so it does not change under scaling by 2^k.

member.name: F:g3.ExactRayTriangle.Miss
member.summary: RayHit*: no crossing at t >= 0

member.name: F:g3.ExactRayTriangle.Ahead
member.summary: RayHit*: the ray crosses the triangle at t > 0

member.name: F:g3.ExactRayTriangle.AtOrigin
member.summary: RayHit*: the origin lies on the triangle (t = 0)

member.name: M:g3.ExactRayTriangle.SecondPoint(g3.Vector3d,g3.Vector3d)
member.summary: The second point of the ray's line: origin + 2^m direction, with 2^m chosen from the exponents of the largest coordinates of origin and direction so that the scaled direction is at least twice the origin's largest coordinate (so p != origin, and the rounding of the sum changes the line's direction by at most about 2^-51 relative). 2^m depends only on the exponent difference, so scaling origin and direction by 2^k (or the origin alone, with the 2^k scaled into 2^m) scales p by 2^k exactly. Returns origin if the direction is 0 or a value is not finite (no hits then).

member.name: M:g3.ExactRayTriangle.EdgeSign(g3.Vector3d,g3.Vector3d,g3.Vector3d,g3.Vector3d)
member.summary: The sign of Orient3d(o', p', a, b) for o' = o + (ε⁴, ε⁸, ε¹²), p' = p + (ε, ε², ε³), ε → 0+: never 0 unless a == b. With f(o, p) = det[p - o, a - o, b - o] (the value whose sign Orient3d(o, p, a, b) is), affine in o and in p, the expansion is f + Σ ε^(1,2,3) ∂f/∂p_(x,y,z) + Σ ε^(4,8,12) ∂f/∂o_(x,y,z) + Σ ε^(i+j) ∂²f/∂p∂o (no other terms: f is linear in p, affine in o, and the exponents 1..15 are all distinct), with ∂f/∂p_x = ((a - o) x (b - o))_x = orient2d of o, a, b in the (y, z) plane, likewise (z, x) and (x, y); ∂f/∂o_x = -orient2d of p, a, b in the (y, z) plane, likewise (z, x) and (x, y); ∂²f/∂p_i∂o_j = (e_j x (a - b))_i: for (p_y, o_x) -(a - b)_z, (p_z, o_x) (a - b)_y, (p_x, o_y) (a - b)_z, (p_z, o_y) -(a - b)_x, ..., (p_i, o_i) 0. The first nonzero coefficient in the order of the exponents is the sign. It is reached by exponent 11 at the latest if a != b ((a - b)_z at 6, (a - b)_y at 7, (a - b)_x at 11).

member.name: M:g3.ExactRayTriangle.LineCrossing(g3.Vector3d,g3.Vector3d,g3.Vector3d,g3.Vector3d,g3.Vector3d)
member.summary: The crossing of the perturbed line (o', p') with the triangle (a, b, c): +1 if it crosses the triangle's interior with (p - o) . N > 0, N = (b - a) x (c - a) (the normal Orient3d(a, b, c, .) is positive along), -1 if it crosses with (p - o) . N < 0, 0 if it does not cross (also for a triangle of no area). The edge signs sum to (p' - o') . N (Σ det[d, a - o, b - o] over the edges is d . N), so when they agree that is their sign.

member.name: M:g3.ExactRayTriangle.ClosedCrossing(g3.Vector3d,g3.Vector3d,g3.Vector3d,g3.Vector3d,g3.Vector3d)
member.summary: The crossing of the line (o, p) with the closed triangle (a, b, c): +1 if it meets the triangle (interior, edge or vertex) with (p - o) . N > 0, -1 with (p - o) . N < 0, 0 if it does not meet it or lies in its plane (all three signs 0; also every line for a triangle of no area). The edge signs sum to (p - o) . N, so when none is opposite to another and not all are 0, the nonzero ones have the sign of (p - o) . N.

member.name: M:g3.ExactRayTriangle.RayHitClosed(g3.Vector3d,g3.Vector3d,g3.Vector3d,g3.Vector3d,g3.Vector3d)
member.summary: Does the ray from o through p hit the closed triangle (a, b, c): Miss, Ahead (at t > 0) or AtOrigin (o lies on the triangle: a ray that starts on the surface hits it at t = 0, as upstream). The side of o is exact: the crossing is ahead iff Orient3d(a, b, c, o) is opposite to the crossing sign; a crossing implies (p - o) . N != 0, so with o in the plane the crossing is o itself.

member.name: M:g3.ExactRayTriangle.RayHitPerturbed(g3.Vector3d,g3.Vector3d,g3.Vector3d,g3.Vector3d,g3.Vector3d)
member.summary: Does the perturbed ray from o' through p' cross the triangle (a, b, c): Miss, Ahead (at t > 0) or AtOrigin (o lies on the triangle: either answer is consistent for a point on the surface). The side of o is exact: the crossing is ahead iff Orient3d(a, b, c, o) is opposite to the crossing sign. With o exactly in the triangle's plane: if p is in it too (the line lies in the plane), the perturbed line crosses the plane behind o' (both (o' - a) . N and (p' - o') . N lead with the first nonzero coordinate of N, so t' < 0): Miss, as the perturbation decides, and as upstream ("parallel: no intersection"). Otherwise the crossing is at o itself, on the closed triangle: AtOrigin.

member.name: T:g3.ExactSlopeKernel
member.summary: Exact geometry of the slope envelope (docs/design/TERRAIN_1A_PLAN.md): planes through three double points, lines in XY where two planes have the same height or through two double points, and vertices where two lines cross or at a double point. Every decision (side of a line at a vertex, orientation of three vertices, order along a line) is the sign of a polynomial in the input doubles: interval arithmetic first (ExactInterval), then exact (ExactDyadic). Constructed values (the rounded vertex position, a plane's height there) are rounded once, to nearest, from the exact rational value.

member.name: T:g3.ExactSlopePredicates
member.summary: Exact slope predicate of a triangle given by double coordinates (docs/design/TERRAIN.md 5.4, oracle (i)). With n = (b - a) x (c - a), the slope (magnitude of the gradient over XY) is sqrt(nx^2 + ny^2) / |nz|. The comparison against a limit is a polynomial sign, decided by interval arithmetic (ExactInterval) and, if the interval contains 0, exactly (ExactDyadic). The orientation does not matter (both sides are squares).

member.name: T:g3.FixedPoint3
member.summary: A canonical ExactPoint3 in fixed width, for the exact points of ExactMeshArrangement (docs/design/FIXED_WIDTH_EXACT_POINTS.md): X, Y, Z, W as sign and magnitude, the magnitudes in four 64-bit limbs each. member.name: T:g3.IndirectPredicates
member.summary: Exact sign predicates generated from their formulas by tools/PredicateCompiler (docs/design/INDIRECT_PREDICATES.md). Inputs within the bound of a predicate are evaluated on FixedArith, every value with the limbs its derived bound allows (the comments), on a FixedArena of the derived scratch; inputs beyond it in BigInteger. No allocation on the FixedArith path. A predicate with several sign factors is 0 when any factor is 0: an indirect predicate is also 0 when its point does not exist (denominator d = 0: a line parallel to the plane, a degenerate triangle, dependent planes); a caller that must tell this apart checks d itself. Orient3d*(..., a, b, c) is the sign of det(x - c, a - c, b - c) = ExactPredicates.Orient3d(a, b, c, x) for the implicit point x.

member.name: T:g3.TransformSequence
member.summary:
TransformSequence stores an ordered list of basic transformations. This can be useful if you need to construct some modifications and want to use the same set later. For example, if you have a hierarchy of objects with relative transformations and want to "save" the nested transform sequence without having to hold references to the original objects.
Use the Append() functions to add different transform types, and the TransformX() to apply the sequence

member.name: M:g3.Vector3d.ComputeOrthogonalComplement(System.Int32,g3.Vector3d,g3.Vector3d@,g3.Vector3d@)
member.summary: this function is ported from GTEngine. Compute a right-handed orthonormal basis for the orthogonal complement of the input vectors. The function returns the smallest length of the unnormalized vectors computed during the process. If this value is nearly zero, it is possible that the inputs are linearly dependent (within numerical round-off errors). On input, numInputs must be 1 or 2 and v0 through v(numInputs-1) must be initialized. On output, the vectors v0 through v2 form an orthonormal set.

member.name: T:g3.DMesh3
member.summary:
Dynamic indexed triangle mesh with full connectivity (vertices, edges, triangles and their adjacency), the main mesh type of geometry3Sharp. Supports optional per-vertex normals, colors and UVs and per-triangle group IDs, and local editing (SplitEdge, CollapseEdge, FlipEdge, RemoveTriangle, ...).
IDs are stable: removing elements leaves gaps, so always iterate with VertexIndices() / TriangleIndices() (or Vertices() / Triangles()), and use MaxVertexID / MaxTriangleID only to size arrays; VertexCount and TriangleCount are the numbers of live elements. Check IsCompact, or copy with new DMesh3(mesh, true) to remove the gaps.
Topology is kept manifold at edges: AppendTriangle refuses a triangle that would give an edge more than two triangles (returns NonManifoldID); bowtie vertices are allowed. Triangles are [a,b,c] counter-clockwise seen from the side the normal points to. Timestamp / ShapeTimestamp change on every edit and are used by caches such as DMeshAABBTree3. Not thread-safe for concurrent modification. Use CheckValidity() to test the internal consistency after construction or editing.

member.summary: Ultimate generic mesh-builder, pass it arrays of floats/doubles, or lists of Vector3d, or anything in-between. Will figure out how to interpret. Vertices: float/double (3 per vertex), Vector3f or Vector3d. Triangles: int (3 per triangle), Index3i or Vector3i. Normals (optional): one per vertex, same element types as Vertices. TriGroups (optional): one per triangle. Vertex IDs are the input indices. Triangles that cannot be added (invalid or non-manifold) are silently skipped, so check TriangleCount if this matters. Throws NotSupportedException for other element types, and if the normal or group counts do not match. The type arguments must be given explicitly (NType cannot be inferred when Normals is omitted), eg DMesh3 m = DMesh3Builder.Build<double, int, double>(new double[] { 0,0,0, 1,0,0, 0,1,0 }, new int[] { 0,1,2 });

member.name: T:g3.MeshConstraintUtil
member.summary: Helpers that fill a for common cases, for use with and . The overloads that take a Remesher create its constraints object if it has none. Without constraints the refiners move, split and collapse boundary edges freely (boundaries shrink and lose detail), so constrain them when the boundary must be kept: FixAllBoundaryEdges keeps the boundary exactly (its edges are not changed at all), PreserveBoundaryLoops lets boundary vertices slide along the original boundary curve (edges can be split and collapsed, so the boundary is remeshed too), and PreserveBoundaryAndFeatures additionally keeps sharp feature edges and pins corners.

member.name: M:g3.MeshConstraintUtil.FixEdges(g3.MeshConstraints,g3.DMesh3,System.Collections.Generic.IEnumerable{System.Int32})

member.name: M:g3.MeshConstraintUtil.PreserveBoundaryAndFeatures(g3.MeshConstraints,g3.DMesh3,System.Double,System.Double)
member.summary: Constrain boundary loops and sharp feature edges (normals differ by more than creaseAngle degrees) for remeshing: vertices on them stay on these curves (MeshTopology spans/loops as projection targets), junctions are pinned, and so are corners along the curves, where the curve turns by more than cornerAngle degrees (default: creaseAngle). Without pinned corners, collapses and smoothing slide corner vertices along the curve and round off eg the corners of the outer boundary ring. Bowtie vertices (fans of triangles that meet only there, eg two cones tip to tip) are pinned too: otherwise a collapse removes them and joins the fans, and the smoothing moves them with all fans.

member.name: M:g3.MeshConstraintUtil.PreserveBoundaryAndFeatures(g3.Remesher,System.Double,System.Double)
member.summary: PreserveBoundaryAndFeatures on the remesher's mesh and constraints (created if null)

member.name: M:g3.MeshConstraintUtil.PinSharpVertices(g3.MeshConstraints,g3.DMesh3,System.Double)
member.summary: Pin the vertices where the surface comes to a point that is no junction of feature curves: the apex of a cone made of many slices, whose side edges are too flat to be creases, so PreserveBoundaryAndFeatures does not see it and the remeshers round it off (smoothing, collapses). A vertex is pinned if the absolute value of its angle deficit (2 pi minus the sum of its triangle angles, gs.MeshCurvature.AngleDeficit; the Gaussian curvature concentrated at the vertex) is at least minAngleDeficit degrees: 360 (1 - sin a) for the apex of a circular cone of half angle a (eg 199 degrees for a = 26.6, 75 for a = 52, 48 for a = 60); a negative deficit (a saddle point) counts by its absolute value. It tends to 0 at the vertices of a finely tessellated smooth surface, but a coarse tessellation has large deficits everywhere (60 degrees at every vertex of an icosahedron, 90 at a cube corner), so there every vertex above the threshold is pinned. Interior, manifold vertices only (no boundary, no bowtie, finite one-ring; degenerate triangles at the vertex are fine, their angles count in the deficit), without a constraint: the vertices of feature curves are left to the curve constraints (they have a deficit from the crease alone, eg 360 / slices degrees at the rim of a capped cylinder; corners and junctions are pinned there), so call it after PreserveBoundaryAndFeatures. Pinned in place (VertexConstraint.Pinned: two pinned vertices are not collapsed together). Returns the number of vertices pinned. Angles only: invariant under scaling, rotation and translation up to rounding.

member.name: M:g3.MeshEditor.CutAlongEdges(System.Collections.Generic.IEnumerable{System.Int32})
member.summary: Cut the mesh open along the given interior edges. At every endpoint the triangle fan is split where it crosses a cut edge, and each piece after the first (largest) gets its own copy of the vertex; a cut edge becomes two boundary edges where this separates its two triangles. It does not where the fan of neither end is split: eg an edge whose ends are both inside the mesh with no other cut edge at them (a slit needs a hole or a boundary to open into), or a fan with a single cut edge. Fans at the endpoints that were already separate (bowties) are split as well. Returns the number of vertices added.

member.name: T:g3.MeshMeasurements
member.summary: Static measurement functions for meshes: volume and surface area, mass properties (center of mass, inertia tensor), centroids, axis-aligned and oriented bounds, extents along an axis, and genus. None of these modify the mesh. Volume integrals assume a closed mesh whose triangle normals point outward (the convention of the mesh generators); for such meshes the volume is positive, for inside-out meshes it is negative, and for open meshes it is not meaningful.

member.summary: Computes mass (= volume, assuming unit density), center of mass and 3x3 inertia tensor for a closed triangle set. You provide an enumerator over triangles and a vertex accessor. If bodyCoords is true, the inertia tensor is relative to the center of mass, otherwise it is relative to the world origin. The inertia tensor is row-major. Ported from WildMagic5 Wm5PolyhedralMassProperties.

member.name: T:g3.MeshRefinerBase
member.summary: Base class of the edge-collapse based mesh refiners (, and their subclasses). Holds the mesh, which is modified in place, the optional , cancellation (Progress) and the shared validity tests for collapses and flips.

member.name: F:g3.MeshRefinerBase.AllowCollapseFixedVertsWithSameSetID
member.summary: If true, then when two Fixed vertices have the same valid (non-negative) FixedSetID, we treat them as not fixed and allow collapse (to the midpoint). Default true.

member.name: P:g3.MeshRefinerBase.EdgeFlipTolerance
member.summary: If the dot product of a triangle normal before and after a collapse or flip is less than or equal to this, we consider it a normal flip and reject the operation. If nonzero, the normals are normalized first. Clamped to [-1,1]. default = 0

member.name: F:g3.MeshRefinerBase.MinCollapseTriangleQuality
member.summary: If > 0, reject edge collapses that would create a triangle with quality below this value (unless it was already worse before). Quality is 4*sqrt(3)*area / sum of squared edge lengths: 1 for equilateral, 0 for degenerate. Without this, collapses can create near-zero-area triangles, which only pass the normal flip test because they do not flip.

member.name: F:g3.MeshRefinerBase.CollapseQualityAgainstWorst
member.summary: (internal; Reducer only) MinCollapseTriangleQuality with an exception for collapses that remove the worst triangle around the collapsed edge (both one-rings): if one of the two triangles the collapse removes is that worst triangle, a new triangle below the threshold and worse than its own predecessor (refused without this) is allowed as long as it is better than the removed one. So a collapse can remove a sliver of the input although its new triangles stay below the threshold; elsewhere the rule is the one without the option. The worst quality around the edge never drops below min(threshold, worst before).

member.name: M:g3.MeshRefinerBase.TriangleQuality(g3.Vector3d@,g3.Vector3d@,g3.Vector3d@)
member.summary: 4*sqrt(3)*area / sum of squared edge lengths: 1 for equilateral, 0 for degenerate
