member.name: T:g3.Reducer
member.summary:
Mesh Simplication - implementation of Garland & Heckbert Quadric Error Metric (QEM) Simplification.
Collapses edges in place, cheapest quadric error first, until a target is reached: ReduceToTriangleCount(), ReduceToVertexCount(), ReduceToEdgeLength() or ReduceToMaxQuadricError(). The mesh passed to the constructor is modified; vertex and triangle ids are not compacted. There is no return value: a target can be missed when no allowed collapse is left (collapses that would flip a normal, break the link condition, violate constraints, move boundary vertices, exceed MaxDeviation or create self-intersections are skipped), so check mesh.TriangleCount afterwards.
Boundaries: with PreserveBoundaryShape (default) boundary vertices are never moved (a collapse keeps the boundary vertex), so the boundary only loses vertices. For a guaranteed geometric tolerance set MaxDeviation (certified one-sided bound to the input surface). Use via SetExternalConstraints() to fix vertices or edges.
Prefer Reducer to lower the triangle count while keeping the shape. Use instead for uniform, well-shaped triangles of a given edge length (Reducer keeps long thin triangles in flat regions).

member.name: F:g3.Reducer.MinimizeQuadricPositionError
member.summary: if true (default), we try to find position for collapsed vertices that minimizes quadric error. If false we just use midpoints. Note: using midpoints is *significantly* slower, because it results in may more points that would cause a triangle flip, which are then rejected. (Also results in more invalid collapses, not sure why though...)

member.name: F:g3.Reducer.AreaWeightedQuadrics
member.summary: Weight each triangle's plane quadric by its area (default). If false, every plane counts once, so errors are sums of squared distances to the original planes; small triangles at sharp corners then keep their full influence (useful with ReduceToMaxQuadricError).

member.name: F:g3.Reducer.BoundaryQuadricWeight
member.summary: If PreserveBoundaryShape is set, each boundary edge adds a plane through the edge, perpendicular to its triangle, to the quadrics of its vertices (Garland-Heckbert boundary constraint), weighted by this times the plane weight of a triangle. Removing a corner of the boundary ring then has a cost, while vertices on straight boundary runs can still be collapsed.

member.name: F:g3.Reducer.FeatureAngle
member.summary: If > 0, edges whose triangle normals differ by more than this angle (degrees) are feature edges. The planes of both their triangles are added to the quadrics of the edge vertices with weight FeatureQuadricWeight, so sharp edges and corners are preserved even next to large triangles.

member.name: F:g3.Reducer.FeatureQuadricWeight
member.summary: weight of the feature edge planes, relative to a triangle plane (see FeatureAngle)

member.name: F:g3.Reducer.QuadricRegularization
member.summary: The optimal collapse point minimizes the quadric plus QuadricRegularization * (trace(A)/3) * |x - edge midpoint|^2. This keeps the solve well-conditioned and independent of the mesh scale (directions the planes do not constrain, eg along a flat region, stay at the midpoint), as with probabilistic quadrics (Trettner and Kobbelt 2020). Small enough not to move corners noticeably.

member.name: F:g3.Reducer.MaxDeviation
member.summary: If > 0, a collapse is only done if every point of the new triangles stays within MaxDeviation of the input surface (checked with the certified bounds of TriangleDeviationBounds, so the reduced surface is guaranteed to lie within this distance of the input). One-sided: input features thinner than the tolerance (eg a spike) can still be cut off. The reference is the mesh at the first reduction with MaxDeviation (so repeated ReduceTo... calls stay within MaxDeviation of the original), or the one given to SetDeviationReference. Not covered: the projection of a ProjectionTarget (Reproject) after the collapses.

member.name: F:g3.Reducer.PreventSelfIntersections
member.summary: If set, a collapse is only done if its new triangles intersect no other triangle (exact test, ExactTriangleIntersection.IntersectsBeyondShared, against a grid of the current triangles), so the reduction cannot push the surface through nearby parts of itself (thin walls, narrow gaps). Folds are prevented by the usual flip check. Costs about 2-3x the reduction time.

member.name: F:g3.Reducer.PreventFoldOver
member.summary: If true (default), a collapse is also rejected if one of its new triangles turns away from the input surface it stands for: its unit normal must have a positive dot with the reference normal of its corners, the sum of the area-weighted input normals each corner has absorbed (summed on every collapse). The usual flip check compares with the current triangle only, so a chain of collapses, each turning a normal by less than 90 degrees, can fold the surface over (meshoptimizer issue 346). Where the absorbed normals nearly cancel (a sharp crease, the rim of a thin plate: the reference shorter than ReferenceNormalMinLength of their summed lengths) the reference says nothing, and only the usual flip check applies. The references are taken from the mesh at the start of each reduction, like the quadrics. False gives the reductions of upstream geometry3Sharp.

member.name: F:g3.Reducer.BoundaryTriangleMinNormalDot
member.summary: (PreventFoldOver) a new triangle with two boundary edges, eg one on three consecutive vertices of a straight border after an interior vertex was collapsed onto the border, must have a dot of more than this with its reference normal (default 0.7, about 45 degrees), not just a positive one: such a triangle can stand at right angles to the surface (a wall along the border) and still pass the sign test, as the reference of border vertices tilts towards the border. (Triangles with one boundary edge, eg all of a band one cell wide, need only the positive dot.)

member.name: F:g3.Reducer.ReferenceNormalMinLength
member.summary: (PreventFoldOver) the reference normal of a triangle is used only if its length is at least this fraction of the summed lengths of the normals it was summed from (default 0.25: they spread by less than about 150 degrees); otherwise they nearly cancel and the sign of a dot with it is noise

member.name: F:g3.Reducer.MaxDeviationDepth

member.name: T:g3.QuadricError

member.name: M:g3.QuadricError.OptimalPoint(g3.Vector3d@,g3.Vector3d,System.Double)
member.summary: minimizer of the quadric + lambda * |x - center|^2, with lambda = lambdaRel * trace(A)/3: always well-conditioned and scale independent; directions the quadric does not constrain stay at center. The Reducer then takes an endpoint or the midpoint of the edge.

member.name: M:g3.RegionRemesher.RepairPossibleNonManifoldEdges
member.summary:
After remeshing we may create an internal edge between two boundary vertices [a,b]. Those vertices will be merged with vertices c and d in the base mesh. If the edge [c,d] already exists in the base mesh, then after the merge we would have at least 3 triangles at this edge. Dang.
A common example is a 'fin' triangle that would duplicate a 'fin' on the border of the base mesh after removing the submesh, but this situation can arise anywhere (eg think about one-triangle-wide strips).
This is very hard to remove, but we can at least avoid creating non-manifold edges (which with the current DMesh3 will be prevented, hence leaving a hole) by splitting the internal edge in the submesh (which presumably we were remeshing anyway, so changes are ok). Called by BackPropropagate() by default.

member.name: M:g3.RegionRemesher.BackPropropagate(System.Boolean)
member.summary:
Remove the original submesh region from BaseMesh and merge in the remeshed version. You can call this multiple times as the base-triangle-set is updated (CurrentBaseTriangles).
By default, we allow the submesh to be modified to prevent creation of non-manifold edges (RepairPossibleNonManifoldEdges). You can disable this, however then some of the submesh triangles may be discarded.
Returns false if there were errors in insertion, ie if some triangles failed to insert. Does not revert changes that were successful.

member.name: T:g3.Remesher
member.summary:
Isotropic remeshing in place (Botsch and Kobbelt style): each BasicRemeshPass() splits edges longer than MaxEdgeLength, collapses edges shorter than MinEdgeLength, flips edges to improve vertex valence, then applies tangential-ish Laplacian smoothing and (optionally) projects the vertices onto a target surface. Call SetTargetEdgeLength() and then BasicRemeshPass() several times (typically 5-20 passes; ModifiedEdgesLastPass gives a convergence hint). There is no return value; the mesh (passed to the constructor) is modified directly, vertex and triangle ids are not preserved. A pass that would turn a closed component inside out (a target edge length far above the wall thickness) is rolled back and counted in InvertingPassesRejected (RejectInvertingPasses).
Important behaviour: without a projection target the smoothing shrinks and rounds the surface, so for shape-preserving remeshing call SetProjectionTarget(MeshProjectionTarget.Auto(originalMesh)). Boundary edges and vertices are split, collapsed and smoothed like interior ones unless constrained, use (FixAllBoundaryEdges, PreserveBoundaryLoops, PreserveBoundaryAndFeatures) or SetExternalConstraints(). PreventNormalFlips is off by default. The default (buffered) parallel smoothing gives the same result as the serial one; only EnableSmoothInPlace with parallel smoothing depends on the thread timing.
See for a faster variant (queue-based passes and a FastestRemesh/SharpEdgeReprojectionRemesh driver), to remesh only part of a mesh, and for simplification to a triangle count or error (Remesher only targets edge lengths).

member.name: F:g3.Remesher.MinTriangleQuality
member.summary: Opt-in quality safeguards, 0 = off (default, the original behaviour; `g3cli remesh` uses 0.2, chosen with the fidelity measures of benchmarks/RemeshQualityBenchmark). If > 0 (eg 0.2), with quality 4*sqrt(3)*area / sum of squared edge lengths (1 equilateral, 0 degenerate): - vertices on constraint curves are smoothed along their curve (towards their two neighbours across edges constrained to the same target; junctions and curve ends stay) instead of with the surface smoothing, so the projection onto the curve keeps them in place along it (otherwise they could land on another part of the curve, on a corner or on an edge); - a smoothing move is rejected if it flips an incident (not flat) triangle, or leaves one below this quality and worse than before; a projection move that would flip one is shortened to a half, quarter or eighth step, or rejected (the next pass gets closer); - the buffered smoothing and projection passes revert the moves of every triangle the moves together would still flip; the projection pass is then buffered too, so the result does not depend on the order or thread timing (not with EnableSmoothInPlace, whose parallel pass reads positions being written); - an edge whose triangle pair contains a triangle below this quality is flipped if that at least doubles the pair's minimum quality and keeps the orientation; - an edge with a flat neighbouring triangle (its opposite vertex on the edge) is not split, which would put the new vertex onto that vertex; - collapses and flips that would flip a triangle normal are rejected (as with PreventNormalFlips); - a collapse that would create a flat triangle (eg two vertices of a straight feature curve joined over a third one on it) is rejected. Other collapses are not restricted: blocking poor but not flat results (eg with MinCollapseTriangleQuality) keeps short edges that the splits around them multiply. Not guarded: the projection of a new vertex after a split. Together, on 20 Thingi10K meshes remeshed with creases kept, 28% of the poor (q < 0.1) and 13% of the flat (q < 1e-3) triangles and 16% of the self-intersecting pairs remain (benchmarks/RemeshQualityBenchmark). RemesherPro queues the edges of a vertex whose move was rejected. With a target edge length far above the wall thickness the result is undefined with and without this option: the walls are folded through each other (self-intersections); passes that turn a closed component inside out are rolled back (RejectInvertingPasses).

member.name: F:g3.Remesher.RejectInvertingPasses
member.summary: Roll back a pass (BasicRemeshPass, RemesherPro.RemeshIteration) that turns a closed component of the mesh inside out (an outer surface or a cavity): after it, the number of closed components with a positive or with a negative signed volume differs from before, or a component has another sign than most of its vertices had before (a volume within 1e-9 area^1.5 of zero counts as neither, so a component flattened to zero volume is rolled back too). This happens when the target edge length is far above the wall thickness (the walls are folded through each other), with or without MinTriangleQuality. The mesh and the constraints are restored to their state before the pass and InvertingPassesRejected is incremented; the next pass starts from there again (and is usually rolled back too, so the result stays at the last pass that kept the orientation). Costs a copy of the mesh and the constraints per pass if the mesh has a closed component. The rollback is for the whole mesh: one small part that keeps inverting (eg a coarse cone among finer parts) stops the remeshing of all other parts too. In RemesherPro.FastestRemesh a rolled-back last iteration leaves the state after an iteration without projection. Not guarded: the other passes (FullSmoothPass, FullProjectionPass, RemesherPro.FastSplitIteration, TrackedFaceProjectionPass) and a cancelled pass. Default true (false in EdgeLoopRemesher).

member.name: F:g3.Remesher.InvertingPassesRejected
member.summary: status: the number of passes rolled back by RejectInvertingPasses so far

member.name: F:g3.Remesher.PreventSelfIntersections
member.summary: Opt-in (default false): reject the edge operations and vertex moves that would make a triangle intersect another one (exactly, ExactTriangleIntersection.IntersectsBeyondShared, the test of MeshRepairMetrics.SelfIntersections): a collapse, flip or split whose new triangles intersect a triangle outside the changed ones (or each other; a split too: its rounded midpoint is not exactly on the edge, and a pair that shared a vertex before need not share one after), the projection of a vertex created by a split onto its constraint curve (it stays at the edge midpoint), and in the buffered smoothing and projection passes (also RemesherPro's tracked and face-aligned passes) the moves of every triangle pair that intersects after the pass (reverted until no pair with a moved vertex intersects, and with MinTriangleQuality until no triangle at a reverted vertex flips; the first round in parallel when the pass is, each round as a set, so the result does not depend on the thread timing). The inline projection of a collapse or smoothing move is part of the checked position. Triangles kept in a hash grid that is rebuilt when the mesh was changed outside the remesher. A mesh without self-intersections stays without them; intersections the mesh already has are not removed, and the operations and moves near them are blocked. Not guarded: EnableSmoothInPlace, and in RegionRemesher the rest of the base mesh (only the region is checked). The first round of the move check finds candidates with DMeshAABBTree3, whose boxes are padded by an absolute 6e-6: for coordinates beyond about 1e10 a touching pair can be missed there (the later rounds use the exact grid boxes). Rejections are counted in SelfIntersectionsRejected. Expensive: with the g3cli remesh settings about 17x the time on Thingi10K (11.3 -> 195.7 s for 20 meshes; mostly the exact tests of neighbouring triangles), see benchmarks/RemeshQualityBenchmark, measured before TriangleTriangleFilter in front of those tests (2 to 4 times faster on flat and axis-flat meshes, same results: benchmarks/SelfIntersectionBenchmark). Thin walls far below the edge length stay intersection-free but end far from the input (the folds are blocked, not avoided).

member.name: F:g3.Remesher.TargetEdgeLengthF
member.summary: Opt-in local sizing (default null): the target edge length at a point (eg the midpoint of an edge). An edge is split if it is longer than 1.33 times the target at its midpoint and collapsed if shorter than 0.66 times it, as SetTargetEdgeLength does globally; the field is capped by MinEdgeLength / MaxEdgeLength, so it can only make edges shorter than the global target (eg below the local wall thickness: RemeshSizing.FromWallThickness). A non-finite or non-positive value means the global target. RemesherPro queues edges by these local lengths too; its tracked passes call the field in parallel, so it must be thread-safe (RemeshSizing's fields are). Called once per processed edge (and per queued edge in RemesherPro): its cost adds to every pass.

member.name: T:g3.DualContouring
member.summary:
Dual Contouring (Ju et al. 2002) of an implicit function on a uniform grid. One vertex per cell, placed by minimizing a QEF built from the surface points and normals ("Hermite data") on the cell's sign-changing edges, which reproduces sharp edges and corners. Produces far fewer triangles than MarchingCubes at the same feature quality.
Hermite data comes from HermiteF if it is set (eg project the edge crossing onto an input mesh), otherwise from linear interpolation of the field and its central-difference gradient.
Each cell gets one vertex per surface patch (the patches marching cubes would create in it), as in manifold dual contouring (Schaefer et al. 2007), so thin walls and gaps do not create non-manifold edges.
Sparse mode: if CandidateCells is set, only those cells (and the cells around their sign-changing edges) are contoured, and grid node values come from NodeValueF instead of sampling Implicit on the whole grid. Cell (i,j,k) spans Bounds.Min + CellSize * [i,i+1] x [j,j+1] x [k,k+1].
Local refinement (sparse mode, see SetRefinement): a set of cells is replaced by cells RefineFactor times smaller. Where refined cells meet unrefined ones, the fine grid nodes on the shared faces and edges get signs topologically equivalent to the coarse face (see edge_decision / face_decision): the real field signs if they are, otherwise imposed ones. Each fine sign change on such a face then belongs to one surface patch of the coarse cell, and the polygons of fine edges on the faces of coarse cells (triangles for edges inside a coarse face) connect to that patch's vertex, as in octree dual contouring. The result stays closed and manifold.
Notes: - inside is where the field is greater than IsoValue (eg winding number); set InsideIsLess for SDFs - quads that would still create a non-manifold edge (an ambiguous face where both cells have a single patch) are left out and counted in NonManifoldTriangles; the result then has small holes

Return true and the surface point and normal to use, or false to fall back to the interpolated point and field gradient. Must be thread-safe if ParallelCompute is true.

The cells there merge both sides of the gap, which can make the surfaces intersect. Counted in HiddenGapEdges; refining the grid until there are none avoids this. Called at most once per grid edge (results are kept across FindCrossings calls).

member.summary: Sparse mode: replace the given cells (grid cell coordinates) by factor^3 cells each (factor a power of two). fineCandidateCells are cells of the fine grid (cell (i,j,k) spans Bounds.Min + CellSize / factor * [i,i+1] x ...) inside the refined cells where the surface may pass, fineNodeValueF the field at fine grid nodes (it is not called at nodes of the coarse grid, those come from NodeValueF). member.name: F:g3.DualContouring.ResolveSelfIntersections
member.summary: Neighbouring polygons can fold through each other: around vertices on sharp features (QEF of rank 2 or 3: edges, corners), where fine and coarse cells meet, and where several thin sheets pass through few cells (eg a winding number field of a non-orientable input). If set, intersecting triangles are found with exact predicates and their vertices moved until none are left: halfway to a fallback position four times, then onto it (the QEF solution on the dominant plane only, which stays on one input surface), then onto a last resort (the center of a fine cell with one patch, where polygons between such cells become non-intersecting squares between cell centers; else halfway between the patch's crossing centroid and the cell center, or in a coarse cell the crossing centroid).

member.name: T:g3.TubeGenerator
member.summary:
Sweep a 2D Profile Polygon along a 3D Path. Supports closed and open paths, and capping open paths. However caps are triangulated using a fan around a center vertex (which you can set using CapCenter). If Polygon is non-convex, this will have foldovers. In that case, you have to triangulate and append it yourself.
If your profile curve does not contain the polygon bbox center, set OverrideCapCenter=true and set CapCenter to a suitable center point.
The output normals are currently set to those for a circular profile. Call MeshNormals.QuickCompute() on the output DMesh to estimate proper vertex normals

member.name: T:g3.MarchingCubes.RootfindingModes
member.summary: How vertex positions are found along cell edges: one linear interpolation, repeated interpolation, bisection, or LinearEdges: one linear interpolation of the original corner samples, without the endpoint nudges and with no skipped triangle. LinearEdges requires finite samples and edge coordinates, no sample exactly at IsoValue and crossings strictly inside their edges (a sample that differs from IsoValue by a tiny amount can still round a crossing onto a corner); it never repairs a violation: Generate() then throws InvalidOperationException (a crossing on a grid corner, a collapsed triangle, or as a guard a rejected one) or ArgumentException (non-finite values), also from the parallel path (InvalidOperationException preferred if several cells fail), and the partial mesh must not be used. MarchingCubesPro additionally needs a finite positive CubeSize and at most 65535 cells per axis for Generate(), 65534 for GenerateContinuation() (its 16-bit grid hash), whose seeds must lie in the grid (cell indices 0 to n), and otherwise throws ArgumentException before any work. The mode alone certifies nothing about an arbitrary field: the conditional enclosure recipe and its further preconditions are in docs/design/CONSERVATIVE_MC_AUDIT.md.

member.summary: Generate a mesh of a sphere by first generating a mesh of a cube, and then normalizing the vertices and moving them to sphere of desired radius. The sphere is centered at Box.Center (the origin by default); EdgeVertices (inherited, default 8) sets the resolution, giving 12*(EdgeVertices-1)^2 triangles. All vertices lie exactly on the sphere, so the mesh is slightly smaller than the true sphere (volume and area converge to 4/3 pi r^3 and 4 pi r^2 from below). With the default NoSharedVertices = false the mesh is closed, with outward normals and genus 0. Example: DMesh3 m = new Sphere3Generator_NormalizedCube() { Radius = 1, EdgeVertices = 20 }.Generate().MakeDMesh();

member.name: T:g3.ExactMeshArrangement
member.summary:
Exact arrangement of the triangles of several meshes: every triangle is split along its intersections with the triangles of the other meshes, so that the pieces only meet along shared edges and vertices.
All input coordinates are converted exactly to one integer grid (a double is m * 2^e). New points are implicit: an edge crossing a triangle plane, two coplanar edges crossing, or three planes (the triangle planes, and for each triangle edge the plane through the edge perpendicular to the triangle). A point is stored as its construction with a double approximation and a bound on its error; the predicates decide from the approximations when the bounds allow it, and compute the point as a canonical rational (ExactPoint3) only when they do not. The same construction gives the same point id; coincident points from different constructions are merged afterwards (merge_points), so equal points have one id. Each split triangle is retriangulated with an exact constrained Delaunay triangulation in a coordinate projection. A point on an edge is always also computed by the triangles on the other side of the edge (it is the end of their intersection with the same triangle), so the pieces stay connected.
Intersections between triangles of the same mesh are computed if SelfIntersections is set; then also T-junctions (a vertex on the edge of a neighbour, closed by a degenerate triangle) are split, since the triangles touch along a segment. Degenerate (zero-area) triangles are not part of the output.
Sources (implemented from the papers, no code taken over; see docs/SOURCES.md): Zhou, Grinspun, Zorin, Jacobson, "Mesh Arrangements for Solid Geometry", 2016 (exact arrangement); Attene, "Indirect Predicates for Geometric Constructions", 2020, and Cherchi, Livesu, Scateni, Attene, "Fast and Robust Mesh Arrangements using Floating-point Arithmetic", 2020 (implicit points with filters); Shewchuk, "Adaptive Precision Floating-Point Arithmetic and Fast Robust Geometric Predicates", 1997 (error bounds); Sloan, "A fast algorithm for generating constrained Delaunay triangulations", 1993.

member.name: T:g3.TriangleBoxTree
member.summary: Bounding volume hierarchy of boxes with closed overlap tests and no padding, so that it never misses a pair of touching boxes (for exact computations). Above MedianSplitBelow boxes they are sorted once along a Morton curve of their centres (as Geogram's MeshFacetsAABB, Lévy; Lauterbach et al. 2009; the coordinates as ranks where one far box would squeeze the others into a few cells) and every range splits where the highest differing bit of its codes changes (Karras 2012); smaller trees keep the median split on the longest axis. On Thingi10K this gives tighter nodes than the median split on the longest axis used before (docs/perf/EXACT_BOOLEAN_PERFORMANCE.md). The order only steers which boxes share a node: the boxes a query finds, and the pairs, are the same.

member.name: T:g3.ExactMeshBoolean
member.summary:
Boolean operations (union, intersection, difference) of two triangle meshes, with exact arithmetic: the intersection curves, the retriangulation and the inside/outside decisions are computed exactly (ExactMeshArrangement), so touching, coplanar and nearly degenerate configurations give a closed result, at any scale. Only the output vertex coordinates are rounded to double.
The solid of a mesh is where its winding number is positive (Zhou et al., "Mesh Arrangements for Solid Geometry", 2016), so self-intersecting meshes, nested and overlapping shells and duplicated faces are handled. The triangles of both meshes are split along all intersections, also of a mesh with itself. For each patch of pieces between intersection curves, the winding numbers of both meshes on its front side are counted exactly along a ray (signed crossings); the back side differs by the orientations of the triangles at the patch. A piece is part of the result if the operation is true on one side and false on the other, oriented towards the false side. Pieces where several triangles coincide are output once.
The winding numbers are exact for meshes that are closed in the winding number sense (every edge used equally often in both directions; non-manifold edges and self-intersections are allowed). For other (open) meshes the generalized winding number is used (Jacobson et al. 2013, fast approximation), with the solid where it is above 0.5; then the result is generally not closed, also along edges where an open boundary of an input meets other pieces and the kept pieces run the edge the same way (ConflictEdges). An inside-out mesh (winding number -1) has an empty solid. A mesh with inconsistently oriented triangles (flipped faces) is first oriented consistently per component (triangles connected across edges with two triangles, by vertex position), keeping the orientation of the larger part by area (ReorientedTriangles); components that cannot be oriented are left as they are. Where solids touch along an edge, the result is non-manifold there when welded by position, by design (as in Manifold): the triangles at such an edge are split into manifold pairs with copies of its vertices (NonManifoldEdges); Contacts counts the positions with two or more vertices, so that a caller that welds (eg writes STL) knows. Two different exact points that round to one double would be such a contact as well, one the exact solid does not have: SafeRounding separates them (see MeshRoundingRepair.InitialFalseContacts) and RoundingClean requires that none is left. Degenerate (zero-area) input triangles are dropped. The rounding of new vertices can create tiny self-intersections, and intersection points that nearly coincide give degenerate slivers: SafeRounding repairs both after the rounding (MeshRoundingRepair, verified with exact predicates on the doubles), ComputeExactVertices gives the exact rational coordinates of the vertices instead. New vertices that lie exactly inside a flat region of the result or on a straight edge between two flat regions (eg the crossings of the edges of overlapping coplanar faces) are removed and the regions retriangulated (SimplifyFlatRegions, ExactPlanarSimplify), so that repeated booleans do not split the faces again and again at rounded points.
Usage: construct with the two meshes and the operation, call Compute(), and read Result (a new mesh; the inputs are not modified). Compute() returns false and sets Error for null inputs, non-finite coordinates, open meshes when AllowOpenMeshes is false, or a result that is not clean with StrictRounding; it throws InvalidOperationException in the (not expected) case that no non-degenerate ray is found. Result has no normals, colors, UVs or groups. Compute() can be called again after changing the meshes or the operation.
Cost: exact predicates behind floating-point filters (BigInteger only where the filters cannot decide); slower than floating-point methods, the phases run in parallel. Prefer this class over (floating-point, not robust, union of closed meshes only). Use instead when a remeshed, volumetric result is acceptable and very broken input (triangle soups) must give a closed mesh.
Implemented from the papers cited here and in ExactMeshArrangement, no code taken over (docs/SOURCES.md).

member.name: F:g3.ExactMeshBoolean.WindingPredicate
member.summary: if set, decides instead of Operation where the result's solid is (Zhou et al. 2016): called with the winding numbers of all input meshes at a point (entry i for mesh i, in the order of Meshes, or A, B), returns true for inside. The winding numbers are exact integers for closed meshes; for open meshes the generalized winding number w is rounded to ceil(w - 1/2) (so w > 1/2 is at least 1). Called on both sides of every patch, from one thread; the array is reused and must not be modified or kept. A point far from all meshes has all winding numbers 0, so a predicate that is true there gives an unbounded solid and no closed result. Examples: AtLeast(k), (w) => (w[0] > 0) != (w[1] > 0) (symmetric difference).

member.name: F:g3.ExactMeshBoolean.SafeRounding
member.summary: after rounding the vertices to double, repair the self-intersections and degenerate triangles (area below 1e-12 of the squared diagonal; the diagonal of the result's largest connected component, here and below) the rounding left, by local edits checked with exact predicates on the doubles (MeshRoundingRepair: contractions of short edges, flips, tiny vertex moves, removal of closed components that keep a sliver and are tiny or thinner than RoundingMaxDisplacement (1e-5) of the diagonal, counted in Rounding.RemovedComponents; a thin one that holds real volume for its area is kept and counted in Rounding.ScaleDisparity, not clean). Input vertices are kept where possible, and sheets that touch at duplicated vertices still touch, at the same points; vertices of different exact points that rounded to one double (a contact the rounding made, not one of the exact solid) are moved apart by a few units in the last place where that adds no defect (Rounding.InitialFalseContacts, RemainingFalseContacts; Contacts counts the positions with several vertices left). Not every case can be repaired: Compute() still succeeds (Status Success) if defects remain (unless StrictRounding); RoundingClean tells whether the result is verified free of both, Rounding has the counts. On by default (since October 2026; before, off): on the Thingi10K benchmark it makes about 1.6 times as many results clean, for about 1.2 to 1.9 times the time of the boolean (benchmarks/MeshRepairBenchmark README). Off, the new vertices are only rounded to the nearest double.

member.name: M:g3.ExactMeshBoolean.orient3d_filter(g3.Vector3d@,g3.Vector3d@,g3.Vector3d@,g3.Vector3d@)

member.name: M:g3.ExactMeshBoolean.orient3d_filtered(g3.Vector3d@,g3.Vector3d@,g3.Vector3d@,g3.Vector3d@)
member.summary: sign of the homogeneous 4x4 determinant of orient3d for points given approximately by doubles (relative error at most 2^-52 per coordinate, positive weights), or 2 if the error bound does not decide (also for coordinates below TinyCoordinate, NaN or infinite ones). det4 [a 1; b 1; c 1; d 1] = -det3 [b-a; c-a; d-a]; the rows u, v, w of the 3x3 determinant are computed with absolute errors eu, ev, ew (inputs and subtraction), which change the determinant by at most (|u|+eu)(|v|+ev)(|w|+ew) - |u||v||w| (expanding it multilinearly, Hadamard's inequality for each term); the evaluation adds at most 1e-15 times the permanent (Shewchuk's orient3d bound).

member.name: M:g3.ExactMeshBoolean.assemble(System.Boolean[],System.Boolean[])

member.name: T:g3.ExactPlanarSimplify
member.summary:
Removes the vertices of a boolean result that the shape does not need: new points (not input vertices) that lie inside a flat region, or on a straight edge between two flat regions, and retriangulates the region around each one. Such points come from the arrangement splitting coplanar overlapping triangles along each other's edges and diagonals (for example the faces of overlapping boxes); rounded to double, they lie slightly off the faces and edges, and repeated booleans split at them again and again.
All decisions are exact: the triangles of a region lie in the same plane (their source triangles have the same plane, compared as normalized integer planes) with the same orientation, and the retriangulation uses the arrangement's exact orientation and incircle predicates in the plane's coordinate projection. A point is removed only if its triangles form one closed fan whose edges are all used by exactly two triangles, and either all of them are in one region, or exactly two of its edges separate two regions of different planes (then both edges lie on the line where the planes meet, on opposite sides of the point). The hole (a star-shaped polygon) is triangulated by ear clipping, then edges inside regions are flipped towards the Delaunay triangulation of the projection (Lawson), for better shaped triangles. The surface covers the same set, so it stays closed and keeps its exact volume; the remaining vertices keep their exact coordinates.
Whether a point can be removed does not depend on the other removals (a removal keeps the regions and the lines between them), and the points are removed in a deterministic order (ComparePoints).

Points are inserted into the triangle that contains them, constraint segments by edge flips (Sloan 1993), then non-constrained edges are flipped to Delaunay (Lawson). Points must be distinct, inside the closed outer triangle, and constraint segments must not cross each other or pass through points (split them first).

member.name: T:g3.LaplacianMeshSmoother
member.summary:
Global Laplacian smoothing by a sparse least-squares solve: finds vertex positions x that minimize |L x|^2 + sum over constrained vertices of (w_i |x_i - p_i|)^2, where L is a (uniform-like) graph Laplacian of the mesh and p_i, w_i are soft constraints set with SetConstraint(). The target Laplacian is zero, so unconstrained regions become as smooth (flat/minimal) as the constraints allow; the weights control how strongly vertices are held. Without any constraints the problem is singular and the result degenerates, so always constrain some vertices (eg the boundary, or all vertices with a small weight to their current position for mild smoothing).
Solve() writes the result to an array; SolveAndUpdateMesh() writes it to the mesh in place. Both return false if the conjugate-gradient solve does not converge (the mesh is then not changed). Initialize() (called automatically by the first solve) captures the mesh topology and positions, so do not change the mesh topology afterwards. RegionSmooth() smooths a set of triangles with a fixed border. For simple local smoothing with a fixed number of steps see .

member.summary: Solve the normal equations (L^T L + W^2) x = W^2 p of the least-squares problem (default). Appendix C from http://sites.fas.harvard.edu/~cs277/papers/deformation_survey.pdf . Must be set before Initialize().

member.summary: Apply LaplacianMeshSmoother to subset of mesh triangles. border of subset always has soft constraint with borderWeight, but is then snapped back to original vtx pos after solve. nConstrainLoops inner loops are also soft-constrained, with weight falloff via square roots (defines continuity) interiorWeight is soft constraint added to all vertices. nIncludeExteriorRings expands the region by that many one-rings first; if bPreserveExteriorRings, the added vertices are snapped back to their original positions after the solve. The mesh is modified in place (only the region's vertex positions).

member.name: T:g3.MeshBoolean
member.summary:
Experimental floating-point union of two closed meshes: each mesh is cut along its intersection with the other (), the triangles inside the other mesh (winding number above 0.9 at the triangle centroid) are removed, and the two remaining parts are appended into Result.
Only union is supported (there is no operation setting). The parts are not welded: Result has open boundaries along the intersection curve, with duplicate vertices on both sides (missing cut vertices are inserted by edge splits within VertexSnapTol, so they can be merged afterwards, for example with MergeCoincidentEdges). Not robust for coplanar or touching faces. Both inputs must be closed: this is checked with Util.gDevAssert, which throws (or breaks into the debugger) otherwise. Compute() always returns true; the inputs are not modified (copies are cut).
Not robust across scales: VertexSnapTol (and the MergeCoincidentEdges tolerance, twice that) is an absolute 1e-5, so at millimetre scale it throws ("unsortable vertex") and at UTM coordinates it can hang or give a different result (docs/ROBUSTNESS_SWEEP.md R6). Scale VertexSnapTol to the model if you use it. Prefer (exact, robust, all operations, closed result), or for a volumetric result from broken input.

member.name: T:g3.MeshExtrudeMesh
member.summary:
Extrude all faces of a mesh, and stitch together any boundary loops. Steps are: 1) make a copy of all triangles in mesh 2) offset copy vertices 3) connect up loops with triangle strips
Works in place on Mesh: the original triangles are kept (reversed for a positive offset) and the offset copy and stitch strips are appended, so an open surface becomes a closed shell (a closed mesh just gets a second, offset copy). The default ExtrudedPositionF moves each vertex by its vertex normal (computed if the mesh has none), ie an offset of 1; set it for another distance. Extrude() returns false if a boundary loop could not be stitched (the mesh then has a hole there).

member.name: T:g3.MeshIterativeSmooth
member.summary: Explicit iterative Laplacian smoothing of a set of vertices, in place: in each of Rounds rounds every listed vertex moves the fraction Alpha towards its smoothed position (one-ring centroid for Uniform, or cotangent / mean-value weighted), computed from the positions of the previous round (Jacobi style, so the result does not depend on the order or the threads). Each round shrinks the surface a little (no volume preservation); ProjectF can project the smoothed positions back onto a surface. Smooth() always returns true. For a global solve with soft constraints see .

member.name: T:g3.MeshMeshCut
member.summary:
Cuts the curves where CutMesh intersects Target into Target, in place (floating-point): Compute() splits the triangles of Target so that the intersection curves run along its edges. CutMesh is not modified. Afterwards RemoveContained() deletes the triangles of Target that are inside CutMesh (winding number above 0.9 at the centroid), which leaves Target open along the cut.
Intersection points within VertexSnapTol are merged with existing vertices. Not robust: segments that cannot be inserted are counted in FailedSegmentInsertions (the cut then has gaps), and only intersection segments are used, so coplanar overlaps (intersection polygons) are not handled. Used by ; for robust booleans use . VertexSnapTol is an absolute 1e-5: scale it to the model (millimetre models and UTM coordinates fail with the default, docs/ROBUSTNESS_SWEEP.md R6).

member.name: T:g3.MeshPlaneCut
member.summary:
Cut the Mesh with the Plane, in place. The *positive* side, ie (p-o).n > 0, is removed. If possible, Cut() returns the boundary loop(s) along the cut in CutLoops, and open boundary pieces in CutSpans (this happens if the cut intersects holes in the mesh; FoundOpenSpans is set). Also FillHoles() for a topological fill of the closed loops. Or use CutLoops and fill yourself.
Cut() returns true (it throws if an edge split fails); check CutLoopsFailed for the loop extraction. Vertices within 16 * MathUtil.Epsilon times the largest coordinate (of the mesh bounds and the plane origin) of the plane count as on the plane, ie within the rounding of (p-o).n (use a unit-length normal). Crossing edges are split at the exact plane intersection. Use MeshPlaneCut to trim a mesh or open it along a plane; to cut a mesh with another mesh see and .
Algorithm is: 1) find all edge crossings 2) Do edge splits at crossings 3) delete all vertices on positive side 4) (optionally) collapse any degenerate boundary edges 5) find loops through valid boundary edges (ie connected to splits, or on-plane edges)
[TODO] could run into trouble w/ on-plane degenerate triangles. Should optionally discard any triangles with all vertex distances < epsilon. But this complicates boundary edge tracking...

member.name: T:g3.MeshRoundingRepair
member.summary:
Repairs what rounding exact vertex coordinates to double leaves behind (eg the output of ExactMeshBoolean, whose intersection points are rational): self-intersections, and degenerate triangles (needles and caps where intersection points nearly coincide), by local edits whose result is checked with exact predicates on the doubles. Only edits that create neither a new intersection nor a new degenerate triangle in their neighbourhood and remove at least one are applied, so the counts never grow and the repair terminates.
The edits follow the modification stage of Milenkovic and Sacks ("Geometric rounding and feature separation in meshes", CAD 2019), applied after rounding: contract a short edge (length at most MaxDisplacement times the diagonal; the kept vertex at one of the two ends, which keeps the coordinates as they are, or at the midpoint), flip an edge (caps), and, beyond the paper, move a single vertex by a tiny amount (along the normal of the triangle it intersects or away from the base of a cap), which separates intersections that no contraction can (sheets that come within a rounding unit of each other), and zip two caps on both sides of an edge whose apexes lie on it (a flip would give two caps again: both are removed and the neighbouring edges along the segment split at the apexes), and, generalizing the zip, zip a strip: degenerate triangles and slivers connected across edges along a line (eg fans of nearly collinear points in degenerate input, where every flip gives slivers again), a disk whose boundary runs strictly monotone along the segment between its two farthest boundary vertices on both sides and all of whose vertices, the inner ones too, lie between them along it, is removed, and the triangles outside it along both sides (distinct, their third corners outside the strip) are split at the vertices of the other side, so that both share one chain (StripZips). Where the coordinates are coarse (far from the origin compared to the mesh's size, see UlpFactor), a vertex of valence 3 that the rounding put onto the position of another vertex is removed, its three triangles replaced by the one of its neighbours (VertexRemovals), and FixedVertexF is not used if FixedWhereCoarse is false (the fixed vertices carry rounding errors of the size of the bound there themselves). The contractions keep the mesh manifold (link condition, DMesh3.CollapseEdge). Edits at the boundary of open meshes stay on the boundary curve: a boundary vertex keeps its coordinates in a contraction and is removed only by contracting a boundary edge into its other end (an interior edge between two boundary vertices, which would pinch the mesh, is not contracted; an interior vertex may be contracted into a boundary vertex), and it moves only along one of its boundary edges of the input whose other end has not moved (not past that end, and over several moves towards the same end); flips and zips do not change boundary edges. So the boundary keeps its loops, every boundary vertex left stays where it was or on the input curve, and the curve moves by at most the length of a contracted edge or a move. Bowtie vertices on the boundary are not edited. No triangle may turn over in an edit (a fold, which is not an intersection), except slivers (below 100 times the degenerate area) and triangles not higher than twice the distance a vertex moves (a move cannot turn over a triangle higher than the move, so the rule matters for flips and zips: tiny triangles may turn over, they are only checked for intersections and degeneracy). Closed components that keep a degenerate triangle or were edited, and are tiny (below 1e4 times the degenerate area, eg a flat tetrahedron between intersection points that nearly coincide) or thinner than MaxDisplacement times the diagonal (eg the slivers that are the difference of two nearly coincident solids), are removed if RemoveTinyComponents, as Milenkovic and Sacks do. Open components are kept (they may close the rest of the mesh by position), so an isolated sliver that no edit can repair is left and counted in RemainingDegenerate.
The degenerate test is the one of MeshRobustRepair.NotCleanReason (area below DegenerateArea times the squared diagonal, or exactly collinear corners); intersections are those of MeshRepairMetrics.SelfIntersections (exact, also between neighbours that overlap). With SharedPositionsTouch, vertices at the same position count as shared, so that sheets which touch at duplicated vertices (ExactMeshBoolean splits where solids touch) do not count as intersecting there; then no edit moves a vertex onto a position where other vertices are (which would make a new, uncounted contact), and a contraction keeps the contact points as they are (the kept vertex at its own position). Where the caller knows the exact point of each vertex (ExactMeshBoolean), vertices of different exact points that the rounding put at one position are not a contact of the solid but a defect: after the passes, the vertices of the other points are moved off the position, one at a time (towards its neighbours or along its normal, a few units in the last place first), checked like every edit, so that they then meet the other sheet nowhere; the point with the most vertices there stays, and a point with several vertices there is not moved apart, so a contact of one exact point is kept (InitialFalseContacts, RemainingFalseContacts; IsClean requires none left).
Usage: construct with the mesh (modified in place), optionally set FixedVertexF to the vertices whose position should be kept where possible (eg input vertices), call Apply(). Apply() returns IsClean: RemainingDegenerate is counted again at the end, RemainingIntersections too if there were any (no edit adds one: each is checked exactly against all triangles near it), so a clean result is free of self-intersections and degenerate triangles (Milenkovic and Sacks get the same guarantee by separating the features before rounding; this works on the rounded mesh and has no guarantee that every case can be repaired).
Bounded displacement: every vertex has a drift, 0 at the start; it is a charge, not a bound on how far that vertex itself moved (an edit charges its apex, which need not be a vertex it moves). An edit gives its apex, a vertex of every triangle it adds (all vertices of the triangles it removes and adds if it has none: zips, strip zips of longer loops, ear contractions; docs/design/ROUNDING_DRIFT_APEX.md), the largest drift among the vertices of the triangles it removes and adds plus a bound on how far it moves the surface: the distance a vertex moves (moves, slides, contractions: the kept vertex's new position from both ends), for a flip the smallest of twice the distance between the flipped edge and the new one, a bound from the distances of the corners to the other side's triangles (each bounded by the distance to the nearest edge), and 0 for a convex quad in one plane (exact), for a zip twice the distance of the apexes to the edge, for a vertex removal the distance of the vertex to the new triangle (with the vertex moved to its nearest point there, its three triangles tile the new one), for a strip zip twice the largest distance of the strip's vertices to the line through its ends (with them moved onto it, in their order along it, the old and the new triangles cover the same set). An edit after which a drift would exceed maxLength (MaxDisplacement times the diagonal, or the ulp or the absolute term, see UlpFactor) is not applied. By induction over the edits, every point of a triangle lies within the largest drift of its vertices of the surface at the start, and every point of that surface within it of the repaired one (every added triangle has a vertex with the edit's drift): each edit moves every point of the triangles it removes to within its bound of the triangles it adds or of a simplex spanned by their vertices, and back (a contraction of an ear, whose vertex has a single triangle, adds none: that triangle goes to the edge across, which is in an untouched triangle with both ends among the edit's vertices). Edits stay within one connected component. So the Hausdorff distance between the repaired surface and the surface at the start (the rounded mesh), both without the components removed as tiny or thin, is at most MaxDrift <= maxLength, up to the rounding of the distance computations: an absolute error of a few units in the last place of the largest coordinate per edit, negligible against maxLength unless the mesh lies far from the origin compared to its size. The volume of a closed solid changes in a move or a contraction by at most the edit's bound times the area of the triangles it removes (the change is a third of the move times the area vector of the link); flips and zips change it by the volume between the old and the new triangles (a tetrahedron for a flip), measured at most a third of the same product (strip zips at most 0.18 of it, over 9039 strip zips of poked-sphere clusters with w >= 1e-13, at most 0.07 with the offsets in the surface). Removed components add their volume (thin ones: below maxLength times half their area; tiny ones: area below 1e4 times the degenerate area). Cost: one global exact self-intersection check (two or more if there are intersections), plus local work per defect. Implemented from the paper, no code taken over (docs/SOURCES.md).

member.name: T:g3.PlanarHoleFiller
member.summary:
Try to fill planar holes in a mesh. The fill is computed by mapping the hole boundary into 2D, filling using 2D algorithms, and then mapping back to 3D. This allows us to properly handle cases like nested holes (eg from slicing a torus in half).
PlanarComplex is used to sort the input 2D polyons.
MeshInsertUVPolyCurve is used to insert each 2D polygon into a generated planar mesh. The resolution of the generated mesh is controlled by .FillTargetEdgeLen
In theory this approach can handle more geometric degeneracies than Delaunay triangluation. However, the current code requires that MeshInsertUVPolyCurve produce output boundary loops that have a 1-1 correspondence with the input polygons. This is not always possible.
Currently these failure cases are not handled properly. In that case the loops will not be stitched.
Usage: construct, AddFillLoop(s), SetPlane, Fill() (or construct from a MeshPlaneCut, which sets loops and plane). The loop vertices must lie in the plane (within about 1e-6, the merge tolerance), otherwise the fill cannot be merged and cracks remain. The fill is appended to the mesh in place, as a new triangle group, even when Fill() returns false.

member.name: T:g3.MeshBoundaryLoops
member.summary:
Extract the boundary EdgeLoops (holes) of a mesh; the constructor computes them by default. Enumerate the object, or use Loops / Count / this[i]. Each loop is a simple cycle (bowtie vertices split walks into simple loops) oriented along the boundary orientation (as required by the hole fillers), or along the majority of its edges if the triangles around it are inconsistently oriented (see IsConsistentlyOriented, SawInconsistentOrientation). A closed mesh has no loops.
Can also extract EdgeSpans for open (unclosed) boundary chains, which come mainly from EdgeFilterF but can also happen on meshes with bad bowties. By default (SpanBehavior = Compute, FailureBehavior = ConvertToOpenSpan) they are collected in Spans and SawOpenSpans is set; no exception is thrown unless a ThrowException behavior is selected. The mesh is not modified.

member.name: T:g3.ARAPParameterization
member.summary:
As-rigid-as-possible parameterization with the local/global method of Liu, Zhang, Xu, Gotsman and Gortler (2008): minimizes Sum_T A_T |J_T - R_T|^2 over the UVs and a rotation R_T per triangle, so that lengths and angles are preserved as well as possible (natural scale, free boundary). The local step takes the rotation closest to each Jacobian, the global step solves a cotan Laplacian system, whose factorization is computed once. Triangles that are degenerate on the surface take part with mollified cotangents.
Starts from LSCM (or InitialUV). Works on any connected mesh with a boundary. Does not guarantee a flip-free result (use SLIM for that): a map with flipped, zero-area or degenerate UV triangles is reported as ParameterizationStatus.FlippedTriangles, not as a success.

member.name: F:g3.ARAPParameterization.ConvergenceTolerance
member.summary: stop when the energy decreases by less than this fraction in an iteration

member.name: F:g3.ARAPParameterization.InitialUV
member.summary: optional initial UVs by vertex id (default: LSCM, scaled to the surface area)

member.name: M:g3.ARAPParameterization.Energy(g3.ParamMesh,System.Double[],g3.Vector2d[],System.Double[],System.Double[],System.Double[])
member.summary: ARAP energy per unit area, Sum_T A_T |J_T - R_T|^2 / A, with R_T the closest rotations (stored in angle): the rotation that best maps the 2D edges e onto the UV edges (for a non-degenerate triangle the one closest to J_T, since Sum_k w e e^T = A I). The mollified degenerate triangles are stiff, so their terms stay negligible (about 1e-6 of the energy on a curved T-junction).

member.name: T:g3.BoundaryFirstFlattening
member.summary:
Boundary First Flattening (Sawhney and Crane 2017): a conformal flattening of a disc that is fully controlled by the boundary. Either the scale factors u (log of the length change) or the exterior angles (geodesic curvature) along the boundary are prescribed; the other one follows from a Dirichlet-to-Neumann (or Neumann-to-Dirichlet) map of the cotan Laplacian (discrete Yamabe equation, flat interior). The boundary curve is then integrated from its target lengths and angles, closed with a minimal change of the lengths, and extended into the interior as a holomorphic function (harmonic x coordinate and its harmonic conjugate) or harmonically (exact boundary).
Boundary modes: MinimalAreaDistortion (u = 0 on the boundary: lengths preserved, the conformal map with least area distortion), Disk (the boundary becomes a circle), TargetScaleFactors and TargetAngles (eg exterior angles of pi/2 at four corners give a rectangle). Only linear solves with two factorized Laplacians, so it is fast. Flips are possible near very sharp target corners.

member.name: F:g3.BoundaryFirstFlattening.ExtensionModes.Conformal
member.summary: harmonic x and its harmonic conjugate y: conformal, boundary close to the target curve

member.name: F:g3.BoundaryFirstFlattening.ExtensionModes.Harmonic
member.summary: both coordinates harmonic: boundary exactly the target curve, slightly less conformal

member.name: F:g3.BoundaryFirstFlattening.TargetScaleFactors
member.summary: TargetScaleFactors: log scale factor by boundary vertex id (missing vertices: 0; interior vertices are ignored, so a per-vertex field can be passed)

member.name: F:g3.BoundaryFirstFlattening.TargetAngles
member.summary: TargetAngles: exterior (turning) angle in radians by boundary vertex id (missing vertices: 0); the angles must sum to 2 pi

member.name: F:g3.BoundaryFirstFlattening.ScaleToSurfaceArea
member.summary: scale the result so that the UV area equals the surface area

member.name: F:g3.BoundaryFirstFlattening.BoundaryScaleFactors
member.summary: target scale factors u per boundary vertex id after Compute()

member.name: T:g3.ConeFlattening
member.summary:
Boundary First Flattening with cone singularities (Sawhney and Crane 2017, cones): a conformal flattening of a closed surface (or of a surface with boundary) in which the curvature is concentrated at a few cone vertices, so that the rest becomes flat with little area distortion.
1. Cones: given (Cones), or placed greedily (Ben-Chen, Gotsman and Bunin 2008; Springborn, Schröder and Pinkall 2008): solve the discrete Yamabe equation C u = -K for the log scale factors u with u = 0 at the cones and on the boundary (C the cotan Laplacian, K the angle defects), and make the vertex of largest |u| a cone, until max |u| <= MaxScaleFactor or MaxCones. On a closed surface the first cone is where the scale factor of the uniform curvature flow is largest. The curvature that each cone gets is ConeCurvature = K + C u at the cone; all other interior vertices become flat. 2. Cut through the cones into a disc (MeshDiscCut with the cones as required vertices). 3. BFF of the cut disc with the scale factors u prescribed on its boundary (Dirichlet-to-Neumann map): both sides of each seam get the same lengths, and the angles around cut vertices sum to 2 pi except at the cones, so the seams match up to a rigid motion.
Cone sets that can not be flattened fail with InvalidConstraints: a cone that would get a curvature of 2 pi or more (no angle left, eg MaxCones = 1 on a sphere), or a closed surface of Euler characteristic other than 0 without cones. Degenerate triangles count with their angles (a cap adds about pi), so slivers do not attract cones.
On a cube, the eight corners become cones and the faces are unfolded without distortion. The result is conformal and flip-free in practice, but not guaranteed to be globally injective (check with UVOverlap; the parts can overlap for long, winding seams).

member.name: T:g3.FoldoverFreeParameterization
member.summary: Fixed-boundary untangling from Garanzha et al. (2021), sections 2.2-2.3 and 4.1. A serial modified-Newton solver; convergence within the iteration budget is not guaranteed. Success certifies finite, nondegenerate, positively oriented triangles, not global injectivity. Input mesh and UVs are not modified. All boundary vertices retain their original double values. Energy is the normalized shape/area objective at InitialEpsilon; a retained earlier best map is not marked Converged. Unrepresentable output distortion is a solver failure even if normalization succeeded.

member.name: T:g3.LSCMParameterization
member.summary:
Least squares conformal map (Lévy, Petitjean, Ray, Maillot 2002), equivalently discrete conformal parameterization (Desbrun, Meyer, Alliez 2002): minimizes the conformal energy E_C = E_Dirichlet - A(uv), which is zero exactly for conformal maps, with a free boundary. A(uv) is the signed UV area, written as a sum over the boundary edges. Triangles that are degenerate on the surface get the cotan weights of their intrinsically mollified lengths.
Works on any connected mesh with at least one boundary loop (discs, annuli, ...). Two (or more) pinned vertices fix the similarity transform; by default two boundary vertices far apart are pinned, and the result is scaled to the surface area. On a surface that is not developable the map depends on which vertices are pinned (beyond a similarity), so a mirror-symmetric input gives a mirror-symmetric map only with pins at a mirrored pair (set PinnedVertices; the automatic pair need not be one, eg when two mirrored pairs are equally far apart). Triangles can flip on strongly curved inputs (and on annuli the free inner boundary can collapse): such a map is reported as ParameterizationStatus.FlippedTriangles, not as a success; use SLIM for a guaranteed flip-free map.

member.name: F:g3.LSCMParameterization.PinnedVertices
member.summary: fixed UV positions by vertex id (at least two). Null: pin two boundary vertices far apart.

member.name: F:g3.LSCMParameterization.ScaleToSurfaceArea
member.summary: with automatic pins, scale the result so that the UV area equals the surface area

member.name: T:g3.MeshChartSegmentation
member.summary:
Segments a mesh into charts: connected regions of triangles with similar normals, for a texture atlas.
Region growing in the style of variational shape approximation (Cohen-Steiner, Alliez and Desbrun 2004, L2,1 metric) with the compactness term of D-Charts (Julius, Kraevoy and Sheffer 2005): each chart has a proxy (normal N, centroid C); the charts are grown from seed triangles in order of the cost area * (|n - N|^2 + Compactness * |c - C|^2 / D^2) (D the bounding box diagonal of the region), then proxies and seeds are updated (Lloyd iterations). While a triangle deviates from its chart's normal by more than MaxNormalAngle degrees and there are fewer than MaxCharts charts, a chart is seeded at the worst triangle (the farthest point heuristic) and the charts are regrown. Every chart is connected (grown through edges). Triangles of less than 5% of the mean area are ignored in the deviation (the normals of slivers are noise). Charts are not guaranteed to be discs; MeshDiscCut cuts them if needed.

member.summary: largest angle in degrees between a triangle normal and the normal of its chart

member.name: F:g3.MeshChartSegmentation.Compactness
member.summary: weight of the distance to the chart centroid in the growing cost (compact, round charts)

member.summary: chart index by triangle id (-1 for unused ids) after Compute()

member.name: T:g3.MeshDiscCut
member.summary:
Cuts a mesh into topological discs (one per connected component) along seams, so that it can be parameterized: closed surfaces of any genus, surfaces with several boundary loops, bowtie vertices.
The cut graph is computed by tree-cotree decomposition (Eppstein 2003) with a shortest path tree from a root vertex and a maximum spanning dual tree weighted by the length of the loop through each edge (Erickson and Whittlesey 2005): on a closed surface the seams are then the greedy shortest system of 2g loops through the root, along edges. Edges of the primal tree may be used in the dual tree where the boundary requires it (paths between boundary loops), and the dangling branches of the cut are removed again, so the seams end on the boundary or at RequiredVertices (eg cone singularities). Closed surfaces of genus 0 are cut along a shortest path from the root to the farthest vertex (or between the required vertices). With FeatureWeight > 0 the seams prefer sharp edges, where they are less visible. Edge costs are edge lengths, so seams follow edge-path geodesics.
The cut is done in a new mesh, CutMesh: vertices on the seams are split into one copy per side (wedge), CutToInputVertex / CutToInputTriangle map back to the input. The input is not changed.

member.name: T:g3.TutteEmbedding
member.summary: Tutte embedding (Tutte 1963; Floater 1997, 2003): the boundary is mapped to a circle by arc length and every interior vertex to the average of its neighbours. For a disc, the map is guaranteed to be a bijection without flipped triangles (the boundary is strictly convex and the weights positive), but it distorts a lot; it is the initialization of SLIM.

member.name: F:g3.TutteEmbedding.ScaleToSurfaceArea
member.summary: scale the result so that the UV area equals the surface area (else the unit circle)

member.name: T:g3.SLIMParameterization
member.summary:
Scalable locally injective mappings (Rabinovich, Poranne, Panozzo, Sorkine-Hornung 2017): minimizes the symmetric Dirichlet energy Sum_T A_T (|J|^2 + |J^-1|^2), which goes to infinity when a triangle degenerates, starting from a flip-free map (LSCM if it is injective, else the Tutte embedding; see StartMap). Each iteration solves a reweighted ARAP-like proxy (with weights W_T from the singular values of J_T) and does a line search whose step is limited so that no triangle flips (Smith and Schaefer 2015).
The proxy step is -H^-1 grad E, with H the proxy matrix (its gradient at the current UVs is the energy gradient). With ReuseFactorization, the factorization of H is kept for further iterations (a lagged Hessian) while each step lowers the energy at least at the average rate since the factorization was made, counting the factorization as 8 steps; this saves most factorizations. Converged means the proxy predicts a decrease below ConvergenceTolerance (the Newton decrement, on a new factorization), not merely that one step decreased little.
Guarantees: for a disc, the result has no flipped (or degenerate) UV triangles, including triangles that are degenerate on the surface. The boundary is free and may in rare cases overlap itself (local, not global injectivity).

member.name: F:g3.SLIMParameterization.ConvergenceTolerance
member.summary: stop when the decrease predicted by the proxy for a full step, relative to the energy, is below this

member.name: F:g3.SLIMParameterization.InitialUV

member.name: F:g3.SLIMParameterization.StartMaps.Auto
member.summary: the LSCM map if it is injective (no flipped triangle, no overlap; exact test) and has no sliver UV triangle (twice its area not above 1e-6 of its longest edge squared), else the Tutte embedding; if SLIM gets stuck from LSCM, it goes on from Tutte with the remaining iterations and keeps the lower energy. LSCM is usually much closer to the minimum: on a 48k vertex ellipsoid cap SLIM needs 4 iterations from it instead of over 100 from Tutte.

member.summary: the Tutte embedding (always injective, but strongly distorted)

member.name: T:g3.UVAtlasGenerator
member.summary:
Builds a UV atlas for an arbitrary mesh (closed or open, any genus, several components): seams or charts, a parameterization of each chart, packing into the unit square, all checked for overlaps with exact predicates.
Per connected component, by Method: - Cones: BFF with cone singularities (ConeFlattening): one chart cut through automatically placed cones. Falls back to Charts if the result overlaps itself. - Charts: chart segmentation by normals (MeshChartSegmentation), each chart cut into a disc if needed (MeshDiscCut) and flattened with BFF (minimal area distortion). - SingleChart: the component cut into one disc (MeshDiscCut) and flattened with BFF. - Auto: Cones if that is overlap-free and within the distortion limits, otherwise Charts. A chart that overlaps itself, has inverted triangles or exceeds MaxAreaDistortion or MaxConformalDistortion is split in two (MeshChartSegmentation.SplitInTwo) and both parts are flattened again, while there are fewer than MaxCharts charts. A chart that still overlaps then gets the flip-free SLIM map (from the Tutte embedding), or the Tutte embedding itself, so the atlas is overlap-free.
The result is a new mesh, AtlasMesh, with the input's triangles on vertices split along the seams (AtlasToInputVertex / AtlasToInputTriangle map back) and vertex UVs in [0,1]^2. The final checks (overlaps, inverted triangles, UV triangles of zero area on non-degenerate surface triangles) are exact on the double UVs. The UVs stored in AtlasMesh are rounded to float, which moves each by at most half an ulp; defects that only this rounding causes (tiny or sliver triangles) are counted in FloatRoundingDefects, not failed. Status says whether the limits are met; the input is not changed.

member.name: T:g3.UVOverlap
member.summary:
Exact test of a UV layout for overlaps: pairs of UV triangles whose interiors intersect, and UV triangles that are inverted (clockwise) or degenerate (zero area). Uses the exact orientation predicate (ExactPredicates.Orient2d) on the double coordinates, so touching triangles (shared edges and vertices, charts that only touch) are never reported and every reported pair really overlaps.
Two triangles with disjoint interiors are separated by the line through one of their six edges (separating axis theorem for convex polygons), which is what is tested. Candidate pairs come from a hierarchy of uniform grids over the UV bounding box (cells of twice the median size of the triangles of each level), so that mixed triangle sizes stay near linear.

member.name: T:g3.UVPacker
member.summary:
Packs the UV charts of a mesh into the unit square without overlap. A chart is a set of triangles connected through shared vertices (with per-vertex UVs, seams are duplicated vertices, so every parameterized component is one chart).
Each chart is optionally rescaled to its surface area (so that texel density is uniform), rotated to its minimum-area bounding rectangle (rotating calipers, ContMinBox2), and the rectangles are packed with the skyline bottom-left heuristic (J. Jylänki, A Thousand Ways to Pack the Bin, 2010), trying 90 degree rotations and several bin widths for the smallest square. Charts keep their relative scale. Charts are at least Padding apart and from the border of the square. The placed charts are checked with exact predicates: a chart whose rotated UVs overlap or flip (rounding at exactly collinear vertices) is placed again without the rotation, which keeps the order of each coordinate.

member.name: M:g3.TriangleDeviationBounds.MaxDistance(g3.DMeshAABBTree3,g3.Vector3d,g3.Vector3d,g3.Vector3d,System.Double,System.Double,System.Double,System.Int32,System.Int32,System.Int32,System.Double,System.Int32,System.Double@,System.Double@,g3.Vector3d@)
member.summary: Certified interval [lower, upper] of the largest distance to Target over the triangle (a, b, c): lower is the distance of a point of the triangle (a corner or a subdivision point, returned in worst), and no point of the triangle is farther than upper. Branch and bound as in MeshHausdorffDistance, restricted to this triangle: the piece with the largest upper bound is split into 4 until upper - lower <= tol or after maxSubdivisions splits (then false, with a wider but still valid interval). d_i and n_i are the corner distances and nearest triangles in spatial, whose mesh must be Target. Sequential and deterministic, so it can run in parallel over triangles. Non-finite corners give NaN. A piece whose bound is NaN (rounding in a degenerate piece) counts as unbounded, so upper can be +Infinity if it cannot be resolved within the budget.

member.name: T:g3.FastQuaternionSVD
member.summary:
Fast Approximate SVD of 3x3 matrix that returns quaternions. Implemented based on https://github.com/benjones/quatSVD/blob/master/quatSVD.hpp which was re-implemented from http://pages.cs.wisc.edu/~sifakis/project_pages/svd.html

member.name: T:g3.SingularValueDecomposition
member.summary:
Singular Value Decomposition of an MxN matrix A, M >= N > 1 (A does not have to be symmetric) Computes U/S/V of A = U * S * V^T
Useful Properties: S = square-roots of eigenvalues of A^T * A (the singular values, not the eigenvalues of A) U = eigenvectors of A * A^T V = eigenvectors of A^T * A U * V^T = orthogonal matrix closest to A (if A is square) V * Inv(S) * U^T = psuedoinverse of A (Inv(S) inverts only the nonzero singular values)
U and/or V are rotation matrices but may also contain reflections Detection: det(U) or det(v) == -1 Removal: if ( det(U) == -1 ) { U *= -1; S *= -1 } if ( det(V) == -1 ) { V *= -1; S *= -1 } (negating flips det only for odd dimension, eg 3x3)

member.name: T:g3.SparseCholesky
member.summary:
Sparse Cholesky factorization A = L L^T of a symmetric positive definite matrix, for systems that are solved many times (parameterization, Laplacians with fixed boundary values). The caller makes sure the matrix is positive definite; a singular one is not reliably rejected (see IsValid).
Usage: Add() the entries, Factorize(), then Solve() any number of right-hand sides. To refactor a matrix with new values, Clear() and Add() again; if the nonzero pattern is the same, the ordering and the structure of L are reused and only the numeric factorization runs.
The unknowns are ordered by approximate minimum degree (on the graph of blocks of BlockSize unknowns, eg 2 for interleaved u,v coordinates) to limit fill. The structure of L comes from the postordered elimination tree, the values from a left-looking supernodal Cholesky with dense blocks. Written from the papers and textbooks named in the code and in docs/SOURCES.md, no code taken over.

member.name: P:g3.SparseCholesky.IsValid
member.summary:
The last Factorize() ran to the end: every pivot was positive, above 1e-14 times the absolute value of the diagonal entry of A it came from (false before the first Factorize() and after Clear()). False for clearly indefinite matrices, and for singular ones only where rounding leaves a pivot at or below the bound (eg the Laplacian of a small graph with integer weights, whose last pivot is 0).
It is not a test for singularity: on a positive semidefinite matrix the last pivots are rounding noise, and they can come out positive and above the bound, eg on a graph Laplacian without a fixed vertex with edge weights of different magnitudes. IsValid is then true and Solve() returns values dominated by a huge, arbitrary multiple of the null vector. No bound on the pivots can fix this (a matrix with condition number near 1e16 is indistinguishable from a singular one in double precision), so make the matrix definite before factorizing it: fix (pin) at least one unknown per connected component of a Laplacian, or add a mass term.

member.summary: Add v to A[r,c] and, by symmetry, to A[c,r]: each off-diagonal entry is added once, in either order.

member.summary: solve A x = b (b is not modified; x and b may be the same array)

member.name: M:g3.SparseCholesky.SolveLog(System.Double[],System.Double[])
member.summary: Solve A x = b in the log domain, for an M-matrix A (positive diagonal, off-diagonal entries <= 0) and b >= 0: logB[i] = log(b[i]) (negative infinity for 0), logX[i] = log(x[i]). The Cholesky factor of an M-matrix has no positive off-diagonal entries, so both substitutions only add non-negative terms: every entry of x is as accurate as with Solve(), relative to itself, and none underflows (eg heat 1000 edge lengths from its source, below 1e-308). Returns false (logX undefined) if the factor has a positive off-diagonal entry, ie A is not an M-matrix.

member.name: T:g3.SparseCholesky.MinimumDegree
member.summary: Minimum degree ordering on the quotient graph (A. George, J. Liu, The Evolution of the Minimum Degree Ordering Algorithm, SIAM Review 1989), with the approximate external degrees of P. Amestoy, T. Davis, I. Duff, An Approximate Minimum Degree Ordering Algorithm, SIAM J. Matrix Anal. Appl. 1996. An eliminated node becomes an element (the clique of its neighbours, stored as a list) instead of adding the clique edges, so the cost stays close to the size of the input graph.

member.name: T:g3.DMeshAABBTree3
member.summary:
Hierarchical Axis-Aligned-Bounding-Box tree for a DMesh3 mesh. This class supports a variety of spatial queries, listed below.
You must call Build() (or pass autoBuild = true to the constructor) before any query. The tree does not update itself: if the mesh is modified afterwards (any vertex position or topology change, see DMesh3.ShapeTimestamp), queries throw an Exception until Build() is called again. Check IsValid to see if a rebuild is needed. Building is roughly O(n log n); queries are typically O(log n). Queries return triangle/vertex IDs (DMesh3.InvalidID if nothing is found); use the MeshQueries helpers (eg MeshQueries.TriangleDistance, MeshQueries.TriangleIntersection) to get points and distances. Ray queries require a normalized ray direction.
Various construction strategies are also available, the default is the fastest to build but if you are doing a *lot* of queries, you might experiment with the others (eg TopDownMedian)
Available queries: - FindNearestTriangle(point, maxdist) - FindNearestHitTriangle(ray, maxdist) - FindAllHitTriangles(ray, maxdist) - TestIntersection(triangle) - TestIntersection(mesh) - TestIntersection(otherAABBTree) - FindAllIntersections(otherAABBTree) - FindNearestTriangles(otherAABBTree, maxdist) - IsInside(point) - WindingNumber(point) - FastWindingNumber(point) - DoTraversal(generic_traversal_object)

member.name: M:g3.DMeshAABBTree3.IsInside(g3.Vector3d)
member.summary: Returns true if point p is inside this mesh, using a ray-crossing parity test: a ray in a fixed direction is cast from p and the point is inside if it crosses the surface an odd number of times. The crossings are exact, with a symbolic perturbation of the ray (ExactRayTriangle.RayHitPerturbed): a ray through an edge or a vertex crosses it once, a ray in the plane of a triangle not at all, so the parity is right for every closed mesh (each edge in two triangles) without self-intersections and every p off its surface (p on the surface: either answer). For open, non-manifold, self-intersecting or noisy meshes the parity has no meaning: use WindingNumber(p) > 0.5 (the general inside test for such inputs is ROADMAP Phase 5 #5, generalized winding numbers).

member.name: M:g3.DMeshAABBTree3.CountCrossings(g3.Vector3d,g3.Vector3d)
member.summary: The number of crossings of the ray from origin along direction (need not be normalized) with the mesh, each counted once (ExactRayTriangle.RayHitPerturbed: a ray through an edge or a vertex crosses exactly one triangle of a closed fan; FindAllHitTriangles counts every triangle there). IsInside's parity.
