member.name: M:g3.DMeshAABBTree3.WindingNumber(g3.Vector3d)
member.summary: Evaluate the generalized winding number of the mesh at point p (exact sum of triangle solid angles / 4pi). For a closed mesh with outward-facing normals this is 1 inside, 0 outside (-1 inside for an inside-out mesh, and n inside n nested shells). For open meshes it varies smoothly, and WindingNumber > 0.5 is a robust inside test. To do this, we must construct additional information to short-circuit tree branches. This happens on the first evaluation. This does consume some additional memory, mainly temporary memory during construction. (eg on a 500k sphere, about 30mb to construct, but then only 2-5mb is stored at the end) If you don't want this, just use Mesh.WindingNumber() directly. Also note that if you are only evaluating a few times, it is not sensible - assume you need at least hundreds of evaluations to see speed improvements. The cache is built on first use (under a lock), so this can be called from multiple threads.

members.member: collect all triangles under iBox, find open edges [a,b], and add them all to a list associated with iBox. An edge between two triangles that run along it in the same direction (inconsistent orientation) is part of the boundary of the patch too, twice; without it the winding number is wrong.

member.name: M:g3.DMeshAABBTree3.FastWindingNumber(g3.Vector3d)
member.summary: Fast approximation of the winding number at p using far-field (dipole) approximations (Barill et al. 2018, Fast Winding Numbers). Same conventions as WindingNumber(p) (1 inside, 0 outside for a closed outward-oriented mesh), but the result is approximate (errors of a few percent up to about 0.1 are normal); accuracy is controlled by FWNBeta and FWNApproxOrder. The cache is built on the first call (thread-safe). Much faster than WindingNumber for many queries on large meshes.

member.name: T:g3.HashGridCells
member.summary: The cell range of a hash-grid query (PointHashGrid2d/3d, SegmentHashGrid2d). Upstream cast the range ends to int in the indexer: beyond 2^31 cells (eg UTM coordinates with small cells, or an infinite query point or radius) .NET 9 and later saturate to int.MaxValue, and `for (i = min; i <= max; i++)` wrapped around forever; .NET Framework gives int.MinValue, so the range was wrong or reversed and nearby points were missed. A huge range took as long as its cell count (docs/ROBUSTNESS_SWEEP.md R4). The range is now computed in double; one that is not finite or leaves the int range scans every occupied cell, one with more cells than are occupied scans the occupied cells inside it. Scans visit the cells in the loop order (z, then y, then x), so ties go the same way.

member.name: T:g3.MeshBatchQueries
member.summary:
Batch ray and point queries against a DMeshAABBTree3 (docs/design/BATCH_QUERIES.md). Every result equals the result of the single call for the same tree and query, bit for bit: a batch runs the same single queries (the tree's FindNearestHitTriangle and FindNearestTriangle, the triangle tests of IntrRay3Triangle3 and DistPoint3Triangle3) and only reorders independent queries (Morton order, for cache coherence) and runs them in parallel, writing each result at the index of its query. So the results do not depend on the options, the thread count or the order of the queries.
Thread safety: the tree and its mesh are only read; the mesh must not change during a call, and a DMeshAABBTree3.TriangleFilterF must be thread-safe with Parallel (the default). A batch does not throw for a bad query (see RayStatus and PointStatus), and a stale or unbuilt tree is BatchStatus.MeshModified instead of the single call's exception (an unbuilt tree of an empty mesh is not told apart from a built one: every query has no result). An exception of the user's TriangleFilterF, or a mesh modified during the call, ends the batch as it ends a single call (several at once from the worker threads as AggregateException) with the results partly written.

member.name: M:g3.MeshBatchQueries.IntersectBatch(g3.DMeshAABBTree3,g3.Ray3d[],g3.RayHit[],g3.RayStatus[],g3.BatchOptions)
member.summary: For every ray the nearest hit, as tree.FindNearestHitTriangle(ray, options.MaxDistance) (smallest ray parameter, the lowest id among equal ones; hits behind the origin ignored; front and back faces), with its ray parameter (that of IntrRay3Triangle3.Intersects, as MeshQueries.TriangleIntersection(...).RayParameter). hits has at least rays.Length entries; status (optional) the same, and tells the rays the single query would reject (not normalized) or cannot answer (not finite): those get no hit.

member.summary: For every ray whether it hits the mesh closer than options.MaxDistance: hit[i] is tree.FindNearestHitTriangle(ray, MaxDistance) != DMesh3.InvalidID. (It runs the nearest-hit query: an early-out traversal needs the tree's internals, which this class does not use.)

member.name: M:g3.MeshBatchQueries.NearestPointBatch(g3.DMeshAABBTree3,g3.Vector3d[],g3.NearestPointResult[],g3.PointStatus[],g3.BatchOptions)
member.summary: For every point the nearest triangle, as tree.FindNearestTriangle(p, out dSqr, options.MaxDistance), the closest point on it and its barycentric coordinates (DistPoint3Triangle3.DistanceSqr on that triangle, as MeshQueries.TriangleDistance) and the distance Math.Sqrt(dSqr) of the tree query. A point with no triangle strictly closer than MaxDistance (or any, for an empty mesh) gets Triangle = DMesh3.InvalidID, Distance = double.MaxValue and a zero Point and Bary.

member.name: M:g3.MeshBatchQueries.IsInsideBatch(g3.DMeshAABBTree3,g3.Vector3d[],g3.InsideStatus[],g3.InsideMethod,g3.BatchOptions)
member.summary: For every point whether it is inside the mesh: results[i] is Inside or Outside as tree.IsInside(p) (method Crossings, the default: exact, for closed meshes) or as tree.FastWindingNumber(p) > 0.5 (method WindingNumber: for any mesh), Invalid for a point that is not finite. options.MaxDistance does not apply (it is still checked to be >= 0). An empty mesh has no inside. The winding number cache is built once before the parallel part.

member.name: T:g3.MeshSignedDistanceGrid
member.summary:
Compute discretely-sampled (ie gridded) signed distance field for a mesh The basic approach is, first compute exact distances in a narrow band, and then extend out to rest of grid using fast "sweeping" (ie like a distance transform). The resulting unsigned grid is then signed using ray-intersection counting, which is also computed on the grid, so no BVH is necessary
If you set ComputeMode to NarrowBandOnly (the default), result is a narrow-band signed distance field. This is quite a bit faster as the sweeping is the most computationally-intensive step. Outside the band, samples keep a large placeholder magnitude ((ni+nj+nk)*CellSize) but still get the correct sign.
Usage: var sdf = new MeshSignedDistanceGrid(mesh, cellSize); sdf.Compute(); then read sdf[i,j,k], sdf.Grid, sdf.GridOriginD and sdf.CellSize. Sample (i,j,k) is located at GridOriginD + CellSize*(i,j,k) (see CellCenter). Sign convention: distances are NEGATIVE INSIDE the mesh and positive outside (with the default ParityCount mode this assumes outward-facing triangle normals). The grid covers the mesh bounds plus 2*ExactBandWidth cells (plus ExpandBounds) on each side. Memory and time grow with the cube of (mesh size / cellSize). To get a mesh back from the grid, wrap it in DenseGridTrilinearImplicit and run with IsoValue = 0.
Caveats: - the "narrow band" is based on triangle bounding boxes, so it is not necessarily that "narrow" if you have large triangles on a diagonal to grid axes
Potential optimizations: - Often we have a spatial data structure that would allow faster computation of the narrow-band distances (which become quite expensive if we want a wider band!) Not clear how to take advantage of this though. Perhaps we could have a binary grid that, in first pass, we set bits inside triangle bboxes to 1? Or perhaps same as current code, but we use spatial-dist, and so for each ijk we only compute once? (then have to test for computed value at each cell of each triangle...)
This code is based on the C++ implementation found at https://github.com/christopherbatty/SDFGen Original license was public domain. Permission granted by Christopher Batty to include C# port under Boost license.

member.name: T:g3.PointHashGrid3d`1
member.summary:
Hash Grid for 3D points. You provide the 'point' type. If you have an indexable set of points this can just be int, or can be more complex point data structure (but be careful w/ structs...)
Does not actually store 3D points. So, to remove a point you must also know it's 3D coordinate, so we can look up the cell coordinates. Hence, to 'update' a point, you need to know both it's old and new 3D coordinates.
Typical use: var grid = new PointHashGrid3d<int>(cellSize, -1);, InsertPoint(vid, pos) for each point, then FindNearestInRadius(query, radius, (vid) => positions[vid].Distance(query)). Choose cellSize about equal to the typical query radius: a query visits all cells overlapping the box of size 2*radius around the query point. Points can be inserted/removed at any time, no build step is needed.
TODO: if a lot of points are in the same spot, this is still a disaster. What if we had a second level of hashing, where once a list at a level gets too big, we build a sub-hash there?

member.name: T:g3.TriangleHashGrid
member.summary: Grid of triangle ids (non-negative, eg DMesh3 triangle ids) by the cells their bounding boxes overlap, with insert and remove, for meshes that change (eg during a reduction). Hierarchical: level 0 has the given cell size, each further level LevelFactor times larger cells; a triangle is stored on the finest level where its box overlaps at most MaxCellsPerTriangle cells, a query visits every level. So triangles that grow (late in a reduction) or a few large ones among many small ones cost neither a long list that every query visits nor a rebuild with coarser cells for all. Not thread-safe, also not for concurrent queries (Query marks the triangles it has seen).

member.name: T:gs.RemesherPro
member.summary:
Extension to Remesher that is smarter about which edges/vertices to touch: - queue tracks edges that were affected on last pass, and hence might need to be updated - FastSplitIteration() just does splits, to reach target edge length as quickly as possible - RemeshIteration() applies remesh pass for modified edges - TrackedSmoothPass() smooths all vertices but only adds to queue if edge changes enough - TrackedProjectionPass() same
Same options, constraints and in-place behaviour as (set the edge lengths with SetTargetEdgeLength(), a projection target to keep the shape, and constraints to keep boundaries). After the first full pass only queued edges are processed, so it is usually much faster than repeated BasicRemeshPass() calls. Usual entry point: FastestRemesh(). Call ResetQueue() if the mesh is changed externally between iterations. This class is in namespace gs.

member.name: F:gs.RemesherPro.UseFaceAlignedProjection
member.summary: if true, the projection pass moves vertices to align triangles with the face normals of the projection target (requires an IOrientedProjectionTarget), which recovers sharp edges; set by SharpEdgeReprojectionRemesh()

member.summary: number of face-aligned projection passes per RemeshIteration() if UseFaceAlignedProjection

member.summary: remesh mesh m in place

member.summary: the number of edges queued for the next RemeshIteration (for tests)

member.summary: MinTriangleQuality rejected a move of vID: its edges are processed again (eg flipped)

member.name: M:gs.RemesherPro.FastestRemesh(System.Int32,System.Boolean)
member.summary: Converge on remeshed result as quickly as possible: split-only passes until fewer than 1% of the edges split (at most about nMaxIterations), then nMaxIterations queued RemeshIteration() calls (projection only on every other one, and on the last). Modifies the mesh in place; stops early if cancelled.

member.name: M:gs.RemesherPro.SharpEdgeReprojectionRemesh(System.Int32,System.Int32,System.Boolean)
member.summary: This is a remesh that tries to recover sharp edges by aligning triangles to face normals of our projection target (similar to Ohtake RZN-flow): nRemeshIterations remesh iterations with face-aligned projection, then nTuneIterations face-aligned projection passes. Throws if ProjectionTarget is not set or is not an IOrientedProjectionTarget (eg MeshProjectionTarget). Note: leaves FaceProjectionPassesPerIteration at 1.

member.name: M:gs.RemesherPro.ResetQueue
member.summary: Reset tracked-edges queue. Should be called if mesh is modified by external functions between passes, and also between different types of passes (eg FastSplitIteration vs RemeshIteration)

member.name: M:gs.RemesherPro.FastSplitIteration
member.summary: This pass only does edge splits (of edges longer than MaxEdgeLength). Returns number of split edges. The next call only processes the edges created by these splits that are still too long.

member.name: M:gs.RemesherPro.RemeshIteration
member.summary: One remesh pass (split/collapse/flip, smoothing, projection as in Remesher.BasicRemeshPass()). The first call after construction or ResetQueue() processes all edges; later calls only process the edges queued by the previous iteration (around split/collapsed/flipped edges, and edges smoothing or projection changed). ModifiedEdgesLastPass counts the edge operations.

member.name: T:gs.MarchingCubesPro.RootfindingModes
member.summary: How vertex positions are found along cell edges: one linear interpolation, repeated interpolation, bisection, or LinearEdges: one linear interpolation of the original corner samples, without the endpoint nudges and with no skipped triangle. LinearEdges requires finite samples and edge coordinates, no sample exactly at IsoValue and crossings strictly inside their edges (a sample that differs from IsoValue by a tiny amount can still round a crossing onto a corner); it never repairs a violation: Generate() then throws InvalidOperationException (a crossing on a grid corner, a collapsed triangle, or as a guard a rejected one) or ArgumentException (non-finite values), also from the parallel path (InvalidOperationException preferred if several cells fail), and the partial mesh must not be used. MarchingCubesPro additionally needs a finite positive CubeSize and at most 65535 cells per axis for Generate(), 65534 for GenerateContinuation() (its 16-bit grid hash), whose seeds must lie in the grid (cell indices 0 to n), and otherwise throws ArgumentException before any work. The mode alone certifies nothing about an arbitrary field: the conditional enclosure recipe and its further preconditions are in docs/design/CONSERVATIVE_MC_AUDIT.md.

member.name: M:gs.MarchingCubesPro.check_linear_edges_grid(System.Int32)
member.summary: The corner and edge hashes keep 16 bits of each corner index (0 to 65535). Generate() visits the cells 0 to n - 1 of an axis with n = (int)(w / h) + 1 cells, so corner indices up to n: at most 65535 cells. GenerateContinuation() also visits the cell n (GridBounds.Contains is inclusive), corner indices up to n + 1: at most 65534 cells. Beyond that two grid edges alias onto one vertex; LinearEdges refuses such a grid, and a cube size that is not finite and positive, before any work (the legacy modes keep their behaviour). (int)(w / h) + 1 <= maxCells iff w / h < maxCells (also false for NaN and infinity)

member.name: M:gs.MarchingCubesPro.check_linear_edges_seeds(System.Collections.Generic.IEnumerable{g3.Vector3d})
member.summary: LinearEdges: the continuation visits the cells of GridBounds (inclusive: indices 0 to n per axis) and the seed cells, which cell_index does not clamp; a seed cell outside that range (eg a negative index) would alias in the 16-bit hash. cell_index truncates (pos - min) / h toward zero, so its index lies in [0, n] iff -1 < (pos - min) / h < n + 1 (also false for NaN and infinity). The seeds are read once, before any work

member.name: T:gs.AlphaWrapQualityPass
member.summary: Triangle quality pass for a simplified alpha wrap (MeshRobustRepair.AlphaWrapQualityPass): edge flips, tangential vertex moves and, if switched on, cap splits, cap flips and needle collapses around triangles with a small minimum angle (or a large maximum angle), each kept only if - it raises the smallest angle of the changed triangles by at least MinGainDegrees, - no changed triangle turns by more than MaxNormalTurnDegrees or becomes degenerate, - every changed triangle lies within Tolerance of the reference (the unsimplified wrap), certified by TriangleDeviationBounds.IsWithin (with the patch bound), - and, with CheckSelfIntersections, no changed triangle intersects another one (exact test, as the Reducer's PreventSelfIntersections). So the result stays within Tolerance of the reference wherever it changed, and keeps the genus (splits and collapses change the vertices, collapses only under the link condition). The smallest angle of the mesh cannot drop (every operation keeps the smallest angle of its triangles), but the largest one is bounded only by splits and cap flips: a flip, move or collapse may raise the largest angle of its triangles. Serial and in a fixed order: deterministic. Scale invariant (angles and relative thresholds only).

member.name: T:gs.ClothSimulationFilter
member.summary:
Ground filter for airborne / drone LiDAR point clouds, after Zhang et al., "An Easy-to-Use Airborne LiDAR Data Filtering Method Based on Cloth Simulation" (2016). The cloud is turned upside down and a cloth (grid of particles moving vertically) falls onto it under gravity; springs between neighbour particles keep the cloth stiff, so it bridges buildings, vehicles and vegetation (which are holes in the inverted cloud) and settles on the terrain. Points close to the cloth are ground.
Each particle collides with the lowest point (highest after inversion) near it. Rigidness is the number of spring relaxation passes per time step (1 soft .. 3 stiff); the fall speed is limited so that a long fall (deep pits) does not push the cloth through the springs onto objects. Steep faces, which the stiff cloth cannot follow, are handled by a post-processing step (SlopeStep).
Limits: an object on a steep face whose height is less than about the slope times ClothResolution (eg a 2.5 m object on a 51 degree face with a 1 m cloth) cannot be told from the face; and the slope post-processing spreads upwards onto objects lower than SlopeStep (eg light vehicles, 1.5 m: use a SlopeStep below the lowest object height that matters). Low, wide objects (eg a 3 m high building 20 m wide with a 1 m cloth) let the cloth sag onto them: raise Rigidness. Low outliers (multipath points below the ground) hold the cloth up around them: remove them first. Non-finite points are not ground.

member.summary: particle spacing of the cloth (about the point spacing or a bit larger)

member.name: F:gs.ClothSimulationFilter.Rigidness

member.name: T:gs.IntrinsicTriangulation
member.summary:
Intrinsic triangulation of a triangle mesh: the same surface and the same vertices, but triangles whose edges are geodesics along the surface, described only by their lengths (Sharp, Soliman and Crane, "Navigating Intrinsic Triangulations", 2019). FlipToDelaunay() flips edges until the triangulation is intrinsic Delaunay (Bobenko and Springborn 2007): then all cotan weights are non-negative, the cotan Laplacian satisfies a maximum principle and mass + t * Laplacian is an M-matrix, however bad (sliver, obtuse, needle) the input triangles are. The geometry is not changed.
Data structure: halfedges in an array (halfedge 3t+k of triangle t runs from corner k to k+1, in the mesh orientation), which also represents triangulations that are not simplicial complexes (two edges between the same vertices), as they occur after intrinsic flips. Every halfedge carries its length and a signpost: its direction at its tail vertex, as an angle in the vertex' tangent space, measured counter-clockwise from the first edge of the vertex in the input mesh and scaled so that the angles around the vertex sum to 2 pi. Boundary vertices are not scaled: their first boundary edge has the angle 0, the other one the angle sum (so the discrete connection is exactly flat on flat meshes, boundaries included). The signposts give the correspondence with the input mesh (TraceEdge) and the Levi-Civita connection used by the vector heat method.
Degenerate input triangles (zero area, coincident vertices) are handled by intrinsic mollification (Sharp and Crane, "A Laplacian for Nonmanifold Triangle Meshes", 2020): all edge lengths are increased by the smallest delta that makes every triangle inequality hold with a margin of MollifyFactor * mean edge length. Delta is 0 for meshes without (nearly) degenerate triangles.
Vertices must be manifold (one fan of triangles each; split bowtie vertices first); boundaries are allowed. Vertices without triangles are not part of the triangulation.
DelaunayRefine() also inserts vertices (circumcenters, boundary edge midpoints): then the triangulation has more vertices than the mesh; indices from InputVertexCount on are inserted vertices (VertexID -1), located on the input surface by VertexPosition / GetInputLocation. ExtractCommonSubdivision() gives the overlay of the intrinsic and the input triangles.

member.name: M:gs.IntrinsicTriangulation.ExtractCommonSubdivision
member.summary: The common subdivision of this triangulation and the input mesh (see IntrinsicCommonSubdivision): every intrinsic edge is traced over the input (TraceEdge); within each input triangle the traced segments, which cannot cross, cut it into convex faces, and each face is assigned the intrinsic triangle on its side of the segments. The result is checked: every input triangle and every intrinsic triangle must be tiled by its faces (areas to a relative 1e-6); otherwise Status is Inconsistent. Integer (normal) coordinates (Gillespie, Sharp and Crane 2021) would make the combinatorics exact; here they come from the traces, which are exact up to rounding.

member.name: M:gs.IntrinsicTriangulation.BuildDelaunay(g3.DMesh3,System.Boolean,gs.IntrinsicRefinementResult@,System.Double,System.Int32)
member.summary: Intrinsic Delaunay triangulation of a mesh, for its cotan Laplacian (CotanLaplacian, VertexAreas): flipped to Delaunay, and with refine also refined (DelaunayRefine(minAngleDegrees, maxInsertions)), so that the cotan weights are non-negative also at boundary edges opposite obtuse angles. Then the Laplacian and the areas include the inserted vertices (indices from InputVertexCount on, VertexID -1); values at them can be interpolated or eliminated by the caller. result is null without refine.

member.name: M:gs.IntrinsicTriangulation.DelaunayRefine(System.Double,System.Int32)
member.summary:
Intrinsic Delaunay refinement: flips to Delaunay, then inserts vertices until (1) no boundary edge lies opposite an obtuse angle (such edges cannot be flipped and keep a negative cotan weight; they are split at their midpoint, Ruppert's encroached segments), and (2) every triangle has all angles at least minAngleDegrees: the circumcenter of a bad triangle is located by walking straight from its barycenter across the intrinsic triangles and inserted (Chew's second algorithm); if the walk leaves the surface, or the circumcenter lies in the diametral circle of a boundary edge of its triangle, that boundary edge is split instead. After each insertion the triangulation is flipped back to Delaunay. So afterwards all cotan weights are non-negative, also on the boundary.
minAngleDegrees is clamped to [0, 30] (above about 30 degrees termination is not guaranteed); 0 only splits the boundary edges opposite obtuse angles. Triangles whose small angle comes from the input (at a vertex with an angle sum below 60 degrees, or whose shortest edge connects two boundary edges of such a vertex) cannot be improved and are skipped (Shewchuk 2002); boundary edges at such vertices are split at powers of two times the mean input edge length from the vertex (concentric shells), so the refinement there terminates. maxInsertions (0: 10 * input vertices + 1000) bounds the work; boundary edges opposite obtuse angles are split up to twice that limit. The geometry is not changed; inserted vertices lie on the input surface.

member.name: M:gs.IntrinsicTriangulation.InsertVertex(System.Int32,g3.Vector2d)
member.summary: Inserts a vertex into triangle t at the point p of its layout (GetTriangleLayout), splitting it into three; the triangulation is not flipped. Returns the new vertex index, -1 if p is not strictly inside.

member.name: M:gs.IntrinsicTriangulation.SplitEdge(System.Int32,System.Double)
member.summary: Inserts a vertex on the edge of halfedge h at parameter s in (0, 1) from its tail, splitting its triangles (boundary edges too); the triangulation is not flipped. Returns the new vertex index, -1 if the edge cannot be split (s outside (0, 1), or both sides of the edge in the same triangle).

member.name: T:gs.MeshAlphaWrap
member.summary:
Alpha wrapping with an offset (Portaneri, Rouxel-Labbé, Hemmer, Cohen-Steiner, Alliez, "Alpha Wrapping with an Offset", ACM TOG 2022): a closed, oriented, 2-manifold surface without self-intersections that strictly encloses any input: triangle soups, open or non-manifold meshes, degenerate triangles, point clouds. The result is computed, not repaired, so it does not depend on the input being valid.
The method refines and carves a 3D Delaunay triangulation (Delaunay3), starting from a box around the input. A ball of radius Alpha "flows" in from outside through Delaunay facets it fits through (the smallest empty ball through the facet's vertices, the paper's Phi(f), larger than Alpha; TraverseByEmptyBall); a cell it reaches is carved (marked outside), unless 1. the Voronoi edge dual to the facet crosses the offset surface (the points at distance Offset from the input): its first crossing, coming from outside, is inserted as a Steiner point; 2. the cell intersects the input: the projection of its circumcenter onto the offset surface is inserted. The result is the boundary between the outside and the remaining cells, made manifold by moving outside cells around non-manifold edges and vertices to the inside.
Guarantees (with the exact predicates of Delaunay3; the result vertices are the triangulation vertices, no rounding): - closed, consistently oriented (outwards), 2-manifold, no self-intersections; - the input is strictly inside: no outside cell comes closer than 1e-6 * Offset to it (the margin of the floating-point distance tests); - the vertices lie on the offset surface (up to rounding), so between them the result can come closer to the input than Offset (by the sagitta of the triangles); it stays within about Offset + Alpha where the facets come from carving. Where the manifold step moved cells inside it can reach farther (measured up to 8.8 (Offset + Alpha) without RefineNonManifold, 1.1 with it, on an 800 mesh Thingi10K sample). Alpha controls the detail: cavities and gaps narrower than about 2 * Alpha are not entered (they are wrapped over), and the result has triangles with a circumradius of at most about Alpha. Smaller Alpha = more detail, more triangles, more time (about 1 / Alpha^2). Offset keeps the result away from the input. Typical values: Alpha 1/100 to 1/20 of the bounding box diagonal, Offset 1/30 of Alpha.
Triangle shape (derived here, not a claim of the paper; up to rounding and the contact margin, with Offset below Alpha / 2): every Steiner point is at least min(Offset, Alpha - Offset) from every other vertex (a rule 1 point is the center of an empty ball larger than Alpha, unless a circumcenter on its dual edge is not finite and the edge is replaced by a long normal segment, see clamp_center; a rule 2 point lies that deep inside an empty circumsphere, see rule_projection). So a result triangle with a circumradius of at most Alpha has a min angle of at least asin(min(Offset, Alpha - Offset) / (2 Alpha)) = asin(Offset / (2 Alpha)) (0.95 degrees at the defaults, 2.9 degrees at Alpha = 10 Offset) and a max angle of at most 180 degrees minus twice that. Larger triangles, without an angle bound, come from the manifold step (outside cells moved inside, up to 179 degrees), from rejected Steiner points (Counts["rejected_points"]) and from PointLimitReached. RefineNonManifold refines at the spots where the manifold step would move cells first, which removes most of them (an 800 mesh Thingi10K sample at Alpha = 10 Offset: triangles below 0.5 degrees 28 -> 5, above 170 degrees 327 -> 40). Rule 2 points projected from the clamped dual edge (Counts["projection_fallbacks"], none measured) have no separation bound.
Not covered by the guarantees: with MaxSteinerPoints reached (PointLimitReached) the box corners can be vertices of the result.
Implemented from the paper, no code taken over (docs/SOURCES.md).

member.name: F:gs.MeshAlphaWrap.RefineNonManifold
member.summary: Refine at the non-manifold spots of the carved surface before the manifold step (default true): the outside cells that the manifold step would move inside get a Steiner point on the offset surface, and the refinement continues (up to 10 rounds). The facets of moved cells were never gates (circumradius above Alpha, caps up to 179 degrees, the result up to several Offset + Alpha from the input); with the refinement most spots become manifold by carving, which keeps the bounds of the class doc there; the spots that remain are made manifold as before, without a bound. Costs about 20 % more time at Alpha = 10 Offset. The extra points count against MaxSteinerPoints: a wrap that reaches it here ends with PointLimitReached (the guarantees of that status), where it had Success without the refinement. A rule 1 point rejected during the refinement fails the result check as any other (Failed, then the retry with the other box). false: the manifold step alone, as before (the order of its candidates differs only where the old score rounded two volumes to the same value). Default on: owner decision 2026-11-02, with the time cost above.

member.name: F:gs.MeshAlphaWrap.TraverseByEmptyBall
member.summary: (tests) gates by the paper's Phi(f) (Definition 2: the smallest empty ball through the facet's vertices, along its dual Voronoi edge) instead of the facet's circumradius (false: the circumradius, as before). Phi(f) is at least the circumradius, so more facets are gates: the obtuse facets whose circumcircle is smaller than alpha but whose empty balls are not. It removes most result triangles above 150 degrees, and the quality refinement needs it (with the circumradius, its points leave such caps, up to 178 degrees). Costs triangles on thin sheets, as the paper's wrap does (a plate of thickness 0 at Alpha = diagonal / 300: twice the triangles, like CGAL's alpha wrap there; a plate of 1e-3: +24 %)

member.name: M:gs.MeshAlphaWrap.facet_empty_ball(System.Int32,System.Int32)
member.summary: The paper's Phi(f) (Definition 2, Fig. 23): the radius of the smallest empty ball through the vertices of facet i of cell c. The balls through the vertices have their centers on the facet's normal line through its circumcenter; the empty ones are those with the center on the dual Voronoi edge. So Phi(f) is the facet's circumradius if the edge passes through the facet's plane, otherwise the radius at the edge's end nearer to it. An alpha ball can pass through the facet if Phi(f) is larger than alpha. At least the circumradius.

member.name: F:gs.MeshAlphaWrap.LocalPinchTrials
member.summary: (Alpha Wrap 2.0 WP3 lever 4b) the trial runs of the manifold step after the first one start only from the vertices whose star changed since the last trial (the cells inserted or carved since; an insertion's new cells have every vertex of the cells it replaced) and those that trial found non-manifold, instead of every vertex on the result. The step processes them in another order, so it can pick other cells, and the refinement other points: not bit-identical (T1, 100 Thingi10K meshes: 6 differ, by at most 0.2 % triangles and 0.06 degrees of p01). A local trial can also miss a spot (the outer remove_pockets of a trial fills or reopens pockets, which changes stars away from the changed cells), so its labels are never kept, and a local trial that finds nothing is confirmed by a full trial before the refinement stops (Counts local_trials_confirmed, and local_trials_missed when the full one found something). The labels of that full trial are reused when it moved nothing (ReuseTrialLabels); otherwise the final manifold step is the full one. The guarantees come from that final step, as before

member.name: M:gs.MeshAlphaWrap.make_manifold(System.Collections.Generic.List{System.Int32})
member.summary: Moves outside cells to the inside until every edge has at most two result facets and the result facets around every vertex form one disk: around a non-manifold edge or vertex, the outside cells are grouped into connected runs (through facets containing the edge / vertex); the run connected to the box boundary, otherwise the largest one, stays outside. If the inside cells around a vertex are not connected, outside cells move inside one at a time (cells joining inside components, small cells and cells without a box corner first). Only inside is added, so the input stays enclosed; every flip moves a cell inside for good, so this terminates. Vertices are checked from a work list (the vertices on the result, then those of flipped cells).

member.summary: The order of the manifold step's candidates for a move inside (a before b): no box corner first, then one that joins inside components, then the smaller volume. Compared as a key, not as a sum with volume / (1 + volume), which rounded to 1 for volumes above about 2^53 (large coordinates) and then tied, and depended on the unit

member.name: T:gs.MeshAutoRepair
member.summary:
Mesh Auto Repair top-level driver: tries to turn a broken triangle mesh (cracks, holes, inconsistent orientation, bowties, tiny edges) into a closed, consistently and outward oriented mesh while keeping the input triangles where possible. Steps: optional removal of interior/occluded triangles (RemoveMode), component orientation (MeshRepairOrientation), crack closing (MergeCoincidentEdges), collapse of tiny boundary edges, hole filling (SimpleHoleFiller / MinimalHoleFill / SmoothedHoleFill), bowtie disconnection, and as a last resort repeated erosion of boundary triangles (ErosionIterations) before filling again. Finally tiny edges are collapsed (MinEdgeLengthTol), the global orientation is solved and optionally MeshPostRepairCleanup runs.
Behaviour: the input mesh is modified in place, and at the end is replaced by a new, compacted copy with vertex normals, so always read the result from . Apply() returns false only if cancelled (see Progress); it returns true even if the mesh could not be closed, so check eg Mesh.IsClosed(). Self-intersections are not removed, and erosion can delete parts of the input. Tolerances are relative to the size of the mesh by default (see ToleranceMode).
Use MeshRobustRepair to get a clean solid in all cases (it runs this class first and falls back to MeshWindingNumberSolidify, which remeshes); use MeshWindingNumberSolidify directly to rebuild any input as a closed surface at a grid resolution; use ExactMeshBoolean.Resolve to resolve self-intersections and nested shells of an already closed mesh exactly.
TODO: - remove degenerate *faces* (which may still have all edges > length) - this is tricky, in many CAD meshes these faces can't just be collapsed. But can often remove via flipping...?

member.name: T:gs.MeshAutoRepair.ToleranceModes
member.summary: Relative (default): the tolerances are fractions of the size of the mesh (RelativeRepairTolerance, RelativeMinEdgeLength times the diagonal of the axis-aligned bounds of the triangles at the start of Apply(), at most 1/100 of the median edge length, at least 16 rounding units of the largest coordinate), so a model gives the same result in mm, um or km, and far from the origin (a rotation can change the axis-aligned diagonal by up to sqrt(3)). RepairTolerance or MinEdgeLengthTol set to a value other than its 1.0.324 default is absolute and used as given in both modes (set to exactly the default, it counts as not set: use Absolute for that). Absolute: RepairTolerance and MinEdgeLengthTol are used as they are (with their defaults: as geometry3Sharp 1.0.324).

member.name: F:gs.MeshAutoRepair.ToleranceMode
member.summary: see ToleranceModes; default Relative

member.name: F:gs.MeshAutoRepair.RelativeRepairTolerance
member.summary: Crack merging distance as a fraction of the diagonal of the triangles (ToleranceModes.Relative, if RepairTolerance is not set). 1e-8 gives the absolute 1e-6 of 1.0.324 for a model of diagonal 100. Also 0 keeps the floor of 16 rounding units of the largest coordinate (coincident edges are still merged).

member.name: F:gs.MeshAutoRepair.RelativeMinEdgeLength
member.summary: Final short edge collapse length as a fraction of the diagonal of the triangles (ToleranceModes.Relative, if MinEdgeLengthTol is not set); 0 disables. 1e-6 gives the absolute 1e-4 of 1.0.324 for a model of diagonal 100.

member.name: F:gs.MeshAutoRepair.RepairTolerance
member.summary: Distance (absolute, model units) within which boundary edges are merged to close cracks (up to 2x this in the second round); boundary edges shorter than half of it are collapsed before that. A value other than the default 1e-6 (MathUtil.ZeroTolerancef) overrides RelativeRepairTolerance; the default itself counts as not set and is only used with ToleranceModes.Absolute (reading it does not give the relative value, see EffectiveRepairTolerance). It sets the merge distance only; the other small lengths (degenerate hole loops, occlusion test offset) stay relative.

member.name: F:gs.MeshAutoRepair.MinEdgeLengthTol
member.summary: At the end, edges shorter than this (absolute, model units) are assumed degenerate and collapsed; 0 disables. A value other than the default 1e-4 overrides RelativeMinEdgeLength; the default itself counts as not set and is only used with ToleranceModes.Absolute (reading it does not give the relative value, see EffectiveMinEdgeLength).

member.name: M:gs.MeshAutoRepair.compute_tolerances
member.summary: The tolerances for the current mesh: explicitly set or Absolute mode: the absolute values; otherwise the relative factors times the diagonal of the triangles, at most 1/100 of the median edge length (one far away or non-finite triangle would otherwise inflate the diagonal and collapse the whole mesh), but at least 16 rounding units of the largest coordinate, so that cracks of rounding noise far from the origin (UTM) still close. All terms scale exactly with the mesh under scaling by a power of two.

member.name: F:gs.MeshAutoRepair.ErosionIterations
member.summary: If the mesh is still open after the first two rounds, up to this many times all triangles touching the boundary are deleted and the repair is repeated. This removes input geometry.

member.summary: If true, run MeshPostRepairCleanup at the end of Apply(). Removes duplicate triangles and bowties that the pipeline leaves behind, and fixes many of the degenerate triangles, folds and inside-out components it introduces (mostly during hole filling).

member.name: F:gs.MeshAutoRepair.CutOrientationSeams

member.name: T:gs.MeshCurvature
member.summary:
Discrete mean and Gaussian curvature per vertex, after Meyer, Desbrun, Schröder and Barr, "Discrete Differential-Geometry Operators for Triangulated 2-Manifolds" (VisMath 2002, published 2003): - mixed area A_M of each vertex (their Fig. 4): the Voronoi area of the vertex in each non-obtuse triangle, (|x_i x_j|^2 cot(angle at k) + |x_i x_k|^2 cot(angle at j)) / 8, and in an obtuse triangle half its area at the obtuse corner and a quarter at the other two; the mixed areas of a mesh sum to its area; - mean curvature normal K(x_i) = (1 / (2 A_M)) sum_j (cot alpha_ij + cot beta_ij) (x_i - x_j) (their eq. 8), computed in the equivalent area gradient form grad A / A_M (Desbrun et al. 1999; the gradient of a triangle's area at a corner is n x e / 2 for its unit normal n and the opposite edge e), which needs no cotangents and stays bounded at slivers; mean curvature H = K . n / 2 with n the angle weighted vertex normal (positive on a sphere oriented outward: 1 / r); - Gaussian curvature by the angle deficit (their eq. 9): (2 pi - sum of the angles at the vertex) / A_M.
Robustness (all thresholds relative to the triangle, none absolute): - a triangle is degenerate if twice its area is at most 1e-12 times its longest edge squared (collinear, coincident corners, zero-length edges): it adds no area and no area gradient (its normal is not defined), but its angles count in the angle sums, so the total angle deficit stays that of Gauss-Bonnet. The angle at a corner with a zero-length edge is not defined: such corners share pi minus the other angles equally (pi / 2 for two coincident corners, pi / 3 for three). The vertices of a degenerate triangle get values (finite) but are not Valid: the part of their fan that the triangle stands for is missing from the area gradient (eg the midpoint of a T-junction sliver gets an in-plane gradient and H = 0); - a triangle with a non-finite corner, or whose edge products (squared lengths, dot and cross products) leave the double range, adds nothing (no angles either), counts as degenerate, and its vertices are not Valid; - boundary vertices get one-sided values: the deficit against pi (the geodesic curvature of the boundary, 0 at a straight boundary of a plane) and the normal part of grad A / A_M over their fan; bowtie vertices (several fans) the values over all fans. Both are computed, but not Valid; - a vertex without area (no triangles, or only degenerate ones) gets 0 and is not Valid; no output is NaN or infinite (a value that would overflow is set to 0 and the vertex is not Valid; the Voronoi areas are formed from the cotangents, so they do not overflow before the area does).
Scale: H scales with 1 / s and K with 1 / s^2 under a scale by s; scaling by a power of two gives the scaled values bit for bit, and a rotation or translation the same values up to rounding. Deterministic, O(n). The existing MeshUtil.DiscreteGaussCurvature (the negative angle deficit, not divided by an area) and MeshWeights.VoronoiArea (absolute thresholds, NaN at coincident vertices) are left as they are.

member.name: T:gs.MeshDeviation
member.summary:
Deviation map of a mesh (eg a scan, a remeshed or simplified result) against a reference mesh: the signed distance of every vertex to the reference surface, positive outside (on the side the reference normals point to), negative inside, plus statistics over the vertices.
The sign is taken from the closest point (Signs): - PseudoNormal: the angle weighted pseudo-normal of the closest feature (face, edge or vertex) of the reference, after Baerentzen and Aanaes, "Signed distance computation using the angle weighted pseudonormal" (IEEE TVCG 2005). Correct for any point when the reference is closed, manifold and consistently oriented; for open references it is the side of the nearest patch. Closed parts that are inside out for their nesting, and an inside-out reference as a whole, are taken with flipped normals (OrientInvertedParts, see MeshWallThickness.InvertedTriangles). - WindingNumber: inside where the absolute generalized winding number of the reference is > 0.5 (Jacobson et al. 2013, via FastWindingNumber; absolute, so that inside-out parts count as solid). Robust to holes, self-intersections and inconsistent orientation of a (nearly) closed reference, but undefined for open sheets. - Unsigned: the plain distance.
The vertex values sample the deviation; the largest one is a lower bound of the one-sided Hausdorff distance from Mesh to Reference. ComputeCertifiedBound adds the certified interval of that distance (MeshHausdorffDistance), which also covers points inside the triangles. ComputeTriangleBounds adds such an interval per triangle (TriangleDeviationLower / Upper), so that the map is reliable between the vertices too: no point of a triangle is farther from the reference than its upper bound.

member.name: F:gs.MeshDeviation.ReferenceSpatial
member.summary: optional spatial data structure of the reference. If null it is built (and rebuilt when Reference changes); for a reference far from the origin (MeshWallThickness.FarFromOrigin) the queries then run on a copy moved to the origin, with its own tree, and this stays null. A tree set here is used as it is (also far from the origin).

member.name: T:gs.MeshEnvelope
member.summary:
Exact containment in an envelope around a triangle mesh, after Wang, Schneider, Hu, Attene and Panozzo, "Exact and Efficient Polyhedral Envelope Containment Check" (ACM TOG 2020). Every triangle t gets a convex prism: the slab |n . (x - t)| <= 0.8 epsilon along its normal, intersected with half-spaces 0.554 epsilon outside t in 14 directions perpendicular to the normal (8 uniform ones and both normals of each edge). The prism lies within t + ball(epsilon) (lateral 0.554 / cos(22.5 deg) = 0.6, and 0.6^2 + 0.8^2 = 1; the rounding of the half-spaces is taken off these offsets), and it contains t.
Contains / ContainsSegment / ContainsTriangle decide exactly (BigInteger arithmetic on the double input, after floating-point filters) whether a point, segment or triangle lies in the union of the prisms. So true guarantees that every point of the query is within epsilon of the mesh, whatever the rounding; false means that some point is outside all prisms (it may still be within epsilon, as the prisms are thinner than the epsilon ball: at least 0.8 epsilon along the normal, 0.554 epsilon sideways).
Triangles are tested by clipping: the query triangle, in its own (u, v) parameters, minus each nearby prism's convex cross-section, until nothing (contained) or a piece of positive area (not contained) remains, or false if more than MaxExactPieces pieces arise (conservative; counted in AbortedQueries). The mesh may be a soup; degenerate and sliver triangles get a prism around their longest edge (or point). The envelope is a snapshot: later changes to the mesh are not seen. Queries may run in parallel.

member.name: T:gs.MeshFidelityMetrics
member.summary:
Surface fidelity of a mesh (eg a repair, remesh, solidify or wrap result) to a reference (eg its input), beyond the Hausdorff distance and the volume IoU of MeshRepairMetrics, which miss lost features, reversed patches and topology changes: - F-score at thresholds tau (Tatarchenko et al., "What Do Single-view 3D Reconstruction Networks Learn?", CVPR 2019): precision = share of the mesh's surface within tau of the reference, recall = share of the reference's surface within tau of the mesh, F = 2 P R / (P + R); - Chamfer distance: the mean distances of both directions; - normal consistency: |cos| of the angle between the normal at a sample and the normal at its closest point on the other surface (mean, and as a mean angle), in both directions; separately the share of samples within the largest tau whose normals point the other way (cos < -0.001): inverted patches; - Edge Chamfer distance (as in Chen et al., "Neural Dual Contouring", SIGGRAPH 2022): Chamfer distance between the sharp edges (dihedral angle above SharpEdgeAngle, not at slivers narrower than SharpEdgeMinHeight) of both meshes, and the edge precision / recall at the thresholds: feature preservation; - the same against the outer surface of the reference only (OuterSurface), so interior faces that a repair to a solid drops on purpose do not count as lost; - volume IoU of the solids (generalized winding number > 0.5, Jacobson et al. 2013), against the whole reference and against the solid of its outer faces only (OuterVolumeIoU): interior faces, nested shells and double-sided sheets distort the winding number solid of an open reference, not the solid a repair encloses (VolumeSamples); - curvature fidelity (Curvature): discrete mean and Gaussian curvature after Meyer et al. 2003 (MeshCurvature) at corresponding points of both surfaces, and the distance of their distributions; - triangle quality (TriangleQualityStatistics, Verdict definitions) and topology (MeshTopologySummary) of both meshes, and the topology changes.
Sampling: SurfaceSamples points per mesh, area weighted and stratified (sample i lies in the slice [i, i + 1) / n of the cumulative area), uniform inside the chosen triangle; EdgeSamples points per mesh on its sharp edges, stratified by length. The closest point on the other mesh comes from its AABB tree (exact point-triangle distance), on the other mesh's sharp edges from a bounding volume tree of the segments (exact point-segment distance). The normal at a closest point is the angle weighted pseudo-normal of the feature (face, edge or vertex) it lies on (Baerentzen and Aanaes 2005). Cost O((n + s) log n) for n triangles and s samples. Sampling noise of a share is about 1 / s.
All distances and thresholds are relative to the size of the reference (Size: the diameter of the smallest sphere around the area centroid of its triangles that holds them; for a box-like shape about the diagonal of its bounding box, but independent of the rotation), so the results do not depend on position, rotation or scale, and scaling both meshes by a power of two gives the same results bit for bit. The meshes are moved (as copies) to the reference's centroid for the queries, so coordinates far from the origin (eg UTM) do not lose precision in the float boxes of the trees. Deterministic: the samples come from Seed in a fixed order, the queries write per sample and the sums run in sample order, so Parallel = false gives the same results bit for bit.
Usage: var f = new MeshFidelityMetrics(input, result); if (f.Compute()) use(f.FScore[0]); The meshes are not modified. Weld triangle soups first: the sharp edges are found by position, but the pseudo-normals at edges and vertices and the topology (each soup triangle is a component) use the mesh's connectivity. Orientation matters for the reversed share only: a correct result of an input with inverted patches shows them as reversed, so orient the reference (eg MeshRepairOrientation) if only the result's orientation is to be judged.

member.name: F:gs.MeshFidelityMetrics.SharpEdgeAngle
member.summary: an edge is sharp if the angle between the normals of its triangles exceeds this (degrees)

member.name: F:gs.MeshFidelityMetrics.SharpEdgeMinHeight
member.summary: edges at triangles whose height (twice the area over the longest edge) is at most this, relative to Size, are not sharp: the normal of such a sliver comes from the rounding of its corners (eg float STL coordinates), not from a feature, and a crease that narrow is far below the thresholds. On Thingi10K inputs every lost "sharp edge" of the repairs that kept the triangles was at a triangle below 1e-5.

member.name: F:gs.MeshFidelityMetrics.OuterSurface
member.summary: also measure against the outer surface of the reference only (OuterRecall, OuterFScore, Outer*): the reference samples where the generalized winding number w of the reference (tested at OuterOffset * Size along the normal, w+ and w-) jumps by one (|w+ - w-| > 0.5: a single layer) and the rest of the reference does not enclose the point (|w+ + w-| / 2 < 0.75: 0.5 on the boundary of a solid, 0 on an open sheet), or one side is outside and the other inside the solid (|w| < 0.25 and > 0.75: coincident duplicate shells, w 0 and 2). Leaves out faces inside the solid (single faces, nested shells: mean 1 or more), internal double walls and double-sided sheets (jump 0), which a repair to a solid drops on purpose; keeps cavity walls, duplicated outer shells and open sheets. Orient inside-out components of the reference first (eg WindingContouring.OrientedCopy).

member.name: F:gs.MeshFidelityMetrics.OuterOffset
member.summary: offset of the two winding number tests of OuterSurface, relative to Size: both faces of a wall thinner than this, and faces across a gap narrower than this, are not outer

member.name: F:gs.MeshFidelityMetrics.VolumeSamples
member.summary: random points for the volume IoUs (VolumeIoU, OuterVolumeIoU; sampled as MeshRepairMetrics.VolumeIoU does, near the components of both meshes); 0 skips them (NaN). Sampling noise of the IoU about sqrt((1 - IoU) / n).

member.name: F:gs.MeshFidelityMetrics.Curvature
member.summary: compare the curvatures (MeshCurvature) of both meshes: at each surface sample within the largest threshold of the other surface, the mean curvature H and the Gaussian curvature K interpolated linearly from the Valid vertices of its triangle, against the same at its closest point on the other mesh (CurvatureMeshToReference, CurvatureReferenceToMesh); the 1-Wasserstein distance of the area weighted distributions of H and K of both meshes (MeanCurvatureDistance, GaussianCurvatureDistance); the total absolute curvatures. H is relative to 1 / Size (H * Size: 2 on a sphere), K to 1 / Size^2. Boundary, bowtie and area-less vertices are not Valid and left out of the interpolation; a sample whose triangle has no Valid vertex is left out. At sharp edges and corners the vertex values grow with the resolution (the curvature is concentrated there) while the area they spread over shrinks, so the means (area integrals) stay comparable, but two meshes with the same crease at different resolutions differ there. H is signed by the orientation, as the reversed share.

member.name: F:gs.MeshFidelityMetrics.OuterVolumeIoU
member.summary: output (VolumeSamples and OuterSurface): the same against the solid of the (oriented) reference's outer faces only: a face is outer unless none of its centroid and its three points (4 a + b + c) / 6 (and permutations) is on the outer surface by the rule of OuterSurface. Interior faces raise or lower each other's winding numbers (of two layers stacked inside a solid the lower one looks like a boundary while the upper one is there, and with many layers a face of the solid itself looks interior), so the faces are removed in rounds, each judging the faces left by the winding number of the faces left and removing only the clearest interior ones: double layers (no jump of the winding number at any test point) and faces that are not outer with a mean winding number (the lowest of their test points) of at least 0.75 and within 0.25 of the largest such mean. Removed faces stay removed; the rounds end when one removes nothing (OuterFacesConverged; at most MaxOuterFaceRounds, OuterFaceRounds). Faces that are not outer with a mean below 0.75 (eg lowered by interior faces in front of them) are not removed in that round. So faces inside the solid, nested shells, internal double walls and double-sided sheets are left out, faces crossing another surface (partly outer) and degenerate ones kept. Not told apart: a face of the boundary next to a one-sided interior sheet facing away from it (both have the winding numbers of an interior face, eg 0.5 and 1.5, and go in the same round); the winding number solid of the rest closes that gap, so the IoU changes little, OuterFaceShare more. NaN if no face is outer (eg every face a double layer: walls thinner than OuterOffset), if the faces enclose no volume, or if the rounds did not converge (OuterFacesConverged). Cost: a winding number tree and up to 8 winding numbers per face per round, O(R n log n) for R rounds; R is small for most inputs and about 1.5 per layer for a stack of interior faces (Objaverse: 3 or fewer for half the objects, more than 16 for one in nine)

member.name: M:gs.MeshFidelityMetrics.SharpEdges(g3.DMesh3,System.Double,System.Double,System.Collections.Generic.List{g3.Vector3d})
member.summary: The sharp edges of the mesh, as endpoint pairs (a0, b0, a1, b1, ...). Edges are identified by the positions of their endpoints, so triangle soups (unwelded STL) give the same edges as welded meshes. An edge is sharp if the angle between the normals of its two triangles exceeds angleDeg, with the normals oriented consistently across the edge (an orientation flip at the edge is not a crease), or if more than two triangles share it (non-manifold). Boundary edges and edges at triangles of height at most minHeight (twice the area over the longest edge; no reliable normal) are not sharp; non-manifold edges are always sharp. In the order of first appearance (triangle order). normals (if given) gets the unit sum of the oriented normals of the first two faces of each sharp edge (zero if one is degenerate). At an edge where two solids only touch (non-manifold, the first two faces from one solid) that direction points into the other solid, and the edge is not outer.

member.name: T:gs.MeshGeodesicDistance
member.summary:
Geodesic distances along a triangle mesh with the heat method (Crane, Weischedel and Wardetzky, "Geodesics in Heat", 2013): heat diffused from the sources for a short time t gives the direction to them; its normalized gradient field is integrated by a Poisson equation into the distance. Much closer to the true surface distance than Dijkstra along mesh edges (which zigzags), and the matrices are reused for further sources.
Accuracy (tests on planes, discs, cylinders and terrain): about 2% of the distance plus half the mean edge length; near the sources the distance is smoothed over a few edge lengths. Near open boundaries, and for sources on the boundary, allow 2% plus one mean edge length: the boundary condition of the heat flow (the average of the Neumann and Dirichlet solutions, Crane et al.) is only an approximation there. Regular grids whose diagonals all point the same way are anisotropic and the least accurate; alternating diagonals or irregular triangulations do better. Computed relative to the mesh center, so UTM coordinates are fine (edge lengths are differences of nearby points). Each connected component is measured from its own sources; components without a source (and isolated vertices) get NaN. Far from the sources (beyond about 700 edge lengths) the heat underflows doubles; then it is computed as its logarithm. Computed on the intrinsic Delaunay triangulation of the mesh (IntrinsicDelaunay, IntrinsicTriangulation; Sharp, Soliman and Crane 2019): caps, needles and obtuse triangles, eg along constrained feature lines after remeshing, would otherwise give negative cotan weights and wrong distances. Degenerate triangles are kept by intrinsic mollification (Sharp and Crane 2020). Bowtie vertices are split into one vertex per fan for the triangulation, and joined again in the linear systems (paths through them remain).
Solvers: sparse Cholesky factorizations (SparseCholesky) of the heat flow and the Poisson problem, reused for further sources. The heat system is an M-matrix (cotan weights clamped to at least 0), so its solution is accurate entry by entry; where it underflows it is solved in the log domain (SparseCholesky.SolveLog). Several thousand edge lengths from the sources cost no more than near ones.
Usage: var geo = new MeshGeodesicDistance(mesh); if (geo.Compute(new[] { sourceVid })) d = geo.Distance[vid]; The mesh is not modified. The first Compute() builds the Laplacian (cost grows with the vertex count); later calls with other sources reuse it until the mesh changes (ShapeTimestamp). Distances are in mesh units, 0 at the sources and non-negative elsewhere.

member.name: F:gs.MeshGeodesicDistance.Mesh
member.summary: input mesh (not modified)

member.name: F:gs.MeshGeodesicDistance.TimeFactor
member.summary: diffusion time = TimeFactor * (mean edge length)^2; must be positive and finite (else Compute returns false)

member.name: F:gs.MeshGeodesicDistance.MaxIterations
member.summary: no longer used: the linear systems are solved directly (kept for API compatibility)

member.name: F:gs.MeshGeodesicDistance.IntrinsicDelaunay
member.summary: compute on the intrinsic Delaunay triangulation of the mesh (same surface, edges flipped by length): robust against caps and needles, eg from remeshing with constrained feature lines.

member.name: F:gs.MeshGeodesicDistance.IntrinsicRefine
member.summary: also refine the intrinsic Delaunay triangulation by vertex insertion (IntrinsicTriangulation.DelaunayRefine, with RefineMinAngle and RefineMaxInsertions): boundary edges opposite obtuse angles are split, so all cotan weights are non-negative, and triangles get angles of at least RefineMinAngle degrees (0: only the boundary edges). More vertices (slower), more accurate on poor meshes. The distances are still reported at the mesh vertices. Needs manifold vertices; otherwise Refinement.Status is NonManifoldInput and the flips alone are used.

member.name: F:gs.MeshGeodesicDistance.SplitObtuseBoundaryEdges
member.summary: without IntrinsicRefine: still split the boundary edges opposite obtuse angles (DelaunayRefine with a minimum angle of 0), the only edges whose cotan weights the flips leave negative. Few inserted vertices and no cost per Compute; on a plane of 169 degree triangles the maximum error drops from 0.81 to 0.23 edge lengths (benchmarks/IntrinsicBenchmark). Needs IntrinsicDelaunay.

member.name: T:gs.MeshGeodesicPath
member.summary:
Geodesic paths and loops on a triangle mesh by edge flips (FlipOut: Sharp and Crane, "You Can Find Geodesic Paths in Triangle Meshes by Just Flipping Edges", ACM TOG 2020). The path starts as a path along mesh edges (Dijkstra between the waypoints, or one given), on an IntrinsicTriangulation of the mesh. As long as the path turns at a free vertex by less than pi on one side, the edges inside that wedge are flipped until the outer boundary of the wedge is convex, and the path is rerouted along it, which shortens it. The result is a geodesic in the exact (intrinsic) geometry of the mesh: straight across triangles and edges, through a vertex only where the angle is at least pi on both sides (saddles, boundary corners), in the same homotopy class as the initial path. The mesh is not modified.
Compute(a, b) gives a geodesic between two vertices that is locally shortest; from the Dijkstra path it is usually, but not always, the globally shortest one. ComputeThrough connects waypoints (kept fixed), optionally closed. Shorten tightens a given path along mesh edges; with closed = true and no fixed vertex it gives a closed geodesic (or Collapsed for a contractible loop).
Vertices must be manifold (see IntrinsicTriangulation); boundaries are allowed, a path does not leave the surface. Lengths are intrinsic edge lengths (with IntrinsicTriangulation's mollification, 0 for meshes without degenerate triangles).

member.name: F:gs.MeshGeodesicPath.AngleTolerance

member.name: T:gs.MeshHausdorffDistance
member.summary:
Certified (Pompeiu-)Hausdorff distance between two triangle meshes (or soups): computes an interval [LowerBound, UpperBound] that contains the exact distance, with UpperBound - LowerBound below the tolerance. Sampling vertices or edge points only gives a lower bound, which can be far too small when the farthest point lies inside a triangle (eg over a hole or dip of the other mesh).
Branch and bound after Sacht and Jacobson, "Cascading upper bounds for triangle soup Pompeiu-Hausdorff distance" (SGP 2024): - lower bound: distances of points of A (vertices, then subdivision points) to B; - upper bound per triangle of A, the smallest of * for any triangle t of B, max over the corners of d(corner, t) (the distance to one triangle is convex, so its maximum over a triangle is at a corner). Tried for the nearest triangles of the corners, it is exact when all corners project to the same triangle; * d(corner) + longest edge at that corner (triangle inequality); * max d(corner) + covering radius (every point is that close to some corner); - the triangle with the largest upper bound is split into 4 until the largest upper bound is within the tolerance of the lower bound; triangles whose upper bound is below the lower bound are dropped. The symmetric distance is the max of both directions; the second direction is pruned against the first one's lower bound.
Usage: var hd = new MeshHausdorffDistance(meshA, meshB); if (hd.Compute()) use(hd.UpperBound); The meshes are not modified. Distances are in mesh units; the meshes must be in the same coordinate space. The value is 0 for identical meshes and, for two concentric spheres of radii r1 < r2, about r2 - r1.

member.name: T:gs.MeshInsertProjectedPolygon
member.summary:
Inserts a polygon into a mesh using a planar projection. You provide a projection frame and either the polygon in the frame's XY-coordinate system, or a DCurve3 space curve that will be projected.
Currently you must also provide a seed triangle, that intersects the curve. We flood-fill from the vertices of that triangle to find the interior vertices, and hence the set of faces that are modified.
The insertion operation splits the existing mesh edges, so the inserted polygon will have more segments than the input polygon, in general. If you set SimplifyInsertion = true, then we collapse these extra edges, so you (should) get back an edge loop with the same number of vertices. However, on a non-planar mesh this means the edges will no longer lie on the input surface.
If RemovePolygonInterior = true, the faces inside the polygon are deleted
returns: ModifiedRegion: this is the RegionOperator created to subset the mesh for editing. You can use this to access the modified mesh
InsertedPolygonVerts: the output vertex ID for Polygon[i]. This *does not* include the intermediate vertices, it's a 1-1 correspondence.
InsertedLoop: inserted edge loop on output mesh
InteriorTriangles: the triangles inside the polygon, null if RemovePolygonInterior=true
If you would like to change the behavior after the insertion is computed, you can subclass and override BackPropagate().
[TODO] currently we construct a planar BVTree (but 3D) to map the new vertices to 3D via barycentric interpolation. However we could do this inline. MeshInsertUVPolyCurve needs to fully support working on separate coordinate set (it tries via Get/Set PointF, but it is not 100% working), and it needs to let client know about poke and split events, w/ bary-coords, so that we can compute the new 3D positions.

member.name: T:gs.MeshPostRepairCleanup
member.summary:
Cleanup pass to run after MeshAutoRepair (see MeshAutoRepair.PostRepairCleanup). Fixes defects that AutoRepair leaves behind or introduces: - duplicate (two-sided) triangle pairs - degenerate triangles (collapse needles, flip caps) - folded edges (flip, only if it reduces the local fold count) - bowtie vertices - inside-out closed components that are not cavities of another component Self-intersections are not handled, and holes are not filled (it does not close a mesh).
Works on any mesh, in place (topology changes, no new mesh is created). Apply() returns no status; the statistics fields tell what was changed. Deterministic.

member.name: M:gs.MeshPostRepairCleanup.FindInvertedComponents(g3.DMesh3)
member.summary: Closed components whose orientation contradicts their nesting: an outer shell (inside an even number of other components) must have positive volume, a cavity (odd) negative volume. So inverted solids, and the cavities of a hollow solid that was inverted as a whole, are found. An inside-out component found so is not returned if an odd number of nearly closed open components (|winding number| above 0.75 inside it) enclose it: the cavity of an open shell. Open components can only take back a result, never add one. Returns their triangle sets (empty if there are none or no closed components). Does not modify the mesh. A component whose surface meets (intersects or touches, exactly) that of a component the majority of its interior samples lie in is not nested in it: crossing components have no nesting, and keep their orientation (they are never returned). Cost: the nesting is tested only for components whose box lies inside another one's (found by a sweep, so many components side by side are cheap), with a winding number tree per enclosing component; the surfaces only for a component that would be returned, against the components its samples lie in (so a correctly oriented mesh pays nothing for them).

member.name: M:gs.MeshPostRepairCleanup.interior_samples(g3.DMesh3,System.Int32[],System.Boolean,System.Double)
member.summary: Up to 9 points just inside the closed component tris: centroids of well-shaped triangles (the largest inradius among evenly spread candidates), moved against the outward normal by min(maxOffset, inradius / 2). The caller limits maxOffset by 1e-4 * diag and by a quarter of |volume| / area (about t / 8 for a slab of thickness t), so that a point does not leave a thin component through its opposite side, and all lengths are relative to the component, so the points do not depend on the unit. inverted: the component has negative volume, its normals point inwards. If no candidate is a proper triangle, the plain centroids are returned.

member.name: T:gs.MeshRepairMetrics
member.summary: Metrics for judging a repaired (or remeshed, solidified, boolean) mesh against its input, where no reference result exists (eg Thingi10K): - SelfIntersections: exact count of intersecting triangle pairs, including pairs that share a vertex or an edge and intersect beyond it (folds lying flat on each other); - VolumeIoU: agreement of inside/outside with the input, where "inside" of the input is its generalized winding number > 0.5 (Jacobson et al. 2013; also defined for soups and open meshes); - certified Hausdorff distances: see MeshHausdorffDistance. All functions are read-only (the meshes are not modified) and deterministic.

member.name: M:gs.MeshRepairMetrics.SelfIntersections(g3.DMesh3)
member.summary: Number of triangle pairs that intersect, exactly (ExactTriangleIntersection). Pairs that share a vertex count if they intersect anywhere else; pairs that share an edge count if they overlap (coplanar on the same side). Degenerate (zero area) triangles are skipped. Builds an AABB tree and runs in parallel; 0 for a mesh without self-intersections.

member.summary: SelfIntersections(mesh), but stops counting once more than limit pairs are found (then returns a value > limit, not the full count): cheap test whether a mesh has more self-intersections than a limit

member.summary: interior edges whose two triangles run through them in the same direction (the orientation is not consistent there; 0 for a consistently oriented mesh)

member.name: M:gs.MeshRepairMetrics.FoldedEdges(g3.DMesh3,System.Double)
member.summary: interior edges whose triangles fold over by more than maxAngle degrees (non-degenerate triangles)

member.name: M:gs.MeshRepairMetrics.VolumeIoU(g3.DMesh3,g3.DMesh3,System.Double@,System.Double@,System.Int32,System.Int32)
member.summary: Intersection over union of the solids of input and result, from samples (deterministic): a point is inside the input where the generalized winding number of its oriented copy (WindingContouring.OrientedCopy: inside-out parts flipped, as the solidify fallback does) is > 0.5, inside the result likewise. 1 = same solid. Also returns the parts of the input solid missing in the result (eg lost thin walls) and the result solid not in the input (eg filled cavities), relative to the input solid. NaN if the input encloses no volume (eg a single open sheet), 0 if the input has no triangles, and 0 (missing and extra NaN) if the input's solid is too small to be hit by the samples at all (then the result's solid is far larger). Estimated from samples random points (fixed seed, so repeatable) in the bounds of the triangles of both meshes, or, for meshes with up to MaxSampledComponents components, only near the components (where the winding number can reach 0.5), so components far apart are sampled as densely as a single one; small differences are sampling noise.

member.name: M:gs.MeshRepairMetrics.VolumeIoUAtLeast(g3.DMesh3,g3.DMesh3,System.Double,System.Double@,System.Int32,System.Int32,System.Double)
member.summary: Is VolumeIoU(input, result) at least minIoU? Samples are classified in rounds (samples / 32, then doubling), and after each round the share of the union that is in only one of the solids gets a confidence interval (Wilson score, z standard deviations); the answer is given as soon as the interval lies on one side of 1 - minIoU and the input's solid has been found. An early answer differs from the one with all samples only by chance, about the probability of a z-sigma deviation (z = 4: about 3e-5, times the number of rounds; with cells, two intervals share it). If the oriented input and the result are both winding-closed (ExactMeshBoolean.IsWindingClosed), the samples are drawn only from the cells of an octree that the surfaces touch (VolumeSampleCells); the cells no triangle touches lie inside or outside each solid entirely and count with their exact volume. This estimates the same IoU with less variance and fewer samples (docs/design/VOLUME_CHECK_SAMPLING.md). Otherwise (open meshes) the samples are those of VolumeIoU: with all of them (results close to minIoU) the answer and iou are those of VolumeIoU. iou is the estimate from the samples used; NaN (and true) if the input encloses no volume, as VolumeIoU (no solid to compare with); 0 (and false) if its solid is too small to be hit by the samples. Typically 10-30x cheaper than VolumeIoU for results that clearly agree with the input.

member.name: M:gs.MeshRepairMetrics.normalizing_scale(g3.DMesh3,g3.DMesh3)
member.summary: The power of two that brings the extent of the triangles of a and b into [2^-300, 2^300] when it lies outside, otherwise 1. The volume checks compute volumes (the cube of the extent overflows above about 5e102 and underflows below about 1e-103) and far points at a few times the extent. Outside that range their IoU was NaN, which passed as "no solid" (a result that lost most of a solid of size 1e160 was accepted), and near 1e308 the far points were infinite and the exact predicates threw. Scaling by a power of two is exact (the same inside decisions, the same IoU as at the scaled size; the checks give the same IoU for 2^k scales), except for coordinates that become subnormal (below about 2^-1322 times the extent). 1 if a bound is not finite (a NaN coordinate may not show in the bounds; it stays NaN), or if scaling up would make the coordinates not finite (a tiny extent far from the origin).

member.name: M:gs.MeshRepairMetrics.unit_scale(g3.AxisAlignedBox3d,System.Int32,System.Int32)
member.summary: The power of two (a normal double) that brings the largest extent of box (or, if that is not finite, its largest coordinate) to about 1 (into [1, 4), or below 1 for an extent below 2^-1022) when the extent lies outside [2^lowExp, 2^highExp], otherwise 1 (also for an empty box or one with a coordinate that is not finite). Exact scaling (see normalizing_scale). The scaled coordinates themselves can overflow (a tiny extent far from the origin): scale differences of coordinates, not coordinates

member.name: M:gs.MeshRepairMetrics.unit_scale_for_mesh(g3.DMesh3)
member.summary: The power of two that brings the extent of the triangles of mesh into [1, 4) when it lies outside [2^-100, 2^100] (where the squares of lengths and the products of areas overflow or underflow, and an absolute threshold like 1e-12 * diagonal^2 is infinite or 0), else 1. Also 1 if scaling the coordinates would overflow or leave the normal range (a tiny extent far from the origin, subnormal coordinates): then the caller works on the mesh as it is. A 2^k scale of the vertices is exact, so an operation run on the scaled mesh and scaled back (ScaleVertices) gives the unit-scale result, times 2^k, bit for bit.

member.name: M:gs.MeshRepairMetrics.ScaleVertices(g3.DMesh3,System.Double)
member.summary: the vertices of mesh times s (a power of two from unit_scale_for_mesh: exact)

If both meshes are winding-closed, the samples are drawn only from the cells near the surfaces (VolumeSampleCells), and the cells known to be inside a solid count with their exact volume; otherwise from sample_region. useCells = false: always sample_region (for benchmarks, an A/B in one build, and tests).

member.summary: As above, against a reference solid given by its inside test (eg the exact boolean of the inputs' winding numbers), sampled in box (expanded by 1%). NaN if no sample is inside the reference. referenceInside is called in parallel and must be thread-safe.

member.name: F:gs.MeshRepairMetrics.MinComponentDiagonal
member.summary: Closed connected components of the input whose solid the result lost (the volume IoU does not notice a part below 1 - IoU of the volume, eg a screw of an assembly or a small separate shell). For each component, points are sampled in its box (up to 1024, 256 if none of them lies in the solid) until 32 lie in the input's solid (winding number of its oriented copy > 0.5, as VolumeIoU); the component is lost if fewer than minCoverage of them lie in the result's solid. Open components (sheets, soup triangles: near them the input's solid is that of the parts around, which gave false alarms on Thingi10K) and components with fewer than 8 such points (walls thinner than about 1/100 of their box) are not judged, nor components whose box diagonal is below MinComponentDiagonal of the input's (specks that the repair removes on purpose, eg below MeshAutoRepair.MinEdgeLengthTol, and that a fallback would lose as well). At most maxComponents components, the largest boxes first (beyond that the smallest are not judged). "In the input's solid" is the solid of the whole input, so a box that holds other parts as well is judged by them too (a lost part can then count as kept). Deterministic (seed).
LostComponents does not judge components whose box diagonal is below this fraction of the input's

member.name: F:gs.MeshRepairMetrics.MaxSampledComponents
