member.name: T:gs.MeshRepairOrientation
member.summary:
Repairs triangle orientation in place. OrientComponents() makes the orientation consistent within each edge-connected component (patches of consistent triangles flipped along a spanning tree, see there; KeepShortSeams = false: flood fill from an arbitrary triangle, reversing neighbours that disagree, as geometry3Sharp 1.0.324); SolveGlobalOrientation() then reverses whole components that face inwards, judged by ray casts from far outside (the side of the triangles that is visible from outside should be the front).
Call OrientComponents() first: SolveGlobalOrientation() works on the components it found. Non-orientable components (eg Moebius strips) keep a seam of inconsistent orientation. The global step is a heuristic for open or nested surfaces; for closed meshes MeshPostRepairCleanup.FindInvertedComponents (signed volume and nesting) is an alternative. Used by MeshAutoRepair.

member.name: F:gs.MeshRepairOrientation.Mesh
member.summary: the mesh whose triangles are reoriented in place

member.name: F:gs.MeshRepairOrientation.KeepShortSeams
member.summary: OrientComponents keeps consistently oriented patches together and leaves a short seam in non-orientable components (default). false: the depth-first propagation of geometry3Sharp 1.0.324.

member.name: F:gs.MeshRepairOrientation.DegenerateAreaFactor
M:gs.MeshRepairOrientation.#ctor(g3.DMesh3,g3.DMeshAABBTree3)
member.summary: spatial is an optional prebuilt AABB tree of mesh3 (built on demand otherwise)

member.name: M:gs.MeshRepairOrientation.OrientComponents
member.summary: Make the orientation consistent within each connected component (triangles connected by edges). Patches of triangles that are already consistently oriented with each other are kept together and flipped as a whole: along a maximum spanning tree of the patch adjacency (weight = number of shared edges), each patch is oriented against its parent, starting from the largest patch, which keeps its orientation. An orientable component ends up consistent. A non-orientable one (or one whose patches cannot be 2-coloured) keeps the inconsistent edges between patches off the tree, which are few, where a depth-first propagation from a single triangle could leave a long seam anywhere in it. Whether that is the outward orientation is decided by SolveGlobalOrientation. With KeepShortSeams = false, the depth-first propagation of geometry3Sharp 1.0.324 is used instead.

member.name: M:gs.MeshRepairOrientation.smooth_seams
member.summary: A triangle with two or three inconsistent edges is flipped (fewer inconsistent edges), until there is none: straightens jagged seams.

member.name: M:gs.MeshRepairOrientation.ComputeStatistics
member.summary: For each component found by OrientComponents(), sum the area of triangles hit from the front and from the back by rays from far outside (used by SolveGlobalOrientation).

member.name: M:gs.MeshRepairOrientation.SolveGlobalOrientation
member.summary: Reverse each component (from OrientComponents) that is hit from outside on its back side more than on its front side (area weighted). Does nothing if OrientComponents() was not called.

member.name: T:gs.MeshRobustRepair
member.summary:
Repair that ends with a clean solid wherever possible: MeshAutoRepair (with the post-repair cleanup) first, which keeps the input triangles; if its result is not clean, its self-intersections are resolved exactly (ExactResolve: ExactMeshBoolean.Resolve, which keeps the geometry); if that is not clean either, the repaired mesh is solidified (winding number, adaptive dual contouring), which gives a closed, manifold surface without self-intersections at the cost of remeshing it (deviation about a cell, see SolidifyResolution). If the solidify fails or its result is not clean either (rare: self-intersections where thin sheets meet in few cells), the mesh is alpha wrapped (MeshAlphaWrap, AlphaWrapFallback), whose result is always closed, manifold and free of self-intersections, but wraps over cavities and gaps narrower than about 2 alpha and lies about Offset outside the input (simplified, SimplifyAlphaWrap: within half an Offset of that).
Clean means: closed, no bowties, no degenerate triangles, consistently oriented, no inside-out components and, if CheckSelfIntersections, no self-intersections (exact, MeshRepairMetrics).
A result can still have lost volume (eg a self-overlapping input made non-overlapping by dropping a layer, or parts removed by erosion): if its solid agrees with the input's winding number solid less than MinVolumeIoU, or it lost a whole component of the input (CheckLostComponents: a part too small for the IoU), the input itself is used instead, resolved exactly, solidified or wrapped (its winding number solid is the reference; UsedInput). The solidify and the wrap themselves are not checked (they change the geometry by about a cell or the offset, and lose parts smaller than that).
Components far apart compared to their size (eg a part 1e8 away from parts of size 1): the degenerate area of NotCleanReason, 1e-12 of the squared diagonal of all triangles, then covers their real triangles, and the cleanups of the exact resolve collapse them. If the exact resolve fails and some component has triangles below that area, it runs once more with the cleanups relative to the diagonal of the largest component; if that resolve is clean but for the area of NotCleanReason, Apply() returns false with the resolved mesh in Mesh and ResultReason ScaleDisparity (the solidify and the wrap, relative to the same diagonal, would lose the parts). A resolve the first attempts accept is unchanged.
Behaviour: the result is in after Apply(), a new mesh object. The mesh passed to the constructor is used as the working mesh of MeshAutoRepair and is modified by it (also its unused vertices are removed, they are no part of the solid), so pass a copy if you need the input afterwards. Check UsedExactResolve / UsedSolidify / UsedAlphaWrap / FallbackReason (and ExactResolveReason, SolidifyReason) to see which path was taken. Cost: the self-intersection check and the volume comparison are cheap compared to the solidify fallback, whose cost grows with SolidifyResolution. With the alpha wrap fallback (and CheckSelfIntersections), a solidify whose contour self-intersects is stopped before its cleanup and reduction (MeshWindingNumberSolidify.StopIfSelfIntersecting) and wrapped right away.
Use MeshAutoRepair alone if the input triangles must be kept (no remeshing), MeshWindingNumberSolidify to always remesh, ExactMeshBoolean.Resolve to resolve self-intersections exactly without remeshing.

member.name: F:gs.MeshRobustRepair.CheckLostComponents
member.summary: also a result that lost a connected component of the input (MeshRepairMetrics.LostComponents: a part too small for the volume IoU, eg a screw of an assembly) is treated like one whose volume differs ("parts of the input lost"). Only with MinVolumeIoU > 0 (0 turns off both). Off by default: on the 430 Thingi10K meshes of benchmarks/MeshRepairBenchmark it found no lost part, but rejected 3 repairs whose nested closed parts were oriented differently from the reference (a part inside another taken for a cavity), and the fallbacks from the open input were worse (one mesh fewer repaired). For inputs with separate small parts (assemblies). The fallbacks after such a rejection (solidify, wrap) are not checked for it: their ResultReason can be "" although they lost the same part, see FallbackReason and UsedInput.

member.name: F:gs.MeshRobustRepair.SimplifyAlphaWrap
member.summary: alpha wrap fallback: simplify the wrap (it has many small triangles, about alpha in size, also on flat regions). Collapses create no self-intersections (Reducer.PreventSelfIntersections, exact, also if CheckSelfIntersections is false); the result is kept only if it is clean and certified within half the wrap offset of the unsimplified wrap (one-sided Hausdorff upper bound), so it stays about half an offset outside the input; otherwise the unsimplified wrap is (AlphaWrapSimplified false).

member.name: F:gs.MeshRobustRepair.AlphaWrapQualityPass
member.summary: alpha wrap fallback: after the simplification, improve the triangle quality (before the simplification's quality guard of Alpha Wrap 2.0, the simplified wrap kept slivers down to about 1.7 degrees): edge flips and tangential vertex moves around triangles with a minimum angle below 30 degrees, each kept only if every changed triangle stays within half the wrap offset of the unsimplified wrap (TriangleDeviationBounds.IsWithin) and, like the simplification, creates no self-intersection (exact). Every changed triangle is certified within the distance when it is made, the others keep the simplification's certificate, so the improved mesh is within half the offset by construction; it is kept only if it is clean, otherwise the simplified one (AlphaWrapQualityImproved false). The default settings (DefaultWrapQuality) also split caps above 160 degrees (at most 5 % more triangles), flip caps above 150 degrees, and keep the normals as close to the unsimplified wrap's (0.1 degree slack per operation). The smallest angle of the mesh does not drop; the largest is not bounded globally (flips and moves may raise it locally). Off by default (owner decision 2026-11-08, Alpha Wrap 2.0; on by default from #292 until then): since the simplification no longer creates caps (its quality guard), the pass adds little (the 1 %-worst angle about 0.15 degrees, no triangle below 0.5 or above 170 degrees either way) at about 30 % of the pipeline's time (benchmarks/MeshRepairBenchmark README, "Alpha wrap quality pass"). true runs it as before.

member.name: F:gs.MeshRobustRepair.RejectTopologyChange
member.summary: reject an exact resolve result whose genus differs from the mesh it resolved (TopologyChanged): the fallbacks (solidify, alpha wrap) run instead. Off by default: a union can change the genus legitimately (overlapping parts that form a ring), and in Thingi10K 357788 the extra handles are tunnels the exact union of a crumpled, self-overlapping region really has.

member.name: F:gs.MeshRobustRepair.TopologyChanged
member.summary: exact stage: true if the genus of its result (GenusAfter) differs from the genus of the mesh it resolved (GenusBefore, the repair result or the input) while the number of components stays the same: handles a component gained or lost by resolving its own self-intersections (eg tunnels between self-overlapping layers, Thingi10K 357788). A union of several parts changes the components, and so the genus, by construction (on Thingi10K 76 of 175 exact results): not flagged. Only judged when the resolved mesh is closed and has no bowtie vertices (genus defined); otherwise false and both genera NaN. Reported, not a defect: the result is clean. Valid together with UsedExactResolve: false and NaN when the result is not the exact resolve (a resolve rejected by RejectTopologyChange is reported in ExactResolveReason only).

member.name: M:gs.MeshRobustRepair.OrientedByReference(g3.DMesh3,g3.DMesh3)
member.summary: Compacted copy of mesh with inside-out parts flipped (WindingContouring.OrientedCopy), then each closed component oriented by the solid of reference (where its generalized winding number is > 0.5), sampled just off both sides of its triangles: reversed if the reference has its solid on the outer side and none on the inner (OrientedCopy guesses a cavity or an inverted part from the nesting alone, eg makes a part nested in another one a cavity), and turned outwards if the reference is solid on both sides (an inner shell of a solid, not a cavity).

member.name: M:gs.MeshRobustRepair.CollapseSlivers(g3.DMesh3,System.Double,System.Int32)
member.summary: Collapses the triangles below the degenerate area of NotCleanReason (1e-12 * diagonal^2): for each, its shortest edge that is shorter than maxCollapse * diagonal and whose collapse keeps the mesh valid (link condition), the vertices moved to the midpoint; otherwise an edge flipped, the longest first (caps). Closed components with a sliver and a total area below 1e-8 * diagonal^2 are removed (also a small but real separate part, about 1e-4 * diagonal across). Unlike MeshPostRepairCleanup it does not avoid distorting or folding the neighbours: they are tiny (the slivers come from intersection points that nearly coincide), so the caller has to check for (and resolve) self-intersections afterwards. Returns the triangles collapsed, flipped or removed.

member.summary: Vertices at the same position (eg from splitting a non-manifold vertex or edge into manifold sheets) make their sheets touch there. Each is moved by fraction of the way towards the centroid of its neighbours, so the sheets separate. Returns the number of vertices moved.

member.name: M:gs.MeshRobustRepair.NotCleanReason(g3.DMesh3,System.Boolean)
member.summary: "" if the mesh is clean (see class comment), otherwise the first problem found, one of "empty", "not closed", "bowties", "degenerate triangles" (area < 1e-12 * diagonal^2, of the bounds of the triangles), "inconsistent orientation" (an interior edge whose two triangles run the same way), "inside-out components", "self-intersections". Useful as a test assertion: NotCleanReason(mesh) == "". Stops at the first problem, which can hide the others (eg degenerate triangles hide self-intersections): NotCleanReasons / FindDefects report all of them.

member.name: T:gs.MeshRobustRepair.Defects
member.summary: the checks of NotCleanReason, as flags (FindDefects)

member.name: M:gs.MeshRobustRepair.FindDefects(g3.DMesh3,System.Boolean)
member.summary: every failed check of NotCleanReason (None if the mesh is clean). An empty mesh is Empty only. Every other check runs whatever the earlier ones found: inside-out components are searched among the closed components, self-intersections ignore exactly degenerate triangles. A defect can follow from another one (the volume of a component with inconsistent orientation, and so inside-out, is not meaningful). Costs as much as NotCleanReason on a clean mesh; on an unclean one all checks run (with checkSelfIntersections also the expensive one).

member.name: M:gs.MeshRobustRepair.DescribeDefects(gs.MeshRobustRepair.Defects)
member.summary: the reasons of NotCleanReason for the defects, in its order, separated by ", " ("" for None; bits that are no Defects value are ignored): the first one is what NotCleanReason returns

member.name: M:gs.MeshRobustRepair.NotCleanReasons(g3.DMesh3,System.Boolean)
member.summary: all reasons why the mesh is not clean, eg "degenerate triangles, inside-out components" ("" if it is clean): DescribeDefects(FindDefects(mesh, checkSelfIntersections)). Starts with NotCleanReason(mesh, checkSelfIntersections). For a report: to decide on a single reason, compare NotCleanReason (or test the flags of FindDefects), not this string, which names more than one reason when there are several defects.

member.name: T:gs.MeshTopologySummary
member.summary: Topology of a mesh per connected component (triangles connected across edges): vertices V, edges E and triangles F used by the component, Euler characteristic chi = V - E + F, boundary loops b and genus g = (2 - chi - b) / 2 (chi = 2 - 2g - b for an orientable surface with boundary). The genus is an integer for orientable manifold components; bowtie vertices are counted once (as in the mesh), so a component with bowties can get a genus that is not an integer or not its genus when split there (BowtieVertices says when). Boundary loops are the connected parts of the boundary edges (two loops through one bowtie vertex count as one). Purely combinatorial: invariant under any transform.

member.name: T:gs.MeshWallThickness
member.summary: Wall thickness per vertex and per triangle of a closed, consistently oriented (outward normals) mesh. Three measures, all evaluated at the vertices (with the area weighted vertex normal) and at the triangle centroids (with the face normal): - Ray: length of the ray along the inward normal to the opposite wall. Exact for parallel walls (slabs, concentric shells), but sensitive to noise and to a single unlucky ray. - ShapeDiameter: shape diameter function after Shapira, Shamir and Cohen-Or, "Consistent mesh partitioning and skeletonisation using the shape diameter function" (The Visual Computer 2008): RayCount rays in a cone of ConeAngle (default 120 degrees) around the inward normal, rays whose length is more than one standard deviation from the median are dropped, the rest averaged with weights 1/(angle to the cone axis). Robust, but larger than the wall thickness (oblique rays are longer); it measures the local "diameter" of the part. - InscribedSphere: diameter of the largest ball that touches the surface at the point and lies inside the solid, ie twice the distance to the medial axis along the normal. Computed by the shrinking ball iteration of Ma, Bai, Hu and Kim, "3D medial axis point approximation using nearest neighbors and the normal field" (The Visual Computer 2012), on the exact surface: start with the ball whose diameter is the inward ray, then while a surface point q lies inside the ball, replace the ball by the one tangent at p through q (radius |q-p|^2 / (2 (p-q).n)). Only contacts seen from the ball center at least SeparationAngle away from p count (the angle condition of Dey and Zhao, "Approximate medial axis as a Voronoi subcomplex", CAD 2004): the flat facets of a tessellated curved surface fold into any ball tangent to one of them, but only close to p, while an opposite wall or a crease is seen at a large angle. Independent of the vertex density (large triangles are fine). Creases that fold by less than SeparationAngle count as smooth. The thickness in the sense of a gauge ("does a ball of diameter t fit"), never larger than Ray. A ball tangent at a polyhedral vertex is not defined at creases (it cuts both faces), so vertex values are the area weighted mean of the values of the vertex's triangles. The rays use the watertight ray-triangle test of Woop, Benthin and Wald, "Watertight ray/triangle intersection" (JCGT 2013): a ray through a shared edge or vertex hits at least one of the triangles, so no ray slips through the surface. A ray that leaves the solid through a front face (normal facing the ray) hit an inconsistently oriented or open part; it is ignored. Points without any valid ray get NaN, and so do degenerate triangles (area below 1e-12 times the squared bounding box diagonal), which also do not count as walls. Closed components that are inside out for their nesting, and a mesh that is inside out as a whole, are taken with flipped normals (OrientInvertedParts; the mesh is not changed).

member.summary: optional spatial data structure. member.name: M:gs.MeshWallThickness.InvertedTriangles(g3.DMesh3)
member.summary: Triangles of mesh to reverse so that it is outward oriented: those of closed components that are inside out for their nesting (MeshPostRepairCleanup.FindInvertedComponents); then, only if the mesh has no boundary edges at all, all of them if the signed volume is still negative (a fallback for when FindInvertedComponents does not decide, eg more than 500 components). For an open mesh the sign of the volume says nothing about its orientation (an open terrain with one tall peak has a negative one), so open parts are never flipped. The mesh and its IDs are not changed. Null if none.

member.name: T:gs.MeshWindingNumberBoolean
member.summary:
Volumetric boolean of two meshes: the winding numbers of the inputs are combined into one field (union = max, intersection = min, difference = min(wA, 1 - wB)) and its 0.5 iso-surface is extracted with dual contouring on an adaptive octree (see MeshWindingNumberSolidify).
Works for any input - open meshes, triangle soups, self-intersecting or overlapping shells - and always gives a closed result. Hermite data comes from exact intersections of the grid edges with the input meshes, so faces and the sharp edges where the inputs intersect are reproduced; coplanar faces need no special handling.
The result is a new mesh (the input triangulation and attributes are not kept), and features smaller than CellSize (thin walls, narrow gaps) are lost. For exact booleans that keep the input geometry, use ExactMeshBoolean (mesh arrangement) instead. The inputs are not modified.

member.name: T:gs.MeshWindingNumberSolidify
member.summary:
Rebuilds a (possibly broken) mesh as a closed solid: samples the fast mesh winding number of the input on a grid and extracts the WindingIso surface, which is closed, has no self-intersections and no interior parts. Holes in the input are spanned by the iso-surface.
Methods: - DualContouring: edge crossings are projected onto the input mesh and its triangle normals are used as Hermite data, so flat faces and sharp edges of the input are reproduced. Far fewer triangles than marching cubes. Can produce a few non-manifold spots, which the cleanup pass and the result checks handle. - MarchingCubes: robust, but rounds sharp edges and produces many triangles.
Features smaller than CellSize are lost in both cases.
Behaviour: the input mesh is not modified (an oriented copy is used, with inside-out parts flipped so inverted inputs still give their solid). Compute() writes a new mesh to Result; the input triangulation and attributes are not kept. Cost grows with the resolution: a full grid for Adaptive = false, about the surface area in cells for Adaptive = true (much cheaper at fine resolutions).
Use this to rebuild any input (soups, open, self-intersecting) as a solid; prefer MeshAutoRepair to keep the input triangles, MeshRobustRepair to try that first and solidify only if needed, and ExactMeshBoolean.Resolve for an exact (not remeshed) resolution of self-intersections of closed meshes.

member.name: T:gs.MinimalHoleFill
member.summary:
Construct a "minimal" fill surface for the hole. This surface is often quasi-developable, reconstructs sharp edges, etc. There are various options.
Method: a fan fill (SimpleHoleFiller), remeshed and then collapsed back to a triangulation of the boundary vertices (normally no new vertices remain), followed by edge-flip passes that make it flatter, minimize the Gaussian curvature at the boundary vertices (OptimizeDevelopability) and improve triangle quality (OptimizeTriangles). Good for mechanical / CAD holes; use SmoothedHoleFill for a smooth, evenly tessellated patch, PlanarHoleFiller for (possibly nested) planar holes.
The mesh is modified in place. Apply() returns false only if the initial fan fill fails (eg the fill would create non-manifold edges); no triangles are added then. Its parameters are scale independent.

member.name: M:gs.MinimalHoleFill.flip_existing_base_edges
member.summary: An interior edge of the fill between two loop vertices that are already joined by an edge of the mesh outside the fill (eg the hole a-b-c-d of a tetrahedron without two faces, whose diagonal a-c is an edge of the other two) cannot be inserted: BackPropropagate splits it at its midpoint, and the fill then touches that existing edge there (a self-intersection; pmp-library issue 181). Flip such edges between two loop vertices (the only ones the split looks at) to the other diagonal of their quad where that one is new and the flip turns no triangle normal around (a concave quad would fold); the others are left to the split.

member.name: T:gs.PartitionedReducer
member.summary:
on a fixed spatial partition, the parts in parallel (Reducer / Remesher 2.0, T3): the same quadric edge collapses, but the cost of an expensive guard such as (4 to 5 times the plain reduction on smooth meshes) is shared by the cores. On smooth meshes of 60 to 100k triangles with that guard it takes 1.3 to 2.4 times the plain serial time instead of 4.0 to 5.1 times (4 cores, ReduceToMaxQuadricError at 0.3 % of the box diagonal, docs/design/REDUCER_REMESHER_20.md section 9; a closed box with large flat faces 9.7 instead of 55 times). Opt-in: the plain reduction without such a guard is cheap enough to stay serial.
How it works (the argument, and the tests that pin each part, are in PartitionedReduction): the bounding box is cut into slabs along its longest axis, at quantiles of the vertex coordinates, separated by a gap of one mean edge length. A triangle with all corners in one slab belongs to that slab's part, every other triangle is frozen. Each part is reduced in its own copy, together with the frozen triangles that its slab could touch, which stay as they are, and a collapse may not move a vertex out of the slab, so the parts cannot interfere with each other and the guards of each copy (also the exact self-intersection check) see every triangle that a new triangle could meet. Two rounds (the second with the cuts shifted by half a slab) are followed by one serial pass on the whole mesh. The vertex quadrics and the fold-over references are those of the whole mesh at the start.
Contract: - Deterministic: the result depends on the mesh, the settings and , never on , the number of cores or the timing: is a constant. The same input gives the same mesh, bit for bit, in every run, and for every similarity that scales by a power of two. - It is not the result of one serial run (the collapses happen in another order; the triangle count is usually within a few percent), so a caller that needs the serial result uses the Reducer. - The target is a maximum quadric error (as ); there is no triangle count target. - The input mesh is not modified; the result is a new compact mesh without vertex normals, colours, UVs, triangle groups and isolated vertices (also when the serial fallback is used). Vertices that no triangle uses do not take part (they are removed from the working copy first, so they do not steer the slabs either). - may set guards and weights (PreventSelfIntersections, AreaWeightedQuadrics, the quality and fold-over settings, EdgeFlipTolerance). It must not set MaxDeviation (the deviation reference of each part would be its own mesh, so the bound would add up over the rounds) or external constraints: both are refused with an before any work (Configure is called once on a scratch reducer to check). Projection targets and deviation references cannot be detected and must not be set either (they would be applied to meshes with other vertex ids). Use the Reducer for these. - is called for the reducer of every part and of the last pass (and once more on the whole mesh to compute the quadrics), from the calling thread and from the threads of the parts, so it must be thread-safe and give the same settings every time. Every reducer runs with PreserveBoundaryShape = false (set after ): the boundary of an open mesh is not kept in shape (the plain Reducer keeps it by default); a caller that needs that uses the Reducer. - is called from several threads at the same time (and between the rounds). When it returns true, the mesh reduced so far is returned (a valid mesh, not the full reduction). It is also given to every reducer as Progress, replacing one set by . - An exception thrown while reducing on the partition path (in a part, or by Configure) surfaces as an for every (the serial fallback throws the original). - Falls back to one serial Reducer run (same settings) when the mesh has fewer than triangles (the partition does not pay below about 20k; default 20000), and when the slabs cannot be kept apart (the gap is lost in the rounding of the coordinates). tells. - The instance keeps no state between calls except the outputs; it is not thread-safe. Sources: Garland and Heckbert 1997 (quadrics); the partition with frozen borders is the approach of out-of-core simplification (P. Lindstrom, SIGGRAPH 2000; Ozaki, Kyota, Kanai 2015), here with fixed slabs for determinism (docs/SOURCES.md).

member.name: T:gs.PartitionedReduction
member.summary:
The alpha wrap simplification's Reducer on a fixed spatial partition, the regions in parallel (Alpha Wrap 2.0, option A), then once more serially on the whole mesh.
The bounding box is cut into Slabs slabs along its longest axis, at the quantiles of the vertex coordinates (about the same work per slab), each shrunk by half a gap on both sides, so the shrunk slabs B_i are disjoint. A triangle with all three corners in B_i belongs to region i; every other triangle is frozen. Each region is reduced in its own copy: its triangles plus the frozen triangles whose (closed) box meets B_i, whose edges and corners are fully constrained. A collapse of two free vertices is allowed only if the new position lies in B_i (a collapse onto a pinned vertex keeps that vertex, which lies in B_i). So every triangle of region i stays inside B_i, those of other regions inside their disjoint slabs, and the frozen ones do not change: the exact self-intersection check of each copy sees every triangle that a new triangle could meet. Rounds parallel rounds are run, every second one with the cuts shifted by half a slab (its slabs cover the gaps of the round before), then a serial pass on the whole mesh. The vertex quadrics and the fold-over references (Reducer.PreventFoldOver) are those of the whole mesh at the start, carried through every round: a pinned vertex in region i's slab takes what region i's collapses added to it.
Deterministic: the partition depends only on the mesh and Slabs, never on the number of cores or threads (Slabs is a fixed setting); each region is reduced on its own (no shared state, no reduction across threads); the results are put together in region order. So the result is the same for every MaxThreads (1 is the serial reference) and every run. It is not the result of one serial Reducer run: the collapses happen in another order, and every round evaluates the edges again that a guard refused before (T1, 100 meshes: 3 % fewer triangles at the median).
Differences to one Reducer run, for a caller that has used that: CancelF is called from the regions' threads at the same time (it must be thread-safe); an exception in a region surfaces as AggregateException; the regions run with PreserveBoundaryShape = false (an open mesh loses boundary vertices; the wrap is closed); the result has no vertex normals, colours, UVs or triangle groups. If the slabs cannot be kept apart (the gap is lost in the rounding of the coordinates, or GapEdgeLengths is 0), the partition is not used: one serial Reducer run (SerialFallbacks).

member.name: T:gs.PolyhedralEnvelope
member.summary:
Exact containment in the polyhedral envelope of Wang, Schneider, Hu, Attene and Panozzo, "Exact and Efficient Polyhedral Envelope Containment Check" (ACM TOG 2020), docs/design/ENVELOPE.md. Every triangle gets the open convex polyhedron of the paper's Prop. 3.1 (offset delta = epsilon / sqrt 3: floor and ceiling, three side planes, caps at the acute and right vertices; a box around the longest edge or the point for a degenerate triangle). Each facet is an oriented plane through three double points.
The rounding of those points is taken off the offsets with a proven bound (ENVELOPE.md section 4.4): every point of every polyhedron is within epsilon of its triangle. That the triangle is strictly inside its polyhedron is checked exactly at build. Queries decide exactly whether a point or a segment lies in the union of the polyhedra (Thm. 3.2: the endpoints are inside, and every point where the segment crosses a facet plane of a polyhedron lies in another one), with ExactPredicates.Orient3d and IndirectPredicates.Orient3dLPI. The boundary counts as outside. True guarantees that every point of the query is within epsilon of the mesh.
The polyhedra are a snapshot of the mesh (Mesh is the given instance; later changes to it are not seen); queries may run in parallel. One triangle that cannot get a polyhedron (TooThin, OutOfRange) makes the status of the whole envelope that, as in MeshEnvelope: a partial envelope would answer false for its region.

member.summary: the polyhedron of one triangle (ENVELOPE.md 4.4); internal for the tests, which check its bounds a posteriori

member.summary: Sizing fields for Remesher.TargetEdgeLengthF.

member.name: M:gs.RemeshSizing.FromWallThickness(g3.DMesh3,System.Double,System.Double)
member.summary: Target edge length from the local wall thickness of input (MeshWallThickness, InscribedSphere: the diameter of the largest ball inside the solid at the point): fraction (finite, > 0, else ArgumentOutOfRangeException) times the thickness, but at least minEdgeLength (default: 1e-3 of the bounding box diagonal, so a sliver of zero thickness does not refine without bound). The thickness of a vertex of input is the smallest of its triangles' (a rim between two walls gets the thinner one), and the field at a point is interpolated over the input triangle nearest to it, from its vertices: continuous, so a point on an edge or vertex of input gets the same value whichever of its triangles is the nearest. Vertices without any thickness (NaN: open parts, degenerate triangles) are left out of the interpolation; NaN if none has one, which Remesher reads as the global target. Remesher caps the field by its global lengths and splits an edge above 1.33 times the target, so with fraction 1 the edges near walls thinner than the global target end at about the wall thickness (0.66..1.33 times it; the walls are not folded through each other), and elsewhere as before. Thread-safe (read-only queries). Input is copied (the remesher may change the mesh it got). Relative values only: scale invariant. Null if the thickness cannot be computed (empty mesh).

member.name: T:gs.RemoveOccludedTriangles
member.summary:
Remove "occluded" triangles, ie triangles on the "inside" of the mesh. This is a fuzzy definition, current implementation is basically computing something akin to ambient occlusion, and if face is fully occluded, then we classify it as inside and remove it.
Each triangle (centroid) or vertex (PerVertex) is tested at a point nudged out along its normal by NormalOffset, with the test chosen by InsideMode. member.name: T:gs.TerrainDualContouring
member.summary:
2.5D dual contouring of terrain (height fields such as open-pit mines, dumps, DTMs). Rebuilds the top surface of a (possibly broken) input mesh as a clean height-field mesh with sharp break lines and few triangles:
- the input is sampled with vertical rays on a grid in XY (SamplesPerCell^2 rays per cell), which sees only the top surface, so triangle soups, duplicated, overlapping or inconsistently oriented triangles do not matter; - each cell gets one vertex at the minimum of a QEF of the sampled planes (as in dual contouring), so vertices sit on break lines (crest and toe of each bench) instead of rounding them off; - cells are merged in a quadtree while the QEF error stays below Tolerance (2:1 balanced), so flat berms and uniform slopes become a few large triangles; - the mesh is the dual of the quadtree: one triangle or quad around each cell corner; each quad is split along the diagonal that matches the input better; - the outer boundary (and the rims of holes) is kept: cells on the input boundary get a vertex on the boundary line (2D QEF of the boundary edges, so its corners are kept exactly).
Overhangs and vertical walls cannot be represented by a height field; the top surface is used. All computations are relative to the grid origin, so large (eg UTM) coordinates are fine.

member.name: F:gs.TerrainDualContouring.Points
member.summary: Alternatively a point cloud (eg LiDAR ground points, see ClothSimulationFilter): the height and normal at a sample are fitted to the points within PointRadius (weighted least squares plane). The outer boundary is then where the points end (no boundary edges to follow).

member.name: T:gs.TerrainGreedyTIN
member.summary:
TIN with as few vertices as needed for a guaranteed maximum vertical error at every node of a height grid (eg a DGM / DTM raster): greedy insertion after Garland and Heckbert, "Fast Polygonal Approximation of Terrains and Height Fields" (1995). Starting from the two triangles of the grid's rectangle, the grid node farthest (vertically) from the current TIN is inserted, until no node is farther than MaxError. The triangulation is Delaunay in XY, so the result is a height field (no overlaps in XY) by construction. RemoveVertices removes vertices again where the guarantee allows.
Node (i, j) lies at (X0 + i CellSize, Y0 + j CellSize), height Z[i + NX j]; the TIN uses the integer node coordinates, so the orientation tests are exact. No-data nodes (NaN) are not supported.

member.name: F:gs.TerrainGreedyTIN.MaxError
member.summary: largest vertical distance of any grid node from the TIN

member.name: F:gs.TerrainGreedyTIN.MaxVertices
member.summary: stop earlier at this many vertices (the error is then larger, see AchievedError)

member.name: F:gs.TerrainGreedyTIN.RemoveVertices
member.summary: after the insertion, vertices whose removal (the hole retriangulated, best fitting ears first) keeps every grid node within MaxError are removed again (repeated passes); the guarantee holds. The greedy insertion places many vertices that later ones make unnecessary: on open-pit benches 94% fewer triangles, on smooth terrain about 20%. The result is no longer Delaunay (the ears follow the data, eg along break lines); still a height field. (Data-dependent flips during the insertion, Garland and Heckbert's variant, gave 10-200% more triangles in tests.)

member.summary: RemoveVertices: the number of vertices removed

member.name: F:gs.TerrainGreedyTIN.AchievedError

member.name: T:gs.TerrainOffset
member.summary:
Offset surface of a terrain (TIN / height field) at a perpendicular distance: Distance > 0 above, < 0 below the terrain (eg a safety layer or minimum cover below the surface). The offset is the boundary of the band of points within |Distance| of the terrain on that side: concave break lines stay sharp, convex ones become the round arcs of the true offset.
On each vertical line, starting |Distance| above/below the terrain (where the distance is at most |Distance|), the first point farther than |Distance| is found by stepping and bisection; the direction from its closest terrain point is the exact normal of the offset. The surface is built with TerrainDualContouring, so the normals are Hermite data and it has few triangles.
The result covers exactly the XY footprint of the terrain (its boundary lines are kept, see TerrainDualContouring.FootprintMesh). Beyond the terrain's border there is nothing, so a positive offset does not continue around the border (the round part of the true offset is not produced).

member.summary: cell size of the result (0 = larger XY extent / GridResolution)

member.name: F:gs.TerrainOffset.Tolerance
member.summary: RMS merge tolerance of the quadtree (0 = 0.05 * cell size), see TerrainDualContouring

member.name: T:gs.TerrainBreakLines
member.summary: Break lines of a terrain mesh: edges where the surface bends by more than MinAngle, split into crests (convex, eg the top edge of a bench face, Boeschungsoberkante) and toes (concave, the foot of a face, Boeschungsunterkante), chained into polylines. Best effort: where a break line does not run along mesh edges (on TerrainDualContouring output where it only clips a cell), its bend is spread over several edges, so the lines are about a cell off and can have gaps (open pit test, 1 m cells: 85% of the crest length found). For safety lines use complete, surveyed break lines.

member.name: F:gs.TerrainBreakLines.MinAngle
member.summary: minimum bend angle between the two triangles of an edge (degrees)

member.name: F:gs.TerrainBreakLines.MinLineLength
member.summary: polylines shorter than this are dropped (small kinks along the other kind of break line, eg a slightly convex edge on a toe); 0 = 3 x the mean edge length

member.name: F:gs.TerrainBreakLines.GapClosingDistance
member.summary: end points of open polylines closer than this are joined (the break line runs through a triangle there, eg where it only clips a cell of TerrainDualContouring); 0 = 3 x the mean edge length. Joined parts are straight segments, so the position lists may contain points between vertices; CrestVertices / ToeVertices are not joined.

member.name: T:gs.TerrainSafetyLines
member.summary:
Safety lines at a distance from source lines, eg crests (surveyed break lines or TerrainBreakLines), on the terrain; lines on both sides of the sources are returned. Polylines are open: repeat the first point to close a ring. Sources outside the terrain give no lines there.
- Horizontal (default): the distance measured horizontally, as safety distances from a crest usually are. The edges near the sources are split (the surface stays the same, coarse survey TINs are fine) and the line points found by bisection on them, so they lie exactly at the distance; between them, around convex corners and line ends, the chords of the arcs lie at most Tolerance inside it. - AlongSurface: the geodesic distance along the terrain (heat method), on the band within 3 x SafetyDistance of the sources, cut out and remeshed to EdgeLength (default SafetyDistance / 8) with its boundary and break lines kept; RemeshedTerrain and Geodesic.Distance give the distance field there. The heat method overestimates the distance next to break lines (by up to about 0.27 x EdgeLength in tests with 75 degree faces), which would put the line too close to the crest: the line is drawn at SafetyDistance + SafetyMargin (default 0.35 x EdgeLength). Not guaranteed: on real crests (open pit, 1 m DGM) the heat method still overestimates by up to 1-2 m in places, which puts the line that much too close. - Guaranteed: the straight 3D distance to the sources, which is never more than the distance along the terrain: the line lies on the safe side for certain (computed like Horizontal, at SafetyDistance + Tolerance, so the chords between the line points stay outside SafetyDistance). It is conservative where the path along the terrain bends over another break line or the straight line crosses a gap. How much is certified: shortest paths along the refined terrain (Dijkstra over its vertices and SteinerPoints points per edge, straight through each triangle) are upper bounds of the distance along the terrain; Excess gives, per line point, the upper bound minus SafetyDistance, ie at most how far beyond SafetyDistance the point lies. The whole segments are bounded (samples every ExcessTolerance / 8, the distance is 1-Lipschitz); while not certified, the bound is computed again with twice the points per edge (up to MaxSteinerPoints). Certified if the lines lie at least SafetyDistance (MinLineDistance, exact) and at most ExcessTolerance (default 0.2 m) beyond it; RequireCertified makes Compute fail otherwise. On the open pit test data: median excess 5-18 cm, 3% (5 m) to 44% (20 m) of the points above 20 cm. An empty certificate: with sources off the terrain, or a distance beyond the terrain, Compute returns true, also with RequireCertified, with Certified true, no lines and MinLineDistance double.MaxValue. It means that no line exists and nothing was certified: check Lines.
NoData and outliers: an edge near the sources (within the reach of the mode) with an end at NoDataValue, or steeper than MaxTerrainSlope, makes Compute fail with Status NoDataVertex or OutlierVertex and the vertices in OutlierVertices; the refinement does not start. A single vertex at z = -9999 (a nodata value) next to a source refined until memory ran out (1.8 million triangles for a spike of 1000 m on a 1 m grid, 34 times that at 10 km); remove or fix such vertices, or raise MaxTerrainSlope for real walls.
Limits: Compute fails (Status TooLarge) above MaxCertifySteps, MaxSourcePoints and MaxRefinedTriangles. The last one is an estimate: the horizontal area of the band times the ratio of 3D to horizontal area of the terrain triangles near the sources, and it is no bound. On a 1 m grid the real count was 4.8 times of it on flat terrain, 4.6 times on a plane of slope 1 and 9.3 times at slope 20 (before the 3D ratio: 6.6 and 187 times; the splits at midpoints refine edges to the next power of two). Spikes make needles and far more (95 times for 1000 m): there the outlier check is the guard. It also does not know where the sources leave the terrain, and counts sources on top of each other twice. The limits do not cover slivers narrower than an edge. An exception (eg out of memory, or SteinerPoints too large for an array) leaves Certified false, but Lines, RefinedTerrain, MinLineDistance and UsedSteinerPoints may stay as they were at that point.

member.name: M:gs.Slope.IsNotSteeper(g3.Vector3d,g3.Vector3d,g3.Vector3d,gs.SlopeSpec)
member.summary: exact: the slope of triangle (a, b, c), sqrt(nx^2 + ny^2) / |nz| with n = (b - a) x (c - a), is at most the spec: exactly against the spec as entered for Ratio and Percent, against the double S for Rise and Degrees. The orientation does not matter. False for a triangle that is degenerate in XY (nz = 0), for an invalid spec and for coordinates that are not finite.

member.name: M:gs.Slope.IsSupportedBy(g3.Vector3d,g3.Vector3d,g3.Vector3d,g3.Vector3d,g3.Vector3d,gs.SlopeSpec)
member.summary: exact: IsNotSteeper, and the plane of (a, b, c) lies on or below both toe points p0 and p1 (the end points of the toe piece the triangle is attributed to). Together they prove that the triangle lies below every slope cone z(q) + s |x - q| of the toe segment from p0 to p1 (5.4 (i) and (ii)): the plane L of the triangle has L(q) <= z(q) on the whole segment (both are linear along it), so L(x) <= L(q) + s |x - q|. p0 = p1 for a single toe point (a cone apex).

member.name: T:gs.SlopeComposite
member.summary: The composite terrain from the overlay (TERRAIN_1B_PLAN.md, scope 5): the slope surface clipped to the region (SlopeRegion) and the terrain minus the region. A triangle wholly inside (outside) is kept as it is; a partial one is triangulated by an exact CDT with the boundary of the region in it as constraints, and its part found by parity from outside its triangle. The nodes on the boundary are overlay identities, so neighbouring triangles split their shared edges at the same nodes: along the catch line both parts share their vertices (z on S̃), along the toe and the lateral limits the terrain has its own vertices (a step), moved off the slope side by ulps where rounding put them on it. In a mixed run (Partner) the cut part and the fill part meet at a toe crossing at one XY with different heights (λ_cut below the toe, λ_fill above): a step there too, along the first catch segment of one of them, which the terrain part beside it does not share.

member.name: M:gs.SlopeComposite.SnapDeviation
member.summary: an upper bound of |z - ideal| on the composite triangles at the catch points that the snap, the merge or the partner snap moved, with ideal = max(S_fill, min(T, S_cut)) of the realized surfaces T (the terrain) and S (each run's slope surface, where it lies; one run in a single run), exactly up to the final rounding up: 0 if no catch point moved. TERRAIN.md 5.5 has the proof: f = z - ideal on a composite triangle t is bounded above by max(z - T, z - S_cut) and below by min(z - T, z - S_fill), both piecewise linear on the cells of t's refinement by the triangles of T and of each S, so the bounds are taken at the cells' vertices: t's corners, the vertices of T and S inside t, and the crossings of edges of two of t, T, S_cut, S_fill, each an exact rational point. A run's S counts at a point only through its triangles whose interiors overlap t's (a triangle that only touches t has no cell in it); on a slope triangle of the run itself S is t's own plane (the region is the slope surface as realized: the base budget bounds that)

member.name: T:gs.TerrainSlopeDesign
member.summary:
Slope surface (Böschung) from toe lines, as the lower envelope of the slope cones with apexes on the toe (cut; the upper envelope of the falling cones for fill): docs/design/TERRAIN.md, phase 1a (docs/design/TERRAIN_1A_PLAN.md). Mode: cone envelope (R1). Without a terrain the surface is built up to HeightLimit (cut) or down to it (fill); it ends at HeightLimit - UsedToeLowering (+ for fill), never beyond HeightLimit (the whole map is lowered by the toe lowering, the cap with it, so its lines stay). With a terrain (phase 1b) the catch lines and the composite follow.
Never steeper than specified: every triangle of SlopeSurface is checked exactly, on its stored doubles, before Compute returns true: it is not steeper than the spec of the toe piece it is attributed to (its group id), and its plane lies on or below both end points of that piece (cut; on or above for fill), so it lies below every slope cone of the piece (Slope.IsSupportedBy; for fill on the triangle and the toe points mirrored by z -> -z). Compute never returns a violating triangle: it fails with SlopeViolation and ProblemTriangles. The guarantee holds for the doubles in memory; an export must write them with round-trip formatting.
Conservative: the surface lies at most Tolerance below the exact cone envelope (cut). The toe vertices of the output lie UsedToeLowering below the specified toe (cut; above for fill): the margin the exact check of the support needs, measured on the output (1e-6 m at UTM in the tests, 3e-10 m near the origin), at most about 1.1 x SlopeMargin x slope x reach.

member.name: F:gs.TerrainSlopeDesign.Terrain
member.summary: optional: the terrain (a TIN, height field). With it the catch lines are computed (TERRAIN.md 5.5), and HeightLimit may be NaN: cut then builds up to the highest terrain near the toe, raised while the slope reaches it, at most to the terrain's highest vertex (fill: down to its lowest). Only the terrain within the box of the slope surface must be a height field (else NotHeightField); outside it the composite copies the terrain as given (but an overlap of a cut terrain triangle, which can reach beyond that box, with one outside it is found by the composite's check: CompositeFailed)

With a Terrain and BuildComposite, the composite is within Tolerance of the clamp of the terrain and the envelope (max(S_fill, min(T, S_cut))) except within m of the steps at the toe, the lateral limits and the cap, whose position shifts by m: m is the largest move of a catch point, below UsedMinFeatureSize in a single run (with Direction Auto, the snap at a toe crossing adds up to max(UsedMinFeatureSize, 1e-4 x the toes' size)); a composite that cannot be certified so fails with SlopeViolation (docs/design/TERRAIN.md 5.5)

member.name: F:gs.TerrainSlopeDesign.LocalFrame
member.summary: Compute in a local frame (docs/design/TERRAIN.md 5.8.1). The toes and the terrain are translated in XY to an origin near the toes, and the design is computed there. The toes are copied; the terrain's positions are translated in place and restored when Compute returns (also if it throws), bit for bit, as every translation is checked exact. The terrain's timestamps do not change, so a spatial index the caller holds on it stays valid afterwards. While Compute runs, though, the caller's Terrain is in the local frame: it must not be read, or shared with another design or other work running concurrently (a concurrent change would also be translated back, and could leave the terrain corrupted). A copy instead cost 10-20 % of the run on a 2-million-triangle terrain (docs/design/TERRAIN.md 5.8.1). Every output (SlopeSurface, Pieces, CatchLines, SlopeRegion, Composite, Replacement, TargetHeightLines) is in that local frame: its XY plus UsedOrigin is the input's frame. The derived sizes (UsedMinFeatureSize, the margins, λ) follow from the local coordinates, not from the magnitude of the input's (MinFeatureSize is about 1.5 cm at UTM with the default SlopeMargin, and some micrometres in a local frame of a few hundred metres), so features that the input's frame cannot resolve can be designed. The outputs are not translated back: fl(local + UsedOrigin) rounds each coordinate by up to half an ulp of the input's magnitude, more than the local margins, so the exact guarantees (never steeper, support, no overlaps) hold for the local outputs only. Translating them back is the caller's choice, without that guarantee. With Replacement (CompositeKind.Replacement) the kept triangles are the caller's Terrain, in the input's frame: translate one or the other. If an input coordinate cannot be translated to the origin exactly, the design is computed in the input's frame (LocalFrameFallback, UsedOrigin (0, 0)). That is common near the origin, where the input's frame is local already; at UTM it takes a coordinate of a much smaller magnitude with fine bits (eg a stray terrain vertex near (0, 0)). While Compute runs, Toes and Terrain are in the local frame (a CancelF callback that reads them sees it). Default false: the input's frame.

member.name: M:gs.SlopeMap.FlipNeedles(g3.DMesh3,System.Double,System.Double)
member.summary: Repair of needles: a triangle thinner than minAltitude has its longest edge flipped if the two new triangles are proper (the old diagonal's ends strictly on both sides of the new one, exact; counter-clockwise when the old ones are, and the exact check of every triangle afterwards catches any other) and the thinner of them is thicker than the thinner of the two old ones; both take the piece (group) of the thicker old triangle. A face of the map narrower than the rounding (two creases that meet at an angle of 1e-12, from nearly coplanar tangent planes of neighbouring apexes) can only be triangulated into needles; across its sides the flips remove them. Vertices do not move; the exact check of every triangle decides afterwards. Each triangle carries a bound of its deviation from the realization (0 for the realized ones): a flip changes the surface most at the crossing X of the two diagonals, by |z_ab(X) - z_cd(X)|, so the new triangles get the larger bound of the old two plus that (and the rounding of its evaluation); a flip whose bound would exceed maxDeviation is not made (the share reserved for it, TerrainSlopeDesign.MergeShare and RepairLambda). The new triangles are checked against the thicker old triangle's piece; reaching less than w into a neighbouring piece, they may be steeper than that piece's spec allows only within the reserved shares. Returns the number of flips.

member.name: M:gs.SlopeMap.BandMerge(g3.DMesh3,System.Double,System.Double,System.Boolean,System.Func{System.Int32,System.Boolean},System.Double@)
member.summary: The targeted merge of the band (TERRAIN.md 5.4, "Repair of the band") on a realization: see the static overload; the heights are the planes' at 'lower' (as Realize).

The targeted merge of the band: an edge with XY length at most maxLength (at most MinFeatureSize, so both its triangles are needles: a triangle's altitude is at most its shortest edge), whose ends are on no barrier and have different plane sets (a near-quadruple point, which CollapseShortEdges may not collapse, or nested sets that it left: it refuses a collapse that shrinks a thin altitude, and it measures in 3D), is collapsed onto one end (more labels first, then x, then y). The kept vertex takes the union of the plane sets and the lowest of those planes at its XY ('height', mirrored for fill). Made only if every other triangle of the removed vertex stays counter-clockwise, the link condition holds, and no original position merged into the removed vertex (its own and those merged into it before) moves by more than maxLength in XY (an upper bound of the distance, rounded up): chains (clusters of triple points) are merged, the cumulative move of every position capped by maxLength. Passes until one merges nothing (each merge removes a vertex, so finitely many); in a pass shortest edges first, then by id. Only where a triangle of the edge fails ('fails', the exact checks on the current mesh; null: all qualify), so a needle that passes is left as it is, and not at the mesh's boundary (the cap's level line: a collapse there would move it). Decisions in XY and by those checks, so they depend on the realization through the checks only. Returns the number of merges; 'merged' is an upper bound of the largest move of an original position (0 if none).

member.name: T:gs.TerrainVolumeDifference
member.summary:
Exact cut and fill volumes between two terrain surfaces (TINs / height fields), eg the surveys before and after excavation or a design surface against the current terrain.
The triangles of both surfaces are overlaid in XY: each overlap of a triangle of Before with a triangle of After is a convex polygon on which both surfaces are linear, so the height difference is linear too. The polygon is split at the zero line of the difference and both parts are integrated exactly (area times the difference at the centroid). Only the common footprint counts.
Inputs must be height fields (each XY point covered by at most one triangle per surface); triangle soups and mixed orientation are fine. Triangles overlapping in XY (eg two survey files merged with an overlap, or folds) would be counted twice: they are found with exact orientation predicates, counted in BeforeOverlaps / AfterOverlaps, and Compute fails (RequireHeightField). Computed relative to a local origin, so UTM coordinates do not lose precision.

member.name: T:gs.TriangleQualityStatistics
member.summary: Shape quality of the triangles of a mesh, with the triangle metrics of the Verdict library (Stimpson, Ernst, Knupp, Pebay, Thompson, "The Verdict Geometric Quality Library", Sandia SAND2007-1751; Knupp, "Algebraic mesh quality metrics", SIAM J. Sci. Comput. 2001), implemented from their definitions. For a triangle with edge lengths L0, L1, L2 and area A: - minimum and maximum angle (degrees; equilateral 60); - aspect ratio Lmax (L0 + L1 + L2) / (4 sqrt(3) A) (1 for equilateral, up to infinity); - scaled Jacobian 2 / sqrt(3) * min over the corners of sin(corner angle) (1 for equilateral, 0 for degenerate; unsigned: a surface mesh has no reference normal for Verdict's sign); - condition number (L0^2 + L1^2 + L2^2) / (4 sqrt(3) A) (1 for equilateral, up to infinity). Each metric as a distribution over the triangles, from the bad side (QualityDistribution), and the number of triangles outside Verdict's acceptable ranges (min angle 30-60, max angle 60-90, aspect ratio and condition 1-1.3, scaled Jacobian at least 0.5). Triangles with zero area have aspect ratio and condition infinity, scaled Jacobian 0; with a zero length edge also min angle 0, max angle 180. All metrics are scale invariant (bit for bit under scaling by powers of two). Unweighted: every triangle counts once.

member.name: T:gs.VectorHeatMethod
member.summary:
The Vector Heat Method (Sharp, Soliman and Crane, "The Vector Heat Method", ACM TOG 2019): parallel transport of tangent vectors along shortest geodesics, extension of scalar values to the nearest source, and the logarithmic map (geodesic polar coordinates around a vertex), each by a few prefactored sparse linear solves of short-time heat flow.
Computed on the intrinsic Delaunay triangulation of the mesh (IntrinsicTriangulation; can be turned off with IntrinsicDelaunay = false): its cotan weights are non-negative, so the scalar heat is an M-matrix solve that is accurate however small the heat gets, and poor input triangles (slivers, obtuse angles) do not spoil the result.
Tangent vectors are Vector2d in the tangent space of each vertex, in the signpost coordinates of IntrinsicTriangulation (angle 0 along the vertex' first mesh edge, angles scaled to sum to 2 pi at interior vertices); Triangulation.ToWorld / FromWorld convert to and from 3D vectors. Results are arrays indexed by mesh vertex id, NaN for vertices without a source in their connected component (and for vertices without triangles).
The log map is a robust replacement for MeshLocalParam's discrete exponential map, which accumulates error along Dijkstra paths. Its length is the heat method distance r on the intrinsic triangulation. Its direction: by the Gauss lemma the gradient of r^2 / 2 at a vertex is the log map vector parallel transported along the geodesic, so measured against the transported reference vector of the source (vector heat) it gives the angle at the source. (Diffusing outward vectors from the one-ring of the source instead is biased by the shape of the one-ring, by some 20 degrees on a mesh whose vertices have six neighbours, independently of the resolution.) r^2 is smooth at the source, so the direction is well defined up to the cut locus. Like the heat method distance, it is less accurate within a few edge lengths of boundary corners. At a boundary source whose angle sum exceeds 2 pi (a ruffled boundary) log map angles beyond 2 pi are exact as signposts, but a tangent vector only determines its angle modulo 2 pi, so ToWorld maps them into the first corners.
Heat decays by about a factor 2.6 per edge length; beyond ~600 edge lengths from a source it would underflow, and then the diffusion time is increased automatically (DiffusionTime).

Results are still reported at the mesh vertices.

member.name: T:gs.VolumeSampleCells
member.summary:
The sample region of the volume IoU check (MeshRepairMetrics.VolumeIoUAtLeast) for two winding-closed meshes (ExactMeshBoolean.IsWindingClosed): an adaptive octree over a box (Meagher 1982: inside, outside and boundary cells), refined level by level where a triangle of either mesh touches a cell.
The winding number of a winding-closed mesh is an integer that changes only across its surface (Jacobson et al. 2013), so it is constant on a cell that no triangle touches (decided exactly: TriangleTouchesBox). One exact evaluation at the cell's centre (ExactWinding, a ray with exactly decided crossings) classifies the whole cell: inside both solids, inside one of them, or in neither. Those cells are known exactly and are not sampled (stratified sampling); only the touched cells of the last level are (Sampled, Next). The union of both solids is then covered exactly by the known cells plus the sampled ones (docs/design/VOLUME_CHECK_SAMPLING.md, section 4), and the estimate of the IoU stays unbiased.
Cell-size rule: a level is refined while its 8 children per touched cell fit in the remaining ChildBudget (tests of a child cell), at most MaxDepth levels; the cells are ever smaller near the surfaces, independent of the units (2^k scales give the same cells, scaled). Deterministic: the children are tested in parallel into their own slots and merged in a fixed order.

member.summary: Does the closed triangle (a, b, c) intersect the closed box? Exact (ExactPredicates; no tolerance): the separating axis test with the 13 axes of a triangle and a box (the 3 coordinate axes, the triangle's normal, the 9 cross products of its edges with the coordinate axes), each decided by signs only. Disjoint compact convex sets are strictly separated along one of them. A degenerate triangle (a segment or a point) has zero vectors among these axes, which never separate; the remaining ones are complete for it as well.

member.name: M:gs.WindingContouring.ContourRefined(System.Double@,System.Int32,System.Int32)
member.summary:
ContourAdaptive, refined for hidden gaps and walls (gaps or material thinner than a cell, which the node signs cannot see: the surfaces on both sides cut through each other, or thin walls vanish or break up). Dual contouring needs about two cells across a gap or wall, so the cell size is halved directly as often as the narrowest one needs for that (measured perpendicular to its surfaces), then checked again. Only gaps and walls the levels left can resolve count (at least cellSize / 2^maxLevels wide): narrower ones (eg nearly touching layers of open meshes) are not worth the work. Refinement is done for at least minEdges such edges; fewer are only reported in HiddenGapEdges / HiddenWallEdges. At most maxLevels halvings; cellSize returns the finest size used.
With LocalRefinement, only the cells around the hidden gap / wall edges (RefineMargin more in each direction) are refined, the rest stays at the original cell size (see DualContouring.SetRefinement for the transition between them); the work for the refinement grows with the area of the refined regions only. Otherwise the cell size is halved everywhere, each level costs about 4x.

member.name: T:gs.WindingNumberOctree
member.summary:
Adaptive octree over a mesh that finds the leaf cells the WindingIso surface of the mesh winding number can pass through, evaluating the winding number only at the corners of cells it subdivides. The work grows with the surface area (x4 per level) instead of the volume (x8 per level).
A cell is subdivided if input triangles are near it, or if the winding number crosses WindingIso between its corners (this catches iso-surfaces spanning holes, away from the triangles). SurfaceCells are leaf cells in integer leaf-grid coordinates: cell (i,j,k) spans Origin + LeafCellSize * [i,i+1] x [j,j+1] x [k,k+1]. NodeValue() gives (cached) winding numbers at leaf-grid nodes, for use with DualContouring.CandidateCells / NodeValueF.
For closed, consistently oriented input meshes, most node values are not evaluated but copied from a neighbour node: the winding number of such a mesh is an integer that only changes where the surface is crossed, so if no triangle touches the grid edge to the neighbour, the value is the same. With open borders (holes, cracks) or inconsistent orientation (edges whose two triangles run along them in the same direction act like borders) the winding number varies continuously, so then all values are evaluated. Values that may be copied are computed from the winding numbers rounded to integers, so the result does not depend on the order in which (parallel) evaluations fill the cache.
With several input meshes, node values are CombineF(winding numbers of all meshes), eg max for a union (see MeshWindingNumberBoolean); cells overlapping triangles of any mesh are refined.

member.name: T:gs.MeshWindingNumberGrid
member.summary:
Sample mesh winding number (MWN) on a discrete grid. Can sample full grid, or compute MWN values along a specific iso-contour and then fill in rest of grid by propagating the computed values along x-rows (this is the default, ComputeModes.NarrowBand). Values are winding numbers, not distances: about 1 inside and 0 outside a closed mesh with outward-facing normals, and fractional near holes, so this is useful for open / broken meshes. Extract a surface with at IsoValue = WindingIsoValue (0.5). Usage: var g = new MeshWindingNumberGrid(mesh, new DMeshAABBTree3(mesh, true), cellSize); g.Compute(); The spatial tree must be built. Sample (i,j,k) is located at GridOriginD + (float)CellSize*(i,j,k) (the spacing of the inner MeshSignedDistanceGrid).
TODO: - I think we are over-exploring the grid most of the time. eg along an x-ray that intersects the surface, we only need at most 2 cells, but we are computing at least 3, and possibly 5. - it may be better to use something like bloomenthal polygonizer continuation? where we are keeping track of active edges instead of active cells?

member.name: F:gs.MeshWindingNumberGrid.UseFastWindingNumber
member.summary: Use the fast (dipole-approximation) winding number of Barill et al. 2018 instead of the hierarchical exact one. The exact one is fast for closed subtrees but degrades towards O(N) per query on broken meshes / triangle soups; the fast one stays fast and is accurate to a small fraction near the 0.5 iso-value.
